The official Exam 1 breakdown: 28 questions by topic

Your professor posted how many questions each topic gets, and noted that "the breakdown for both exams is similar." Treat these counts as your study budget. Electric fields and electrical potential together are 15 of the 28 questions, more than half the exam.

Grew the most
Electrical potential: 7 questions, about twice the past papers' 3.4

Expect the Homework 6 style: \(V\) inside and outside charged spheres and cylinders, \(V(r)\) with a chosen zero, \(V\) graphs, \(\Delta V\) across sheets and slabs, and equipotentials. Chapter 7.2–7.5 and the Fall 2018 paper (5 potential questions) are the best preparation.

Biggest block
Electric fields: 8 questions, up from 7.1

Vector sums from point charges and the rod, ring, or arc integral set-up. Every past paper has both. Work the Chapter 5 examples until the components come out without hesitation.

Shrank
Gauss's law 4 (was 6.8) and capacitance 5 (was 7.1)

Probably one layered sphere or cylinder problem plus one sheets-and-slab problem, and one capacitor network plus one dielectric or slab question. Still 9 questions together: do not skip them, just do not over-invest.

Quick points
Flux 2 and work and energy 2

Short conceptual or one-formula questions. Flux: only the enclosed charge matters. Energy: one term per pair, and the work you do is \(q\,\Delta V\).

Split your remaining time by the breakdown

If a topic is already solid (you can do its drill questions cold), move its time to electric potential, the topic that grew the most.

How the exam is built

The syllabus says problems are "standardized from homework sets, sample problems from the text, and examples worked in class." The four past exams in this guide confirm it: every question type on them maps to a lecture example or a homework problem. The recurring question families are:

  1. Vector force / field from a few point charges in a square, triangle, or line (components, then magnitude and angle).
  2. Set-up-the-integral questions for a rod, ring, or arc of charge (pick the right \(dq\), \(r\), and trig factor; evaluate or take a limit).
  3. Gauss's law layer problems: insulating sphere or cylinder inside a conducting shell, with induced surface charges and \(E\) in each region.
  4. Infinite sheets plus a conducting slab: field in each region, induced surface densities, potential difference between two points.
  5. Energy of a charge configuration (work to assemble), potential at a point, work you do to bring one more charge in.
  6. Potential of spheres and cylinders from Gauss's law plus an integral; graphs of \(E(r)\) and \(V(r)\).
  7. Capacitor networks (series/parallel reduction, which elements share charge or voltage, energy in one capacitor).
  8. Inserted conductor or dielectric (what changes when the battery is connected vs. removed; half-filled gaps).
  9. Conceptual one-liners: flux through odd surfaces, field-line reading, equipotential spacing, charging by induction, charge sharing between spheres.

How to use this guide

  • Read a chapter, then immediately try the matching past-exam questions in the Past exams section. Solutions are hidden until you click.
  • Every worked example lists its source (lecture unit, homework number, or exam) so you can go back to the original.
  • The Appendix reproduces the provided equation sheet with notes on which formula for which situation. Learn the sheet's layout now so you are not hunting during the exam.
  • Boxes marked Trap are mistakes that the exam distractors are specifically designed to catch.
  • New to the material? Read the Foundations section first. Throughout the guide, blue boxes labeled Why this is true explain the physical mechanism behind each rule, not just the rule; read them, because the exam's conceptual questions test exactly that reasoning.
  • Interactive parts. Worked examples hide their steps until you click Show step, so attempt each step first. Many examples end with a Your answer box that checks your number (relative tolerance about 3%; scientific notation like 3.35e5 is fine). Green-bordered Explore panels are live models: drag the sliders and watch the numbers and arrows respond.
  • Every letter is defined. Each equation in the chapters is followed by a dashed box, What each letter means, that names every symbol in it and gives its unit. If you meet a symbol anywhere else (exam solutions, the appendix), look it up in Foundations F.6, the full symbol glossary.

Notation used throughout: \(k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\) \(= 8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\), \(\varepsilon_0\) \(= 8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\), \(e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\). Numbers in solutions use \(k = 8.99\times10^9\) unless the source used \(9\times10^9\).

Foundations: The Tools Every Chapter Uses

Vectors and components · the "chop it up, treat each piece as a point, add" method · work, energy, and conservative forces from Physics 2111 · how to read a formula · numbers on the calculator

Chapters 5 through 8 use a small toolkit over and over. If any of the items below feels shaky, spend twenty minutes here first. Everything later assumes these are automatic.

F.1 Vectors: the language of forces and fields

A vector is a quantity with a size and a direction: a force of 3 N pointing northeast, a field of 200 N/C pointing down. A scalar is just a number: 5 kg, 12 volts, −3 joules. Force and electric field are vectors. Energy and potential are scalars. Half the mistakes in this course come from treating one like the other.

Components: the only reliable way to add vectors

Pick axes (usually \(x\) to the right, \(y\) up). Any vector \(\vec A\) with magnitude \(A\) and direction angle \(\theta\) measured from the \(+x\) axis splits into two numbers:

\[ A_x = A\cos\theta, \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta \]
What each letter means
\(\vec A\)
any vector (a force, a field, a displacement); the arrow on top means it has a direction as well as a size
\(A\)
the magnitude (length) of \(\vec A\), always positive, in whatever unit the vector has (N for a force, N/C for a field)
\(A_x,\ A_y\)
the \(x\)-component and \(y\)-component of \(\vec A\): its "shadow" on each axis; these carry signs (negative means pointing in \(-x\) or \(-y\))
\(\theta\)
the direction angle of \(\vec A\), measured counterclockwise from the \(+x\) axis, in degrees or radians
\(\tan^{-1}\)
inverse tangent (arctan): the angle whose tangent is the ratio; your calculator returns \(-90^\circ\) to \(+90^\circ\), so add \(180^\circ\) when \(A_x \lt 0\)

To add vectors, add the \(x\)-parts together and the \(y\)-parts together, separately. To turn the result back into a magnitude and direction:

\[ A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}, \qquad \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{A_y}{A_x}\ \text{(then fix the quadrant by looking at the signs)} \]

Never add magnitudes of vectors that point in different directions. Two 5 N forces can add to anything from 0 N (opposite) to 10 N (same direction).

Why components work, and a shortcut you will use constantly

Components work because motion along \(x\) and motion along \(y\) are independent: a push to the right does nothing to your vertical motion. So the \(x\)-parts of all the forces combine among themselves, and so do the \(y\)-parts.

The shortcut. You rarely need the angle itself. If a force acts along a line from point 1 to point 2, and that line is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with horizontal side \(\Delta x\) and vertical side \(\Delta y\), then \(\cos\theta = \Delta x/r\) and \(\sin\theta = \Delta y/r\) where \(r = \sqrt{\Delta x^2+\Delta y^2}\). The triangle's own sides are the cosine and sine. In Lecture 1's Example 1.3, "\(0.45\ \mathrm{N}\times 2/\sqrt5\)" is exactly this: the force magnitude times (vertical side)/(hypotenuse).

Unit vectors, especially \(\hat r\)

A unit vector has length 1 and only carries direction. \(\hat i\), \(\hat j\), \(\hat k\) point along \(+x\), \(+y\), \(+z\). Writing \(\vec A = A_x\hat i + A_y\hat j\) is just a way of listing components.

The one that matters most here is \(\hat r\): the unit vector pointing from a source charge to the point you care about. If the source is at the origin and the point is at \((x, y)\), then \(\hat r\) \(= (x\hat i + y\hat j)/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Multiplying any magnitude by \(\hat r\) makes a vector of that size pointing away from the source. That is why Coulomb's law and the field of a point charge are written with \(\hat r\): the formula gives the size, \(\hat r\) supplies the direction, and a negative sign on the charge flips it toward the source.

What each letter means
\(\hat i,\ \hat j,\ \hat k\)
unit vectors (length 1, no units) along \(+x\), \(+y\), \(+z\); the hat means "unit vector"
\(\hat r\)
unit vector pointing from the source charge toward the field point; the formula supplies the size, \(\hat r\) supplies the direction
\((x, y)\)
coordinates of the field point relative to the source, in m
\(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\)
the distance from the source to the point (Pythagoras); dividing by it is what makes the vector have length 1
Two products you need to recognize

Dot product (a scalar): \(\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta\), with \(\theta\) the angle between them. It measures "how much of \(\vec A\) lies along \(\vec B\)." It is largest when they are parallel, zero when perpendicular, negative when they oppose. It appears in work (\(W = \vec F\cdot\vec d\)) and flux (\(\Phi = \vec E\cdot\vec A\)).

Cross product (a vector): \(|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta\), perpendicular to both, direction by the right-hand rule. It is zero when the vectors are parallel. It appears in torque on a dipole (\(\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E\)). For this exam you only need its magnitude and the fact that it vanishes at \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\).

What each letter means
\(\vec A\cdot\vec B\)
dot product of two vectors: a single number (scalar), \(AB\cos\theta\)
\(|\vec A\times\vec B|\)
magnitude of the cross product: \(AB\sin\theta\), a vector perpendicular to both
\(A,\ B\)
the magnitudes of the two vectors
\(\theta\)
the angle between the two vectors when their tails are placed together
\(W = \vec F\cdot\vec d\)
work \(W\) (J) done by a constant force \(\vec F\) (N) over a displacement \(\vec d\) (m)
\(\Phi = \vec E\cdot\vec A\)
electric flux \(\Phi\) (N·m²/C) of a uniform field \(\vec E\) through a flat surface whose area vector \(\vec A\) has size equal to the area (m²) and points along the surface normal
\(\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E\)
torque \(\vec\tau\) (N·m) on a dipole of dipole moment \(\vec p\) (C·m) in a field \(\vec E\)

F.2 The method behind every integral in this course

Every formula for a rod, ring, disk, sphere, or cylinder comes from one idea, which Lecture 2 calls "the whole \(dq\) thing":

  1. Chop the object into pieces so small that each piece is effectively a point. A piece of a rod is a tiny segment of length \(dx\); a piece of a surface is a tiny patch of area \(dA\); a piece of a volume is a tiny cube \(dV\).
  2. Find the charge on one piece. Charge density is charge per unit size, so the piece's charge is density times size: \(dq = \lambda\,dx\), or \(\sigma\,dA\), or \(\rho\,dV\). For a uniform object, the density is the total charge divided by the total size (\(\lambda = Q/L\)). The letter \(d\) in front of a quantity means "a tiny amount of it."
  3. Write what one point charge \(dq\) does (its force, its field, or its potential) using the point-charge formula with the distance \(r\) from that piece to the point of interest.
  4. Add up all the pieces. An integral is exactly that: a sum of infinitely many infinitely small contributions. \(\int\) is an elongated S for "sum." The limits of the integral say which pieces are included (the ones that exist), so they run over the charged object and nothing else.
Why the pieces have to be points, and why vectors make it harder

We only have one exact formula for force or field: the one for a point charge. An extended object has no formula of its own until we build one from points. That is the whole reason for the chopping.

When the thing being added is a vector (force, field), each piece's contribution points in a different direction, so you must add components. Usually the geometry has a symmetry axis: for every piece on one side there is a mirror piece on the other, and their sideways components cancel exactly while their along-the-axis components add. So you multiply each piece's contribution by \(\cos\) or \(\sin\) of its angle to keep only the surviving component, and you write that trig factor in terms of the integration variable using the triangle shortcut from F.1. When the thing being added is a scalar (potential, Chapter 7), there are no directions and no trig factors at all, which is why Chapter 7 keeps saying "no sines and cosines."

F.3 Work, energy, and conservative forces (from Physics 2111)

The definitions

Work done by a force on an object as it moves: \(W = \int\vec F\cdot d\vec l\), which for a constant force along a straight path is \(W = Fd\cos\theta\). Positive when the force has a component along the motion, negative when it opposes the motion, zero when perpendicular. Work is a scalar, in joules.

Work-energy theorem: the total work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy: \(W_{\text{net}}\) \(= \Delta K\) \(= \tfrac12mv_f^2 - \tfrac12mv_i^2\). Positive net work speeds things up.

Conservative force: one whose work between two points does not depend on the path taken (gravity, springs, and, as we will see, the Coulomb force). Only for such forces can we define a potential energy \(U\) by \(\Delta U = -W_{\text{by that force}}\). Then energy conservation reads \(\Delta K + \Delta U = W_{\text{other}}\), where "other" means non-conservative forces like your hand or friction.

What each letter means
\(W\)
work done by a force, in joules (J); positive if the force helps the motion, negative if it opposes it
\(\vec F\)
the force doing the work, in newtons (N)
\(d\vec l\)
a tiny step along the path the object follows, in m; the integral adds up \(\vec F\cdot d\vec l\) over every step
\(F,\ d,\ \theta\)
for a constant force on a straight path: the force magnitude, the distance moved, and the angle between force and motion
\(W_{\text{net}}\)
the total work done by all forces together
\(\Delta K\)
change in kinetic energy, in J: \(\tfrac12 mv_f^2 - \tfrac12 mv_i^2\)
\(m\)
mass of the moving object, in kg
\(v_i,\ v_f\)
initial and final speeds, in m/s
\(U\)
potential energy, in J; only defined for conservative forces
\(\Delta U\)
change in potential energy: final minus initial; equals minus the work done by the conservative force
\(W_{\text{other}}\)
work done by non-conservative forces (a hand, friction, a motor), in J
Why \(\Delta U = -W\), with the minus sign, and what it means mechanically

Lift a ball slowly. Gravity pulls down, the ball moves up, so gravity does negative work. The ball's kinetic energy did not change, yet you spent effort. Where did that effort go? Into the ball-Earth system as stored (potential) energy. So negative work by the conservative force means an increase in stored energy: \(\Delta U = -W_{\text{grav}}\). Let the ball fall: gravity does positive work, \(U\) drops, and the same amount shows up as kinetic energy. The minus sign is just the bookkeeping that keeps the total constant.

The electric force works the same way with charge in place of mass. Push a positive charge toward another positive charge: the field's force opposes you, does negative work, and the system stores energy. Release it, and the field's positive work turns that stored energy into speed. Chapter 7 is built entirely on this one idea, and its sign questions all reduce to "which way is the force, and which way is the motion?"

gravitational field \(\vec g\) (9.81 N/kg down)electric field \(\vec E\) (N/C)force per unit "handle"
\(\vec F = m\vec g\)\(\vec F = q\vec E\)negative \(q\) reverses the force
\(U = mgh\)\(U = qV\)\(V\) plays the role of \(gh\), "height"

F.4 How to read a formula so it teaches you something

  • Name every symbol. In \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\): \(E\) is the field magnitude, \(\lambda\) is charge per length on the line, \(\varepsilon_0\) is a constant of nature, \(r\) is the perpendicular distance from the line to the point. If you cannot say what a symbol is, you cannot use the formula.
  • Check the units. \(k\) has units N·m²/C², so \(kq/r^2\) has units N·m²/C² × C / m² = N/C. A result in the wrong units is wrong.
  • Check the limits. Far from any finite object the field must look like \(kQ/r^2\). Inside a hollow shell it must be zero. If your formula disagrees, it is wrong.
  • Check the dependence. Does the answer get bigger or smaller when it should? Doubling the charge should double a force. Halving a distance should quadruple an inverse-square force.
  • Check the sign and direction. Positive charges: field points away. Negative: toward. Like charges: repel. If the sign of the answer surprises you, redo the direction step, not the arithmetic.

On the TI-30, enter \(8.99\times10^{9}\) as 8.99 EE 9 (the EE key, not the multiplication key), and \(1.6\times10^{-19}\) as 1.6 EE (−) 19 using the sign key, not the minus key. Keep three or four significant figures until the final step; exam answer choices are usually separated by factors of 2 or 10 or a sign, so rounding early rarely hurts, but cancellations (like Spring 2015 Q2, where two 0.14 N pieces nearly cancel to 0.007 N) punish early rounding.

Electric Charges, Coulomb's Law, and the Electric Field

On Exam 1: electric fields, 8 of 28 questions, the largest topic.

OpenStax 5.1 Electric charge · 5.2 Conductors, insulators, charging by induction · 5.3 Coulomb's law · 5.4 Electric field · 5.5 Fields of charge distributions · 5.6 Field lines · 5.7 Electric dipoles

5.1–5.2 Charge, conductors, insulators, and how objects get charged

Start with the atom. Every atom has a tiny nucleus of protons (charge \(+e\) each) and neutrons (no charge), surrounded by electrons (charge \(-e\) each). A normal atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so its total charge is zero: it is neutral. "Neutral" never means "no charge inside"; it means the positives and negatives balance. An object becomes charged when that balance is broken, and in ordinary matter the only way to break it is to move electrons: nuclei are locked into the solid, while the outermost electrons of many atoms are loosely held. So a "positively charged" comb is a comb missing some electrons, and a "negatively charged" balloon has extra ones.

In plain words

"Charged" means "unbalanced." A positive object is missing electrons; a negative object has extra electrons. Nothing else ever moves when you rub a balloon or touch a doorknob.

The four facts about charge
  1. Two signs. Like signs repel, opposite signs attract. (Lecture 1: "Why? Why? Why? How?!" is the honest answer to why there are exactly two.)
  2. Quantized. Every charge is an integer multiple of the elementary charge: \(q = Ne\), with \(e = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\). The proton's charge is exactly \(+e\), the electron's exactly \(-e\).
  3. Conserved. Charge is never created or destroyed, only moved. When you rub two objects, one loses electrons and the other gains the same number. (Lecture 1's Fermilab example: a proton and an antiproton, \(+1\) and \(-1\), can annihilate into neutral particles because the total was zero to begin with.)
  4. Charge lives on electrons. In ordinary charging, only electrons move. "Positively charged" means "missing electrons," never "gained protons."
What each letter means
\(q\)
the total charge on the object, in coulombs (C), with its sign
\(N\)
the number of elementary charges: how many electrons were removed (positive object) or added (negative object); a whole number with no unit
\(e\)
the elementary charge, \(1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\): the size of the charge on one electron or one proton. So \(q = Ne\) says "total charge = (how many) × (charge of each)"
Why these facts matter for problem solving

Two signs is what makes the electric force different from gravity: it can attract or repel, and a cluster of charges can add up to zero. That is why a neutral object feels no net Coulomb force from far away, and why "induced" charges (below) can appear without anything being created.

Quantization is why "how many electrons" is a meaningful question and why charges like \(1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\) and its multiples keep appearing. In practice \(e\) is so small that a few nanocoulombs already means tens of billions of electrons, so for calculations charge behaves like a continuous fluid.

Conservation is the tool that fixes induced charges in Chapter 6: if a neutral conducting shell develops \(-Q\) on its inner surface, the \(+Q\) that used to balance it must be somewhere, and the only place left is the outer surface.

Counting electrons
Homework 1, Problem 7 · Homework 1, Problem 8
(a) How many electrons make a charge of \(-6.0\ \mathrm{nC}\)? (b) How many electrons must be removed from a neutral object to leave it with \(+1.1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)? (c) Two small foam balls each carry an excess of \(N = 10^{6}\) protons and are \(2.3\ \mathrm{m}\) apart. What force does each exert on the other?

  1. Write the one equation that links charge to a count

    WhyEvery electron carries the same charge \(e\). The total is (how many) × (charge of each), so the count is the total divided by the charge of one.

    \(\displaystyle q = Ne\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow N\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{|q|}{e}\)
    \(\displaystyle e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\)

    MeansThe absolute value is there because \(N\) is a count, never negative. The sign of \(q\) only tells you whether electrons were added (negative) or removed (positive).

  2. (a) Convert nanocoulombs to coulombs

    Why"n" (nano) means \(\times10^{-9}\).

    \(\displaystyle 6.0\ \mathrm{nC}\) \(\displaystyle = 6.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\)

  3. (a) Divide, numbers first, then powers of ten

    WhyDividing powers of ten subtracts the exponents: \(10^{-9}/10^{-19}\) \(= 10^{-9-(-19)}\) \(= 10^{10}\).

    \(\displaystyle N\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{6.0\times10^{-9}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{6.0}{1.60}\times10^{10}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.75\times10^{10}\)

    MeansAbout 37 billion extra electrons. A charge that sounds tiny in coulombs is an enormous number of electrons.

  4. (b) Same formula, now for electrons removed

    WhyA positive object is missing electrons. The count missing is \(|q|/e\). "μ" (micro) means \(\times10^{-6}\).

    \(\displaystyle N\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{1.1\times10^{-6}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.6875\times10^{13}\) \(\displaystyle = 6.9\times10^{12}\)

  5. (c) First find the charge on each ball

    WhyNow run the formula forwards: \(Q = Ne\). An excess of protons means the ball is positive.

    \(\displaystyle Q = (10^{6})(1.60\times10^{-19})\) \(\displaystyle = 1.60\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{C}\)

  6. (c) Then Coulomb's law

    WhyBoth charges are equal, so \(|q_1||q_2| = Q^2\). The distance is already in meters.

    \(\displaystyle F = \dfrac{kQ^2}{d^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle Q^2 = (1.60\times10^{-13})^2\) \(\displaystyle = 2.56\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle d^2 = (2.3)^2\) \(\displaystyle = 5.29\ \mathrm{m^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle F\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(2.56\times10^{-26})}{5.29}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2.30\times10^{-16}}{5.29}\) \(\displaystyle = 4.35\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{N}\)

    MeansBoth balls are positive, so the force is repulsive. It is absurdly small, because a million protons is still a tiny charge.

(a) N = 3.75×10¹⁰ electrons (b) N = 6.9×10¹² electrons (c) F = 4.35×10⁻¹⁷ N (repulsive)

Conductors vs. insulators

In a conductor (metals, salt water, the human body) some electrons are free to move anywhere in the material. In an insulator (plastic, glass, rubber, dry air) charges stay where they are put. Two consequences you will use constantly:

  • Excess charge on a conductor spreads out and sits on the surface (Lecture 1: "charges always on very edge of conductor"). Chapter 6 proves this with Gauss's law.
  • An insulator can hold charge in its volume (a "uniform volume charge density \(\rho\)"), which is why Gauss's law problems with \(\rho\) always involve insulators, never conductors.
Why conductors and insulators behave differently, and why charge sits on the surface

In a metal, each atom gives up one or two of its outer electrons to a shared "sea" that belongs to the whole crystal. Those electrons are not attached to any particular atom, so a push (an electric field) moves them freely through the material. In an insulator, every electron is tied up in a bond between specific atoms; a field can stretch the bond a little (the atom polarizes) but cannot pull the electron loose. Charge placed on an insulator stays put; charge placed on a metal flows.

Now put extra electrons on a metal ball. They all repel each other, and they are free to move, so they run away from each other as far as they can. "As far as possible" on a ball means the surface, spread out evenly. If any excess charge remained inside, its neighbors would still be pushing it outward, so the arrangement is not finished until the interior holds none. The same logic says the field inside the metal must be zero when everything has settled: a nonzero field would still be pushing electrons around. Chapter 6 turns this argument into a proof with Gauss's law; for now, remember the picture of mutually repelling charges fleeing to the edge.

Why a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall. The wall is an insulator, so its electrons cannot leave their atoms, but the balloon's negative charge pushes each atom's electrons slightly away and pulls each nucleus slightly closer. Every atom becomes a tiny dipole (Section 5.7) with its positive end nearer the balloon. Nearer means stronger, so the attraction of the positive ends slightly beats the repulsion of the negative ends, and the net force is attractive. This is the same mechanism as charging by induction, without the ground wire.

Three ways to charge an object

MethodWhat happensContact?Final sign
Friction (triboelectric)Rubbing transfers electrons from the material higher on the triboelectric series to the one lower. Glass loses electrons (becomes +), rubber and plastic gain them (become −).YesDepends on the pair of materials
ConductionA charged object touches a neutral conductor; charge flows until both are at the same potential (Ch. 7). Identical spheres end up with equal charge.YesSame sign as the charged object
InductionA charged object is brought near a conductor; free electrons shift. Then a ground wire is touched and removed while the object is still near; finally the object is removed.NoOpposite sign to the charged object
Trap · the electroscope question

Spring 2014 Q1 asks which statement about the induction sequence is not true. With a positive rod: negative charge flows in from ground (true), the leaves repel each other afterward because they share the excess negative charge (true), "positive charges will be induced when the rod is moved away" (false: the electroscope is left negative, and nothing is "induced" once the rod is gone). If the rod were negative, every sign would flip: electrons flow out to ground and the object ends positive.

Charge sharing between identical conducting spheres
Fall 2015, Questions 4–5
Two identical isolated conducting spheres 1 and 2 each carry \(Q = 3.8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). A third identical sphere 3, initially neutral, touches sphere 1, then sphere 2, and is then removed. (Q4) What is the final charge on sphere 2? (Q5) With sphere 1 at \(x = 0\) and sphere 2 at \(x = d\), in which region is the field zero?

  1. Know the sharing rule

    WhyWhen two conductors touch, charge flows until they are at the same potential (Chapter 7). Two identical spheres at the same potential must hold the same charge. Charge is conserved, so each ends with half the combined total.

    Identical spheres touching: each gets \(\displaystyle \tfrac12(q_A + q_B)\).

    MeansOnly for identical conductors. Spheres of different sizes share unequally (bigger radius, bigger share).

  2. First contact: sphere 3 touches sphere 1

    WhySphere 3 starts with 0, sphere 1 with \(Q\).

    \(\displaystyle \text{total} = Q + 0\) \(\displaystyle = Q\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \text{each gets } \tfrac{Q}{2}\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac{3.8}{2}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.9\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

  3. Second contact: sphere 3 (now Q/2) touches sphere 2 (still Q)

    WhySphere 2 was never touched before, so it still has its original \(Q\).

    \(\displaystyle \text{total} = \tfrac{Q}{2} + Q\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac{3Q}{2}\)
    \(\displaystyle \text{each gets } \tfrac{3Q}{4}\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac34(3.8)\) \(\displaystyle = 2.85\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

  4. Check that no charge was created

    WhyConservation is a free check on the arithmetic.

    \(\displaystyle 1.9 + 2.85 + 2.85\) \(\displaystyle = 7.6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) \(\displaystyle = 2(3.8)\ \mu\mathrm{C}\ \checkmark\)

  5. (Q5) Locate the zero-field point

    WhySphere 1 (\(1.9\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)) and sphere 2 (\(2.85\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)) are both positive. Between two like charges their fields point in opposite directions, so they can cancel there; outside the pair they point the same way and never cancel.

    Zero field: between them, \(\displaystyle 0 \lt x \lt d\), closer to sphere 1 (the smaller charge).
Q4: 2.85 μC Q5: 0 < x < d

5.3 Coulomb's law and superposition

Coulomb's law (magnitude and direction)
\[ F = \frac{k\,|q_1|\,|q_2|}{r^2}, \qquad k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{\frac{N\,m^2}{C^2}} \]
What each letter means
\(F\)
the magnitude (size) of the force each charge exerts on the other, in newtons (N); the same for both charges
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(q_1,\ q_2\)
the two charges, in coulombs (C); the absolute-value bars mean "use the sizes, drop the signs" when computing the magnitude, then decide the direction from the signs
\(r\)
the center-to-center distance between the two charges, in meters (m); it is squared, so halving \(r\) makes the force four times larger
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

The force is along the line joining the charges. Like signs push apart, opposite signs pull together. Newton's third law holds: the force on \(q_1\) from \(q_2\) is exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on \(q_2\) from \(q_1\), regardless of which charge is bigger.

Vector form with the course's "by-on" notation (\(\vec F_{1,2}\) is the force by 1 on 2, and \(\hat r_{12}\) is the unit vector pointing from 1 to 2):

\[ \vec F_{1,2} = \frac{k\,q_1 q_2}{r_{12}^2}\,\hat r_{12} \]
What each letter means
\(\vec F_{1,2}\)
the force vector by charge 1 on charge 2 (read the subscripts as "by, on"), in N
\(q_1 q_2\)
the product of the two charges with their signs: positive for like charges (result points along \(\hat r_{12}\), repulsion), negative for opposite charges (result points against \(\hat r_{12}\), attraction)
\(r_{12}\)
the distance between charge 1 and charge 2, in m
\(\hat r_{12}\)
unit vector (length 1) pointing from charge 1 toward charge 2; it carries the direction and nothing else

Keep the signs of \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) in this formula: if \(q_1q_2 \gt 0\) the force on 2 is along \(\hat r_{12}\) (pushed away from 1); if \(q_1q_2 \lt 0\) it is opposite to \(\hat r_{12}\) (pulled toward 1).

Using Coulomb's law, one step at a time
  1. Size. Put the sizes of the charges (no signs) and the distance into \(F = k|q_1||q_2|/r^2\). Charges in coulombs, distance in meters.
  2. Square the distance. \(r^2\), not \(r\). Doubling \(r\) cuts the force to a quarter.
  3. Direction from the signs. Like signs push apart; opposite signs pull together. The arrow lies along the line joining the two charges.
  4. Same size on both. Each charge feels the same size of force, in opposite directions.
Why the force goes as \(1/r^2\), what \(k\) is, and why the two forces are equal

The inverse square. Picture a charge sending its "influence" out equally in all directions. At distance \(r\) that influence is spread over a sphere of area \(4\pi r^2\). Double the distance and the same influence covers four times the area, so its intensity at any one spot is one quarter. Anything that spreads out uniformly in three-dimensional space falls off this way: light from a bulb, sound from a speaker, gravity from a planet. The \(4\pi\) in \(k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\) is literally the \(4\pi\) of that sphere's area, which is why the sheet gives \(\varepsilon_0\) two ways of appearing in this course.

The constant. \(k\) is a measured number that converts "charges and a distance" into newtons in our chosen units; there is no deriving it. Its size, \(9\times10^{9}\), says that a coulomb is an enormous amount of charge: two 1 C charges a meter apart would push with \(9\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N}\), the weight of a million tonnes. Real static charges are nanocoulombs to microcoulombs. \(\varepsilon_0\) ("permittivity of free space") is the same constant in a different costume; the equation sheet uses whichever makes the formula look cleanest.

Equal and opposite. The formula contains \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) symmetrically, so the size of the force is the same no matter which charge you call "the one being pushed." This is Newton's third law, and it holds even when one charge is a million times bigger: the big charge feels exactly the force the small one feels. What differs is the acceleration (\(a = F/m\)), which is why a proton barely moves while an electron flies.

Explore · Coulomb's law
Two charges, two forces

Change the charges and the separation. The two arrows always have the same length: Newton's third law holds no matter how unequal the charges are. Halving r quadruples the force.

Order-of-magnitude feel: two paperclips
Lecture 1, Example 1.1
Remove one electron from every atom of a \(1.0\ \mathrm{g}\) iron paperclip, and put all those electrons on a second paperclip \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) away. The mass of one iron atom is \(9.27\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg}\). How big is the force between the clips?

  1. Count the atoms in the clip

    WhyTotal mass divided by the mass of one atom gives the number of atoms. Convert grams to kilograms first: \(1.0\ \mathrm{g}\) \(= 1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}\).

    \(\displaystyle N\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{1.0\times10^{-3}}{9.27\times10^{-26}}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.08\times10^{22}\ \text{atoms}\)

  2. Turn the count into a charge

    WhyOne electron removed per atom, so \(N\) electrons moved. Each carries \(e\).

    \(\displaystyle q = Ne\) \(\displaystyle = (1.08\times10^{22})(1.60\times10^{-19})\) \(\displaystyle = 1.73\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{C}\)

    MeansOne clip is \(+q\), the other \(-q\): they attract.

  3. Coulomb's law

    WhySizes of the charges, distance squared.

    \(\displaystyle q^2 = (1.73\times10^{3})^2\) \(\displaystyle = 2.98\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle F\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(2.98\times10^{6})}{(10)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.7\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{N}\)

  4. Compare with something familiar

    WhyDivide by \(g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\) to find the mass whose weight equals this force.

    \(\displaystyle m = \dfrac{F}{g}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2.7\times10^{14}}{9.8}\) \(\displaystyle = 3\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{kg}\)

    MeansThe weight of a mountain. A coulomb is an enormous charge, which is why real static charges are nanocoulombs to microcoulombs. In a hydrogen atom the electric force is about \(10^{39}\) times gravity, and because both fall off as \(1/r^2\), no separation makes them equal.

F ≈ 2.7×10¹⁴ N

Superposition: the only rule for many charges

The net force on a charge is the vector sum of the individual Coulomb forces from every other charge, each computed as if the others were absent:

\[ \vec F_1 = \vec F_{2,1} + \vec F_{3,1} + \vec F_{4,1} + \cdots \]
What each letter means
\(\vec F_1\)
the net (total) force vector on charge 1, in N
\(\vec F_{2,1},\ \vec F_{3,1},\ \dots\)
the individual force vectors by charge 2 on charge 1, by charge 3 on charge 1, and so on, each computed from Coulomb's law as if the other charges did not exist
\(+\)
vector addition: add \(x\)-components together and \(y\)-components together, never the magnitudes

This is Newton's second law bookkeeping from Physics 2111 (\(\sum F_x = ma_x\), \(\sum F_y = ma_y\)) with a new force. Lecture 1 emphasizes two habits:

What each letter means
\(\sum F_x,\ \sum F_y\)
the sum of the \(x\)-components (and, separately, the \(y\)-components) of every force on the object, in N
\(m\)
the mass of the object, in kg
\(a_x,\ a_y\)
the components of its acceleration, in m/s²; both are zero when the object is in equilibrium (at rest, or "floating")
  • Draw the picture first. Put an arrow on the target charge for each other charge: away from like signs, toward opposite signs. Only then compute magnitudes.
  • Components, not "adding magnitudes." Each force contributes \(F\cos\theta\) to \(x\) and \(F\sin\theta\) to \(y\), with the angle measured for that arrow. Sum the components, then take the magnitude \(\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}\) and angle \(\tan^{-1}(F_y/F_x)\), fixing the quadrant by looking at the signs of \(F_x\) and \(F_y\).
Why superposition holds, and how to turn a picture into components

Why forces simply add. The force that charge 3 exerts on charge 2 does not care whether charge 1 exists; each pair interacts on its own. That is an experimental fact (electric forces are "linear"), and it is what makes every many-charge problem tractable: compute each pair force as if the others were absent, then add the vectors. Nothing fancier is ever needed for point charges.

The procedure, mechanically. (1) Mark the target charge. (2) For every other charge, draw an arrow on the target: pointing away from that charge if the signs match, toward it if they differ. Draw the arrow on the target, not on the other charge. (3) For each arrow, compute the magnitude \(k|q_1||q_2|/r^2\) with \(r\) the straight-line distance between the two charges (Pythagoras when they are not on a common axis). (4) For each arrow, get the components from the triangle whose hypotenuse joins the two charges: \(F_x = F\,(\Delta x/r)\), \(F_y = F\,(\Delta y/r)\), with the signs of \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) taken in the direction the arrow points. (5) Add the \(x\)'s, add the \(y\)'s. (6) Only now convert to magnitude and angle if asked. Step 2 is where the physics lives; steps 3 through 6 are arithmetic.

What each letter means
\(F\)
the magnitude of one pair force, \(k|q_1||q_2|/r^2\), in N
\(F_x,\ F_y\)
its components along \(x\) and \(y\), in N, with signs
\(\Delta x,\ \Delta y\)
the horizontal and vertical separations between the two charges (target minus source, in m); their signs give the direction of \(\hat r\)
\(r\)
the straight-line distance, \(\sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}\), in m; \(\Delta x/r\) and \(\Delta y/r\) are the cosine and sine of the direction angle without ever computing the angle
Force on a charge in 2D, fully worked
Lecture 1, Example 1.3 (numbers as in the figure above)
The target \(q_2 = +10\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) sits at the origin. \(q_1 = -30\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) is at \((-3, -2)\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(q_3 = +25\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) is at \((1, -2)\ \mathrm{m}\). Find the net force on \(q_2\): components, magnitude, and direction.

  1. Draw the two arrows on the target before any numbers

    WhyDirection is decided by signs alone. \(q_3\) and \(q_2\) are both positive: repel, so the arrow on \(q_2\) points away from \(q_3\). \(q_1\) is negative and \(q_2\) positive: attract, so the arrow points toward \(q_1\).

    \(\displaystyle \vec F_{3,2}\): away from \(\displaystyle q_3\), up and to the left.
    \(\displaystyle \vec F_{1,2}\): toward \(\displaystyle q_1\), down and to the left.

    MeansBoth arrows have a leftward part, so \(F_x\) will come out negative. Predicting signs now catches mistakes later.

  2. Find each distance with Pythagoras

    WhyThe distance is the length of the line joining the two charges: \(r = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}\).

    \(\displaystyle q_3\) to \(\displaystyle q_2\): \(\displaystyle \Delta x = 1,\ \Delta y\) \(\displaystyle = 2\), so \(\displaystyle r_{32} = \sqrt{1+4}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt5\) \(\displaystyle = 2.236\ \mathrm{m}\)
    \(\displaystyle q_1\) to \(\displaystyle q_2\): \(\displaystyle \Delta x = 3,\ \Delta y\) \(\displaystyle = 2\), so \(\displaystyle r_{12} = \sqrt{9+4}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{13}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.606\ \mathrm{m}\)

  3. Size of the force from q₃

    WhyCoulomb's law with sizes only. Note \(r^2 = 5\) exactly, no need to square 2.236.

    \(\displaystyle |q_3||q_2| = (25)(10)\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.50\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle F_{3,2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(2.50\times10^{-10})}{5}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2.248}{5}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.4495\ \mathrm{N}\)

  4. Size of the force from q₁

    WhySame steps, \(r^2 = 13\).

    \(\displaystyle |q_1||q_2| = (30)(10)\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.00\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle F_{1,2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(3.00\times10^{-10})}{13}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2.697}{13}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.2075\ \mathrm{N}\)

  5. Components of F₃,₂ from the side ratios

    WhyThe arrow points from \(q_3\) toward \(q_2\) and beyond: 1 unit left for every 2 units up, over a hypotenuse of \(\sqrt5\). So the left part is \(1/\sqrt5\) of the force and the up part is \(2/\sqrt5\).

    \(\displaystyle F_{3,2,x}\) \(\displaystyle = -F_{3,2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\) \(\displaystyle = -(0.4495)(0.4472)\) \(\displaystyle = -0.2010\ \mathrm{N}\)
    \(\displaystyle F_{3,2,y}\) \(\displaystyle = +F_{3,2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\) \(\displaystyle = (0.4495)(0.8944)\) \(\displaystyle = +0.4020\ \mathrm{N}\)

  6. Components of F₁,₂ from the side ratios

    WhyThe arrow points toward \(q_1\): 3 left, 2 down, hypotenuse \(\sqrt{13}\).

    \(\displaystyle F_{1,2,x}\) \(\displaystyle = -F_{1,2}\cdot\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\) \(\displaystyle = -(0.2075)(0.8321)\) \(\displaystyle = -0.1726\ \mathrm{N}\)
    \(\displaystyle F_{1,2,y}\) \(\displaystyle = -F_{1,2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\) \(\displaystyle = -(0.2075)(0.5547)\) \(\displaystyle = -0.1151\ \mathrm{N}\)

  7. Add the x parts, then add the y parts

    WhySuperposition: forces add as vectors, which means component by component. Never add the magnitudes.

    \(\displaystyle F_x = -0.2010 + (-0.1726)\) \(\displaystyle = -0.3736\ \mathrm{N}\)
    \(\displaystyle F_y = 0.4020 + (-0.1151)\) \(\displaystyle = +0.2870\ \mathrm{N}\)

    MeansSigns match the prediction from step 1: left and up.

  8. Magnitude

    WhyPythagoras on the two components.

    \(\displaystyle |F| = \sqrt{(0.3736)^2 + (0.2870)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{0.1396 + 0.08235}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.471\ \mathrm{N}\)

  9. Direction, with the quadrant fixed by hand

    Why\(\tan^{-1}\) only knows the ratio, not which quadrant. Use the sizes to get the angle from the nearest axis, then read the quadrant from the signs: \(F_x \lt 0\), \(F_y \gt 0\) is the second quadrant (up-left).

    \(\displaystyle \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{0.2870}{0.3736}\right)\) \(\displaystyle = 37.5^\circ\text{ above the } -x \text{ axis}\)
    \(\displaystyle \text{from } +x:\ 180^\circ - 37.5^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = 142.5^\circ\)

    MeansA calculator's \(\tan^{-1}(F_y/F_x)\) with the negative \(F_x\) returns \(-37.5^\circ\). That is the wrong quadrant; add \(180^\circ\).

F = (-0.374, +0.287) N |F| = 0.47 N at 142° from +x
N

The same recipe solves Homework 1 Problems 4, 5, 6 (triangle and square configurations) and Spring 2015 Q1–2, Fall 2018 Q1.

Using symmetry before computing
Spring 2015, Questions 1–2
\(Q_1 = +7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at \((-L, 0)\), \(Q_2 = -10.5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at the origin, \(Q_3 = +7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at \((L, 0)\), with \(L = 1.3\ \mathrm{m}\). \(Q_4 = -10.5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) sits at \((0, h)\) with \(h = 2.6\ \mathrm{m}\). Find the \(x\)- and \(y\)-components of the net force on \(Q_4\).

  1. Draw the three arrows on Q₄

    Why\(Q_2\) and \(Q_4\) are both negative: repel, so \(Q_4\) is pushed straight up. \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) are positive and \(Q_4\) negative: attract, so \(Q_4\) is pulled toward each of them, down-left and down-right.

  2. Use the mirror symmetry for Fₓ

    Why\(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) have the same charge and the same distance from \(Q_4\), placed as mirror images across the \(y\)-axis. Their pulls have equal size, so their left and right parts cancel. \(\vec F_2\) is vertical and has no \(x\)-part.

    \(\displaystyle F_x = 0\)

    MeansThat answers Q1 with no arithmetic. Exams reward spotting this.

  3. Size of the push from Q₂

    WhyDistance from the origin to \((0, h)\) is \(h\). Sizes of the charges only.

    \(\displaystyle |Q_2||Q_4|\) \(\displaystyle = (10.5)(10.5)\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.1025\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle F_2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(1.1025\times10^{-10})}{(2.6)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{0.9911}{6.76}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.1466\ \mathrm{N}\ (+y)\)

  4. Distance from Q₁ to Q₄

    WhyPythagoras with legs \(L\) and \(h\).

    \(\displaystyle r^2 = L^2 + h^2\) \(\displaystyle = 1.69 + 6.76\) \(\displaystyle = 8.45\ \mathrm{m^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle r = \sqrt{8.45}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.907\ \mathrm{m}\)

  5. Size of the pull from Q₁

    WhyUse \(r^2 = 8.45\) directly.

    \(\displaystyle |Q_1||Q_4| = (7)(10.5)\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = 7.35\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle F_1\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(7.35\times10^{-11})}{8.45}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.07820\ \mathrm{N}\)

  6. The downward part of F₁

    WhyThe pull points from \(Q_4\) toward \(Q_1\): down a height \(h\) over a hypotenuse \(r\). So the vertical part is the fraction \(h/r\) of the force, pointing down.

    \(\displaystyle F_{1,y} = -F_1\dfrac{h}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = -(0.07820)\dfrac{2.6}{2.907}\) \(\displaystyle = -0.06994\ \mathrm{N}\)

    MeansBy symmetry \(Q_3\) contributes exactly the same downward part.

  7. Add the vertical parts

    WhyOne push up, two equal pulls down.

    \(\displaystyle F_y = 0.1466 - 2(0.06994)\) \(\displaystyle = 0.1466 - 0.1399\) \(\displaystyle = +6.74\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N}\)

    MeansThe big numbers nearly cancel, leaving a small net push up. Keep four significant figures until the last subtraction, or rounding will swamp the answer.

Fₓ = 0 F_y = +0.00674 N
N
Where is the net force on a third charge zero?
Lecture 2, Example 2.2 and clicker · Homework 1, Problem 3 · Fall 2015 Q5
Homework 1, Problem 3: \(+5.9\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) sits at \(x = 0\) and \(-1.1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at \(x = 0.21\ \mathrm{m}\). Where on the \(x\)-axis would a third charge feel zero net force?

  1. Pick the region from the sign rule

    WhyOpposite signs (\(+5.9\) and \(-1.1\)). Between them, both fields on a test charge point the same way (away from + and toward −), so they add and cannot cancel. Outside, they point opposite ways. Cancelling needs equal sizes, which requires being closer to the weaker charge.

    Zero is at \(\displaystyle x \gt 0.21\ \mathrm{m}\) (outside, beyond the \(\displaystyle -1.1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)).

  2. Set the two field sizes equal

    WhyAt the zero point the two contributions are equal in size and opposite in direction. The distance to the first charge is \(x\), to the second is \(x - 0.21\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{k(5.9)}{x^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k(1.1)}{(x - 0.21)^2}\)

    Means\(k\) and the \(10^{-6}\) cancel from both sides, so you can drop them.

  3. Take the square root of both sides

    WhyEverything is positive in this region, so the square root is safe and avoids a quadratic.

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{\sqrt{5.9}}{x}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sqrt{1.1}}{x - 0.21}\)
    \(\displaystyle \sqrt{5.9}\,(x - 0.21)\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{1.1}\;x\)

  4. Put in the numbers

    \(\displaystyle 2.429\,(x - 0.21)\) \(\displaystyle = 1.049\,x\)
    \(\displaystyle 2.429x - 0.5101 = 1.049x\)

  5. Collect the x terms and solve

    WhyMove all \(x\) terms to one side.

    \(\displaystyle (2.429 - 1.049)\,x\) \(\displaystyle = 0.5101\)
    \(\displaystyle x = \dfrac{0.5101}{1.380}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.370\ \mathrm{m}\)

  6. Check the region

    WhyAn answer outside the predicted region means an algebra slip.

    \(\displaystyle 0.370 \gt 0.21\) ✓, beyond the smaller charge.

Same method, like signs. If the second charge were \(+1.1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), the zero is between them: \(\sqrt{5.9}\,(0.21 - x) = \sqrt{1.1}\,x\), so \(0.5101 = 3.478\,x\) and \(x = 0.147\ \mathrm{m}\), closer to the smaller charge as the rule says.

Lecture Example 2.2. \(+4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at 0 and \(+10\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at 0.4 m: \(\sqrt4\,(0.4 - r) = \sqrt{10}\,r\), so \(0.8 = 5.162\,r\) and \(r = 0.155\ \mathrm{m}\) from the \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) charge.

The location does not depend on the third charge at all: if \(\vec E = 0\) there, the force on any charge placed there is zero (Lecture 2 clicker: swapping \(+5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) for \(-5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) changes nothing).

x = 0.370 m
m
Trap

Never solve \(k q_1/x^2 = k q_2/(d-x)^2\) by cross-multiplying into a quadratic unless you must. Taking the square root of both sides is faster and avoids the extra root that lands in the wrong region. Always check the answer is in the region your sign rule predicted.
