E(x) along the line of two charges

q₁ is at x = 0 and q₂ at x = d. The plot is the x-component of the net field along the axis. Flip a sign and watch the zero jump from between the charges to outside them, always on the side of the weaker charge.

Coulomb force balanced by other forces
Homework 1, Problems 1 and 2
Problem 1: \(Q_1 = +5.0\ \mathrm{nC}\) is fixed. A second charge \(Q_2\) with mass \(5.5\ \mu\mathrm{g}\) hovers \(d = 35\ \mathrm{cm}\) directly above it with zero net force. Find the sign and size of \(Q_2\).

  1. Free-body diagram

    WhyOnly two forces act on \(Q_2\): its weight \(mg\), straight down, and the electric force from \(Q_1\), along the vertical line joining them.

    MeansFor the net force to be zero, the electric force must point up.

  2. Decide the sign

    WhyAn upward push from a charge below is a repulsion. Repulsion means like signs.

    \(\displaystyle Q_1\) is positive, so \(\displaystyle Q_2\) is positive.

  3. Write the balance

    WhyUp force equals down force.

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{k|Q_1||Q_2|}{d^2}\) \(\displaystyle = mg\)

  4. Solve for |Q₂|

    Why\(|Q_2|\) is multiplied by \(k|Q_1|\) and divided by \(d^2\). Undo both.

    \(\displaystyle |Q_2| = \dfrac{mg\,d^2}{k|Q_1|}\)

  5. Convert units

    WhyA microgram is \(10^{-6}\ \mathrm{g}\) \(= 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{kg}\). Centimeters to meters.

    \(\displaystyle m = 5.5\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{kg},\) \(\displaystyle d\) \(\displaystyle = 0.35\ \mathrm{m},\) \(\displaystyle Q_1\) \(\displaystyle = 5.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\)

  6. Top and bottom separately

    \(\displaystyle mg\,d^2\) \(\displaystyle = (5.5\times10^{-9})(9.81)(0.35)^2\) \(\displaystyle = 6.609\times10^{-9}\)
    \(\displaystyle k|Q_1|\) \(\displaystyle = (8.99\times10^{9})(5.0\times10^{-9})\) \(\displaystyle = 44.95\)

  7. Divide

    \(\displaystyle |Q_2|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{6.609\times10^{-9}}{44.95}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.47\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.147\ \mathrm{nC}\)

Problem 2 (spring plus two charges), set up in steps. \(q_1 = +q\) at the origin, \(q_2 = +q\) at distance \(r\) along a line at angle \(\theta\), \(q_3 = -q\) at \(3r\) on the same line; \(q_2\) is tied to \(q_1\) by a spring. (1) \(q_1\) pushes \(q_2\) outward along the line with \(kq^2/r^2\). (2) \(q_3\) is also along the line, farther out, and attracts \(q_2\), so it pulls outward too, with \(kq^2/(2r)^2\). (3) Both point along \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\), so they simply add: \(\vec F\) \(= kq^2\left(\frac{1}{r^2} + \frac{1}{4r^2}\right)(\cos\theta\,\hat i + \sin\theta\,\hat j)\). (4) \(q_2\) moves outward and stretches the spring by \(\Delta r\). (5) At the new equilibrium the distances are \(r + \Delta r\) and \(2r - \Delta r\), and the spring force \(-k_s\Delta r\) along the line balances \(kq^2\left(\frac{1}{(r+\Delta r)^2} + \frac{1}{(2r-\Delta r)^2}\right)\).

Q₂ = +0.147 nC

5.4 The electric field

The problem the field solves. Coulomb's law describes two charges pulling on each other across empty space with nothing in between: "action at a distance." That feels wrong, and it is also inconvenient: to know what happens to a new charge placed somewhere, you would have to recompute every pair force from scratch. The field fixes both. We imagine that a charge alters the space around it, and that any other charge placed at a point responds only to the local condition of that space. The condition is \(\vec E\): the force a one-coulomb positive test charge would feel there, per coulomb. Compute \(\vec E\) once from the source charges; then the force on anything you put at that point is just \(q\vec E\). Later in the course the field turns out to be physically real (it carries energy, and light is a traveling field), but for this exam its job is bookkeeping: separate "what the sources do to space" from "what a particular charge does in response."

Definition and the point-charge field
\[ \vec E \equiv \frac{\vec F}{q_{\text{test}}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \vec F = q\vec E \]
What each letter means
\(\vec E\)
the electric field vector: the force per coulomb that a positive test charge would feel at that point, in N/C (= V/m)
\(\vec F\)
the electric force on the test charge, in N
\(q_{\text{test}}\)
a small positive "probe" charge imagined at the point, in C; dividing by it removes the probe from the answer, so \(\vec E\) describes the space, not the probe
\(q\)
any charge placed in the field, in C, with its sign: a negative \(q\) feels a force opposite to \(\vec E\)
\(\equiv\)
"is defined as"; this is a definition, not a law

The field is the force per unit positive charge that would act at a point. It is a property of the space, defined whether or not a test charge is present (Lecture 2: "what if I remove \(q_2\)? Is there anything at that point in space?"). Units: N/C, which equals V/m (Chapter 7). Gravity's analog is \(\vec g = \vec F/m\).

Field of a single point charge \(Q\) at distance \(r\):

\[ \vec E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}\,\hat r \]
What each letter means
\(Q\)
the source charge making the field, in C, with its sign (a negative \(Q\) flips the direction toward itself)
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(r\)
distance from the source charge to the point where you want the field, in m
\(\hat r\)
unit vector (length exactly 1, no units) pointing from the source charge toward the point you care about; it only supplies a direction
\(\sum_i,\ Q_i,\ r_i,\ \hat r_i\)
for many charges: add (as vectors) the field of each charge \(i\), using its own charge, its own distance to the point, and its own direction

with \(\hat r\) pointing from the charge to the field point. Away from positive charges, toward negative charges. Many charges: add the vectors, \(\vec E\) \(= \sum_i \dfrac{kQ_i}{r_i^2}\hat r_i\).

In plain words

The field at a point answers one question: "If I put \(+1\ \mathrm{C}\) here, what force would it feel?" Multiply by the actual charge to get the actual force, \(\vec F = q\vec E\). Positive charges are pushed along \(\vec E\); negative charges are pushed the opposite way.

Why the field points away from positive charges, and what "test charge" means

The definition \(\vec E = \vec F/q\) uses a positive test charge by convention. A positive charge near a positive source is pushed away, so the field of a positive source points away from it. Near a negative source the positive test charge is pulled in, so that field points toward the source. A negative charge placed in any field feels \(\vec F = q\vec E\) with \(q \lt 0\): the same field, the opposite force. The field's direction is fixed by the sources; only the force flips.

The test charge is imagined to be tiny so that it does not disturb the sources (a large test charge would push the source charges around and change the very field you are measuring). In problems you never need to worry about this; it is the reason the field is a property of the sources alone.

Dividing by \(q\) also explains the units: N/C. In Chapter 7 you will meet the same unit as V/m, because a field is also a "potential slope." Both are correct; the equation sheet uses either.

Trap · what changes when you swap the test charge

Lecture 2 clicker: a \(6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) charge feels \(0.18\ \mathrm{N}\) in some field. Replace it with \(9\ \mu\mathrm{C}\): the field is unchanged (it comes from the other charges), so \(F = qE\) \(= 9\times(0.18/6)\) \(= 0.27\ \mathrm{N}\). A negative test charge feels the force opposite to \(\vec E\). Never let the test charge's sign change the direction you draw for \(\vec E\).

Field at the empty corner of a square
Lecture 2, Example 2.1
Charges \(+q\), \(-q\), \(+q\) sit on three corners of a square of side \(d\). Find \(\vec E\) at the fourth corner \(P\).

  1. Put P at the origin and list the positions

    WhyCoordinates turn "directions" into signs you can add.

    Charge 1 (\(\displaystyle +q\)) at \(\displaystyle (-d, 0)\): directly left of \(\displaystyle P\).
    Charge 3 (\(\displaystyle +q\)) at \(\displaystyle (0, -d)\): directly below \(\displaystyle P\).
    Charge 2 (\(\displaystyle -q\)) at \(\displaystyle (-d, -d)\): diagonally down-left.

  2. Field from charge 1

    WhyDistance \(d\). A positive source: the field points away from it. Charge 1 is to the left, so away is \(+x\).

    \(\displaystyle \vec E_1\) \(\displaystyle = \left(\dfrac{kq}{d^2},\ 0\right)\)

  3. Field from charge 3

    WhyDistance \(d\), below \(P\): away is \(+y\).

    \(\displaystyle \vec E_3\) \(\displaystyle = \left(0,\ \dfrac{kq}{d^2}\right)\)

  4. Distance and size for charge 2

    WhyThe diagonal of a square is \(d\sqrt2\), so \(r^2 = 2d^2\).

    \(\displaystyle E_2 = \dfrac{kq}{(d\sqrt2)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq}{2d^2}\)

  5. Direction and components for charge 2

    WhyA negative source: the field points toward it, down-left along the diagonal. A 45° diagonal splits equally: each component is the size times \(1/\sqrt2\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{2x} = E_{2y}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{kq}{2d^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{kq}{2\sqrt2\,d^2}\) \(\displaystyle = -0.3536\,\dfrac{kq}{d^2}\)

  6. Add the components

    WhyFactor out \(kq/d^2\) so only plain numbers remain.

    \(\displaystyle E_x = \dfrac{kq}{d^2}(1 - 0.3536)\) \(\displaystyle = 0.6464\,\dfrac{kq}{d^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle E_y = \dfrac{kq}{d^2}(1 - 0.3536)\) \(\displaystyle = 0.6464\,\dfrac{kq}{d^2}\)

  7. Magnitude and direction

    WhyEqual components mean the field points at 45°, up and to the right. The magnitude is \(\sqrt2\) times one component.

    \(\displaystyle |E| = \sqrt{E_x^2 + E_y^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt2\,(0.6464)\dfrac{kq}{d^2}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.914\,\dfrac{kq}{d^2}\)
|E| = 0.914 kq/d² at 45°
× kq/d²

Fall 2018 Q1–4 uses this same square (\(+2Q\), \(-Q\), \(+Q\) with \(Q = 7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), \(a = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}\)) for force, energy, and potential; see the worked exam.

Field components from two charges, then magnitude and angle
Homework 2, Problem 1 · Fall 2015, Questions 2–3
\(q_1 = 4.2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at the origin and \(q_2 = 6.3\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at \(x = d = 0.85\ \mathrm{m}\). Point \(P\) is \(0.425\ \mathrm{m}\) directly above \(q_2\). (Q2) Find \(E_y\) at \(P\). (Q3) Find \(|\vec E|\) at \(P\).

  1. Field from q₂: size

    Why\(P\) is straight above \(q_2\), a distance \(0.425\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle E_2 = \dfrac{kq_2}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(6.3\times10^{-6})}{(0.425)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{5.664\times10^{4}}{0.1806}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.136\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  2. Field from q₂: direction

    WhyAway from a positive charge that is directly below: straight up.

    \(\displaystyle E_{2x} = 0,\) \(\displaystyle E_{2y}\) \(\displaystyle = +3.136\times10^{5}\)

  3. Distance from q₁ to P

    WhyLegs \(0.85\) (across) and \(0.425\) (up).

    \(\displaystyle r_1^2 = 0.85^2 + 0.425^2\) \(\displaystyle = 0.7225 + 0.1806\) \(\displaystyle = 0.9031\ \mathrm{m^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle r_1 = 0.9503\ \mathrm{m}\)

  4. Field from q₁: size

    WhyUse \(r_1^2\) directly.

    \(\displaystyle E_1\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(4.2\times10^{-6})}{0.9031}\) \(\displaystyle = 4.181\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  5. Field from q₁: components by side ratios

    WhyIt points from \(q_1\) toward \(P\) and beyond: \(0.85\) across and \(0.425\) up over the hypotenuse \(r_1\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{1x} = E_1\dfrac{0.85}{0.9503}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.739\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
    \(\displaystyle E_{1y} = E_1\dfrac{0.425}{0.9503}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.870\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  6. Add: the answer to Q2

    \(\displaystyle E_y\) \(\displaystyle = 3.136\times10^{5} + 1.870\times10^{4}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.32\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
    \(\displaystyle E_x = 3.74\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  7. Magnitude: the answer to Q3

    \(\displaystyle |E|\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{(3.323\times10^{5})^2 + (3.739\times10^{4})^2}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.34\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

    MeansThe exam's choice is \(3.35\times10^{5}\); the tiny difference comes from rounding \(k\). The angle from \(+x\) is \(\tan^{-1}(E_y/E_x) = 83.6^\circ\), nearly straight up because \(q_2\) is so close.

Homework 2 Problem 1 is the same layout with \(Q_1 = +0.35\ \mathrm{nC}\) at the origin, \(Q_2 = -6.5\ \mathrm{nC}\) at \(x = 14.5\ \mathrm{cm}\), and \(P\) \(4.5\ \mathrm{cm}\) above \(Q_2\). The only change in the steps: \(Q_2\) is negative, so its field at \(P\) points down, toward \(Q_2\), and \(E_y\) comes out negative. The angle from \(+x\) is then negative (fourth quadrant).

E_y = 3.33×10⁵ N/C |E| ≈ 3.35×10⁵ N/C
N/C
Explore · Superposition of fields
Field at a point from two charges

Q₁ sits at the origin and Q₂ at (d, 0). Move the field point P and the charges; the arrows show each charge's field at P and their vector sum. Set P directly above Q₂ to reproduce Fall 2015 Q2–3 and Homework 2 P1.

5.5 Fields of continuous charge distributions

The situation. A charged rod, ring, or plate is not a point, so \(kQ/r^2\) does not apply: which \(r\)? Different parts of the object are at different distances and directions from the point where you want the field. The only tool we have is the point-charge formula, so we apply it to each small piece and add. Section F.2 explains the method in general; here it is applied to fields. The exam asks you to set up these integrals more often than to finish them, so the setup steps matter most.

The master recipe (Lecture 2: "it works for all!")

Chop the object into pieces \(dq\), treat each as a point charge, add the vectors with an integral:

\[ \vec E = \int d\vec E = \int \frac{k\,dq}{r^2}\,\hat r \]
What each letter means
\(d\vec E\)
the tiny field made by one tiny piece of the object, in N/C
\(dq\)
the charge of that tiny piece, in C, written as (density) × (tiny length, area, or volume)
\(r\)
distance from that piece to the field point \(P\), in m; it changes from piece to piece, which is why it stays inside the integral
\(\hat r\)
unit vector (length exactly 1, no units) pointing from the source charge toward the point you care about; it only supplies a direction
\(\int\)
integral sign: "add up the contributions of all the tiny pieces"
\(\lambda\)
linear charge density: charge per unit length along a line, rod, or ring, in C/m (\(\lambda = Q/L\) when uniform)
\(\sigma\)
surface charge density: charge per unit area on a sheet or surface, in C/m² (\(\sigma = Q/A\) when uniform)
\(\rho\)
volume charge density: charge per unit volume inside an insulator, in C/m³ (\(\rho = Q/V\) when uniform)
\(dx,\ ds,\ R\,d\theta,\ dA,\ dV\)
the tiny length, arc length (radius times tiny angle), area, or volume of the piece
\(Q,\ L,\ A,\ V\)
the object's total charge, length, area, or volume, used to compute a uniform density
\(dE_x,\ dE_y,\ \theta\)
components of \(d\vec E\) and the angle used to split it; \(\theta\) is measured from an axis you choose
\(h\)
the perpendicular distance from the object to the field point, in m
  1. Write \(dq\) in terms of a geometric variable. Line: \(dq = \lambda\,dx\) or \(\lambda\,ds = \lambda R\,d\theta\) on an arc. Surface: \(dq = \sigma\,dA\). Volume: \(dq = \rho\,dV\). For uniform density, \(\lambda = Q/L\), \(\sigma = Q/A\), \(\rho = Q/V\).
  2. Write \(r\), the distance from that \(dq\) to the field point \(P\), in the same variable (Pythagoras).
  3. Resolve \(d\vec E\) into components. \(dE_x = dE\cos\theta\), \(dE_y = dE\sin\theta\), where the trig factor is a ratio of sides that you write in terms of the integration variable (e.g. \(h/\sqrt{x^2+h^2}\)). This is where the \(\hat r\) goes.
  4. Use symmetry to drop a component that integrates to zero.
  5. Integrate over the object. Then check a limit: far away, the answer must become \(kQ/r^2\).
DensitySymbol and unitsHow to get itGeometry reminders
Linear\(\lambda\), C/m\(\lambda = Q/L\); semicircle \(\lambda = Q/(\pi R)\); full ring \(Q/(2\pi R)\); arc of angle \(\theta_0\): \(Q/(R\theta_0)\)arc length \(s = R\theta\), \(ds = R\,d\theta\)
Surface\(\sigma\), C/m²\(\sigma = Q/A\); sphere surface \(Q/(4\pi R^2)\); disk \(Q/(\pi R^2)\); cylinder side \(Q/(2\pi RL)\)ring on a disk: \(dA = 2\pi r\,dr\)
Volume\(\rho\), C/m³\(\rho = Q/V\); sphere \(Q/(\tfrac43\pi R^3)\); cylinder \(Q/(\pi R^2 L)\)spherical shell: \(dV = 4\pi r^2\,dr\); cylindrical shell: \(dV = 2\pi r L\,dr\)
What each letter means
\(\lambda\)
the rod's charge per unit length, C/m
\(a\)
the length of the rod, in m (it runs from \(x = 0\) to \(x = a\))
\(h\)
the height of the field point \(P\) above the left end, in m
\(x,\ dx\)
the position of a charge element along the rod and the tiny length of that element; \(dq = \lambda\,dx\)
\(\theta\)
the angle at \(P\) between the vertical and the line to the element, so \(\tan\theta = x/h\)
\(E_x,\ E_y\)
the field components at \(P\): \(E_x\) points away from the rod (negative here), \(E_y\) points up
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
Finite rod: the field above one end, derived line by line
Lecture 2, Example 2.3
A rod from \(x = 0\) to \(x = a\) carries uniform charge per length \(\lambda\). Find both components of \(\vec E\) at \(P\), a height \(h\) above the left end.

  1. Pick one small piece of the rod

    WhyThe point-charge formula only works for points. A piece of length \(dx\) is small enough to count as a point.

    \(\displaystyle dq = \lambda\,dx\)

  2. Distance from the piece to P

    WhyHorizontal leg \(x\), vertical leg \(h\).

    \(\displaystyle r = \sqrt{x^2 + h^2}\)

  3. Size of the piece's field

    WhyPoint-charge field of \(dq\).

    \(\displaystyle dE = \dfrac{k\,dq}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda\,dx}{x^2 + h^2}\)

  4. Split it into components

    WhyThe field points away from the piece, along the line from \((x, 0)\) to \(P\) at \((0, h)\): that is \(x\) to the left and \(h\) up, over the hypotenuse \(r\). Side ratios give the components.

    \(\displaystyle dE_x = -dE\cdot\dfrac{x}{r},\) \(\displaystyle dE_y\) \(\displaystyle = +dE\cdot\dfrac{h}{r}\)

    MeansThe minus sign: the \(x\)-part points left, toward \(-x\).

  5. Combine the powers of r

    Why\(dE\) already has \(r^2\) downstairs; the ratio adds one more \(r\). And \(r^3 = (x^2 + h^2)^{3/2}\).

    \(\displaystyle dE_x\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{k\lambda\,x\,dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\)
    \(\displaystyle dE_y\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda\,h\,dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\)

  6. Set up both integrals over the rod

    WhyAdd up every piece: \(x\) runs over the charged object only, from 0 to \(a\). Constants come out front.

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = -k\lambda\displaystyle\int_0^a \frac{x\,dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\)
    \(\displaystyle E_y\) \(\displaystyle = k\lambda h\displaystyle\int_0^a \frac{dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\)

  7. The x integral: substitute u = x² + h²

    WhyThe top \(x\,dx\) is half of \(du = 2x\,dx\). The integral of \(u^{-3/2}\) is \(-2u^{-1/2}\).

    \(\displaystyle \int \frac{x\,dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12\int u^{-3/2}\,du\) \(\displaystyle = -u^{-1/2}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+h^2}}\)
    \(\displaystyle \Big[-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+h^2}}\Big]_0^a\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac1h - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^2+h^2}}\)

  8. So Eₓ is

    WhyFactor \(1/h\) out of the bracket.

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = -k\lambda\left(\dfrac1h - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^2+h^2}}\right)\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{k\lambda}{h}\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{a^2+h^2}}\right)\)

    MeansNegative: the field points left, away from the rod, which lies to the right.

  9. The y integral: substitute x = h tan θ

    WhyThis is the lecture's trick. Then \(dx = h\sec^2\theta\,d\theta\) and \(x^2 + h^2 = h^2\sec^2\theta\), so the \(3/2\) power becomes \(h^3\sec^3\theta\).

    \(\displaystyle \int \frac{dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\) \(\displaystyle = \int \frac{h\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{h^3\sec^3\theta}\) \(\displaystyle = \frac{1}{h^2}\int\cos\theta\,d\theta\) \(\displaystyle = \frac{\sin\theta}{h^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle \sin\theta\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+h^2}}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \Big[\tfrac{x}{h^2\sqrt{x^2+h^2}}\Big]_0^a\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{a}{h^2\sqrt{a^2+h^2}}\)

  10. So Ey is

    WhyMultiply by the constant \(k\lambda h\) that was out front.

    \(\displaystyle E_y\) \(\displaystyle = k\lambda h\cdot\dfrac{a}{h^2\sqrt{a^2+h^2}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda}{h}\cdot\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+h^2}}\)

    MeansPositive: up, away from the rod.

  11. Check two limits

    WhyA formula that fails an easy limit is wrong somewhere.

    Far away, \(\displaystyle h \gg a\): \(\displaystyle E_y \to \dfrac{k\lambda a}{h^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{h^2}\), a point charge \(\displaystyle Q = \lambda a\). ✓
    Very long rod, \(\displaystyle a \to \infty\): \(\displaystyle E_x \to -k\lambda/h\) and \(\displaystyle E_y \to k\lambda/h\), equal sizes, so the field is at 45°. ✓
The infinite line of charge (two ways)
Lecture 2 (integral) · Lecture 4 (Gauss's law)
Extend the rod from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\). Find the field at a perpendicular distance \(h\) from the line.

  1. Use symmetry first

    WhyFor every piece at \(+x\) there is a matching piece at \(-x\). Their fields have equal size; their parts along the line point opposite ways and cancel. Only the part perpendicular to the line survives.

  2. Measure each piece by its angle

    WhyLet \(\theta\) be the angle at the field point between the perpendicular and the line to the piece. Then:

    \(\displaystyle x = h\tan\theta,\) \(\displaystyle dx\) \(\displaystyle = h\sec^2\theta\,d\theta,\) \(\displaystyle r\) \(\displaystyle = h\sec\theta\)

  3. Size of one piece's field in θ

    Why\(dE = k\lambda\,dx/r^2\); the \(\sec^2\theta\) cancels.

    \(\displaystyle dE\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda\,h\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{h^2\sec^2\theta}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda}{h}\,d\theta\)

  4. Keep the perpendicular part

    WhyThe perpendicular direction makes angle \(\theta\) with \(d\vec E\), so multiply by \(\cos\theta\).

    \(\displaystyle dE_\perp\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda}{h}\cos\theta\,d\theta\)

  5. Limits

    Why\(x\) from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\) means \(\theta\) from \(-\pi/2\) to \(+\pi/2\) (Lecture 2 clicker).

  6. Integrate

    Why\(\int\cos\theta\,d\theta = \sin\theta\), and \(\sin(\pi/2) - \sin(-\pi/2)\) \(= 1 - (-1)\) \(= 2\).

    \(\displaystyle E_\perp\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda}{h}\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\,d\theta\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{h}\)

  7. Write it the way the equation sheet does

    Why\(k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\), so \(2k = 1/(2\pi\varepsilon_0)\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{h}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 h}\)

    MeansIt falls as \(1/r\), not \(1/r^2\): moving away, more of the line comes into view. Radially away from a positive line, toward a negative one. Chapter 6 gets the same result in two lines with Gauss's law.

Lecture 2 checkpoint (two parallel lines, both \(+\lambda\)). At the midpoint A the two fields are equal and opposite, so \(E_A = 0\). At B, a distance \(a\) above the top line, both fields point up and add, so \(E_B \gt 0\). Therefore \(E_A \lt E_B\).

Why a line gives \(1/r\) and a sheet gives a constant

Move twice as far from a point charge and its field drops to a quarter: same charge, four times the area to spread over. Now move twice as far from an infinite line. Each individual piece of the line got weaker by the inverse square, but the pieces that contribute most are those within roughly a distance \(r\) along the line on either side of the nearest point, and when you double \(r\) that stretch of line doubles too: twice as much charge is "in play." One factor of \(1/r^2\) times one factor of \(r\) leaves \(1/r\). For an infinite sheet the same thing happens in two directions at once: doubling the distance doubles the width and doubling the height of the patch that matters, four times the charge, cancelling the inverse square completely. The field does not depend on distance at all.

A cleaner way to say it: an infinite line looks exactly the same from any distance except for a scale factor, and an infinite sheet looks exactly the same from any distance, full stop. There is no ruler built into an infinite sheet, so its field has nothing to depend on. This is why the sheet field \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) is such a convenient building block in Chapters 6 and 8.

Rod along its own axis: field at a point beyond the end
Homework 2, Problem 5
A rod of length \(L\) and total charge \(q\) lies from \(x = 0\) to \(x = L\). Point \(P\) is on the axis, a distance \(a\) beyond the right end. Find \(\vec E(P)\), then evaluate for \(q = 470\ \mathrm{nC}\), \(L = 9.05\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(a = 4.1\ \mathrm{cm}\).

  1. Charge on one piece

    WhyUniform charge, so the charge per length is \(\lambda = q/L\).

    \(\displaystyle dq = \lambda\,dx\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q}{L}\,dx\)

  2. Distance from the piece to P

    Why\(P\) is at \(x = L + a\). The piece is at \(x\).

    \(\displaystyle r = (L + a) - x\)

  3. Direction

    WhyEvery piece is to the left of \(P\) and positive, so each \(d\vec E\) points right. Nothing to cancel, nothing to split.

    \(\displaystyle d\vec E = \dfrac{k\,dq}{r^2}\,\hat i\)

  4. Set up the integral

    WhyOnly the charged object: \(x\) from 0 to \(L\).

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq}{L}\displaystyle\int_0^L \frac{dx}{(a + L - x)^2}\)

  5. Substitute u = a + L − x

    WhyThen \(du = -dx\). When \(x = 0\), \(u = a + L\); when \(x = L\), \(u = a\). Flipping the limits absorbs the minus sign.

    \(\displaystyle \int_0^L \frac{dx}{(a+L-x)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \int_a^{a+L}\frac{du}{u^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \Big[-\tfrac1u\Big]_a^{a+L}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac1a - \dfrac{1}{a+L}\)

  6. Combine the fractions

    WhyCommon denominator \(a(a+L)\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac1a - \dfrac{1}{a+L}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(a+L) - a}{a(a+L)}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{L}{a(a+L)}\)

  7. Multiply by the prefactor

    WhyThe \(L\) cancels.

    \(\displaystyle \vec E(P)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq}{L}\cdot\dfrac{L}{a(a+L)}\,\hat i\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq}{a(a+L)}\,\hat i\)

  8. Check the far limit

    WhyIf \(a \gg L\), then \(a + L \approx a\).

    \(\displaystyle E \to \dfrac{kq}{a^2}\ \checkmark\)

    MeansFrom far away the rod looks like a point charge.

  9. Numbers

    WhyCentimeters to meters: \(a = 0.041\), \(a + L = 0.1315\ \mathrm{m}\); \(q = 4.7\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{C}\).

    \(\displaystyle kq\) \(\displaystyle = (8.99\times10^{9})(4.7\times10^{-7})\) \(\displaystyle = 4225\)
    \(\displaystyle a(a+L) = (0.041)(0.1315)\) \(\displaystyle = 5.392\times10^{-3}\)
    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{4225}{5.392\times10^{-3}}\) \(\displaystyle = 7.84\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
E = kq/[a(a+L)] = 7.84×10⁵ N/C, +x
What each letter means
\(q\)
the total charge on the rod, in C
\(L\)
the length of the rod, in m; \(q/L\) is its linear density \(\lambda\)
\(a\)
the distance from the near end of the rod to the point \(P\), in m
\(x,\ dx\)
the position of a charge element along the rod (from 0 to \(L\)) and its tiny length
\(a + L - x\)
the distance from that element to \(P\): the far end is \(a + L\) from \(P\), and the element sits \(x\) closer
\(\hat i\)
unit vector along \(+x\); every piece pushes in this direction, so no components are needed
\(u\)
a substitution variable used to do the integral
N/C
Trap · the multiple-choice integral

Distractors in Homework 2 P5(c) and on exams change one thing at a time: wrong limits (\(0\) to \(a+L\) instead of \(0\) to \(L\)), wrong power (\(1/r\) instead of \(1/r^2\)), a constant distance (\(a+L/2\), which would only be right if the whole rod were at its midpoint), or \(dq\) integrated "from 0 to \(q\)" with an \(x\)-dependent integrand. Check: limits cover the charged object only; integrand has \(r^2\) in the denominator where \(r\) depends on the variable; prefactor uses \(\lambda = q/L\) when \(dx\) is the measure.

Ring of charge on its axis, with the two limits
Lecture 2, Example 2.4 · Fall 2018, Questions 16–18
A ring of radius \(R\) carries total charge \(+Q\) spread uniformly. Find the field at height \(h\) on its axis (Fall 2018 Q16–18: \(\lambda\), the integral, and the far-away limit).

  1. Charge per length (Fall 2018 Q16)

    WhyThe ring's length is its circumference \(2\pi R\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi R}\)

  2. Charge on one piece

    WhyA piece spanning angle \(d\theta\) has arc length \(R\,d\theta\).

    \(\displaystyle dq = \lambda R\,d\theta\)

  3. Distance from any piece to P

    WhyHorizontal leg \(R\), vertical leg \(h\), for every piece around the ring.

    \(\displaystyle r^2 = h^2 + R^2\)

  4. Size of one piece's field

    \(\displaystyle dE = \dfrac{k\,dq}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda R\,d\theta}{h^2 + R^2}\)

  5. Keep only the axial part

    WhyOpposite pieces cancel sideways. The axial part is \(dE\) times \(\cos\theta = h/r\).

    \(\displaystyle dE_z\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda R\,d\theta}{h^2+R^2}\cdot\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+R^2}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda R h\,d\theta}{(h^2+R^2)^{3/2}}\)

    MeansFall 2018 Q17 is exactly this integrand. The distractors use \(R/\sqrt{h^2+R^2}\) (the sideways factor), drop the \(R\) from \(dq\), or have the wrong power.

  6. Integrate around the ring

    WhyNothing in \(dE_z\) depends on \(\theta\), so the integral from 0 to \(2\pi\) just multiplies by \(2\pi\).

    \(\displaystyle E_z\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda R h}{(h^2+R^2)^{3/2}}\cdot 2\pi\)

  7. Put Q back in

    Why\(\lambda\cdot 2\pi R = Q\).

    \(\displaystyle E_z = \dfrac{kQh}{(h^2+R^2)^{3/2}}\)

  8. Far limit (Fall 2018 Q18)

    WhyFor \(h \gg R\), \(h^2 + R^2 \approx h^2\), and \((h^2)^{3/2} = h^3\).

    \(\displaystyle E_z \approx \dfrac{kQh}{h^3}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{h^2}\)

    MeansA point charge, as it must be from far away.

  9. Center and maximum

    WhyAt \(h = 0\) the formula gives 0: at the center every piece is balanced by the opposite one. The field is largest where \(dE_z/dh = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{d}{dh}\left[\dfrac{h}{(h^2+R^2)^{3/2}}\right]\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(h^2+R^2) - 3h^2}{(h^2+R^2)^{5/2}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow h\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt2}\)
E = kQh/(h²+R²)^(3/2)
What each letter means
\(Q\)
the total charge on the ring, in C
\(R\)
the radius of the ring, in m
\(\lambda,\ d\theta\)
the ring's charge per length, \(Q/(2\pi R)\), and the tiny angle spanned by one element, so \(dq = \lambda R\,d\theta\)
\(h\)
the distance along the axis from the ring's center to the field point, in m
\(\sqrt{h^2+R^2}\)
the distance from every element to the field point (the same for all of them)
\(E_z\)
the field along the axis (the only component that survives), in N/C
\(h/\sqrt{h^2+R^2}\)
the cosine of the angle between each element's field and the axis, which picks out the axial part
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
Semicircle of charge: the field at its center
Spring 2014, Questions 5–7
A semicircle of radius \(r = 5.0\ \mathrm{cm}\) lies on the right side of the origin (\(x \gt 0\)) and carries \(Q = +15\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) spread uniformly. (Q5) Find \(\lambda\). (Q6) Set up \(E_x\) at the origin. (Q7) What point charge at \((-r, 0)\) would make the field at the origin zero?

  1. Charge per length (Q5)

    WhyA semicircle's length is half a circumference: \(\pi r\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = \dfrac{Q}{\pi r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{15\times10^{-6}}{\pi(0.050)}\) \(\displaystyle = 9.55\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C/m} \approx 95\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\)

  2. One piece and its distance

    WhyA piece at angle \(\theta\) (from \(+x\)) spans arc length \(r\,d\theta\). Every piece is exactly \(r\) from the center.

    \(\displaystyle dq = \lambda r\,d\theta,\) \(\displaystyle \text{distance}\) \(\displaystyle = r\)

  3. Size of one piece's field

    \(\displaystyle dE = \dfrac{k\,dq}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\lambda\,d\theta}{r}\)

  4. Direction and components

    WhyThe piece sits at \((r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\). Away from it, through the center, is the direction \((-\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)\).

    \(\displaystyle dE_x\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{k\lambda}{r}\cos\theta\,d\theta,\) \(\displaystyle dE_y\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{k\lambda}{r}\sin\theta\,d\theta\)

  5. Set up and integrate (Q6)

    WhyThe semicircle runs from \(\theta = -\pi/2\) (bottom) to \(+\pi/2\) (top). \(\int\cos = 2\) over that range; \(\int\sin = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{k\lambda}{r}\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\,d\theta\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{2k\lambda}{r},\) \(\displaystyle E_y\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

    MeansThe top and bottom halves cancel in \(y\), as symmetry says. The field points \(-x\), away from the arc.

  6. Numbers

    \(\displaystyle |E|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(9.55\times10^{-5})}{0.050}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.43\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  7. Cancel it with a point charge (Q7)

    WhyThe arc's field at the origin points \(-x\). To cancel it, the new charge must make a field pointing \(+x\) at the origin. The new charge is at \((-r, 0)\), to the left; a field pointing right is pointing away from it.

    Away from the charge means the charge is positive.
    \(\displaystyle \text{Size: } \dfrac{kq}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow q\) \(\displaystyle = 2\lambda r\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2Q}{\pi}\)
λ ≈ 95 μC/m E = −2kλ/r (−x) Q7: a positive charge
Two half-rings of opposite charge
Fall 2015, Questions 6–7
A circle of radius \(R\) is made of two curved rods: the top half carries \(+q\) and the bottom half \(-q\). (Q6) Which way does \(\vec E\) point at the center? (Q7) Which integral gives \(E_x\) from the top half, with \(\theta\) measured from the \(y\)-axis?

  1. Top half alone

    WhyPositive charge: its field at the center points away from it. The top half is above the center, so away is down.

    \(\displaystyle \vec E_{\text{top}}\): \(\displaystyle -y\)

  2. Bottom half alone

    WhyNegative charge: its field points toward it. The bottom half is below the center, so toward is down.

    \(\displaystyle \vec E_{\text{bottom}}\): \(\displaystyle -y\)

  3. Add (Q6)

    WhyBoth point down, so they add.

    Net field at the center: \(\displaystyle -y\).

  4. Charge per length on the top half (Q7)

    WhyHalf circumference \(\pi R\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = \dfrac{q}{\pi R},\) \(\displaystyle dq\) \(\displaystyle = \lambda R\,d\theta\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q}{\pi}\,d\theta\)

  5. The x-part of one piece

    WhyWith \(\theta\) measured from the \(y\)-axis, the sideways (\(x\)) part of a piece's field carries \(\sin\theta\); the \(y\)-part carries \(\cos\theta\).

    \(\displaystyle dE_x = \dfrac{k\,dq}{R^2}\sin\theta\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq\sin\theta\,d\theta}{\pi R^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{kq\sin\theta\,d\theta}{\pi R^2}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

    MeansIt integrates to zero, as symmetry demands. Distractors omit the \(\pi\) (wrong \(\lambda\)) or use \(\cos\theta\) (the \(y\)-part).

Q6: −y Q7: ∫ kq sinθ dθ/(πR²)
Arcs with numbers
Homework 2, Problems 3 and 4
Problem 3: an arc of radius \(R = 1.1\ \mathrm{m}\) with opening angle \(\theta_0 = 53^\circ\), symmetric about the \(y\)-axis, carries \(\lambda = -29.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\). Problem 4: a semicircle of radius \(R = 17.4\ \mathrm{cm}\) carries \(Q = 34.7\ \mathrm{nC}\). Find the field magnitude at the center of each.

  1. Problem 3: same set-up as the semicircle, narrower limits

    WhyMeasure \(\theta\) from the symmetry axis. The arc runs from \(-\theta_0/2\) to \(+\theta_0/2\). The sideways parts cancel; the along-axis parts add with \(\cos\theta\).

    \(\displaystyle |E|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k|\lambda|}{R}\displaystyle\int_{-\theta_0/2}^{\theta_0/2}\cos\theta\,d\theta\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2k|\lambda|}{R}\sin\dfrac{\theta_0}{2}\)

  2. Problem 3: numbers

    Why\(\theta_0/2 = 26.5^\circ\), \(\sin 26.5^\circ = 0.4462\).

    \(\displaystyle |E|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(29.5\times10^{-6})}{1.1}(0.4462)\) \(\displaystyle = 2.15\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

    Means\(\lambda \lt 0\), so the field points toward the arc. Whether that is \(+y\) or \(-y\) depends on where the figure puts the arc.

  3. Problem 4: the full semicircle

    WhyNow the angle is \(\pi\), so \(\sin(\pi/2) = 1\), and \(\lambda = Q/(\pi R)\).

    \(\displaystyle |E| = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{R}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2kQ}{\pi R^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle |E|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(34.7\times10^{-9})}{\pi(0.174)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{623.9}{0.09511}\) \(\displaystyle = 6560\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

    MeansAlong the symmetry axis, away from the (positive) arc.

P3: 2.15×10⁵ N/C P4: 6.56×10³ N/C
What each letter means
\(\theta_0\)
the total opening angle of the arc, in radians or degrees
\(R\)
the radius of the arc, in m (every element is this far from the center)
\(\lambda\)
the arc's charge per length, C/m; \(|\lambda|\) means use its size and get the direction from the sign
\(\theta\)
the angle of a charge element measured from the arc's symmetry axis
\(E_y\)
the field at the center along the symmetry axis; the perpendicular part cancels by symmetry
\(2k|\lambda|/R\)
the semicircle result (\(\theta_0 = 180^\circ\), \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\))
N/C
Trap · \(dq\) on an arc

Lecture 2 clicker: the charge in an element \(d\theta\) of a half ring with total charge \(Q\) is \(dq = \dfrac{Q}{\pi}\,d\theta\), not \(Q\,d\theta\) and not \(\dfrac{Q}{2\pi}\,d\theta\) (that is a full ring). Then \(dE_y\) \(= \dfrac{kQ\,d\theta}{\pi R^2}\sin\theta\) (for \(\theta\) from the \(x\)-axis), and integrating \(0\) to \(\pi\) gives \(E = \dfrac{2kQ}{\pi R^2}\) along the axis.

Disk of charge, and the infinite sheet limit
Lecture 2, Example 2.5 · used in Chapters 6 and 8
A disk of radius \(a\) carries uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\). Find the field at height \(h\) on its axis, then let the disk become infinite.

  1. Cut the disk into rings

    WhyA ring of radius \(r\) and width \(dr\), unrolled, is a thin strip: length \(2\pi r\), width \(dr\).

    \(\displaystyle dA = 2\pi r\,dr,\) \(\displaystyle dq\) \(\displaystyle = \sigma\,dA\) \(\displaystyle = 2\pi\sigma r\,dr\)

  2. Use the ring's result for one ring

    WhyReplace \(Q\) by \(dq\) and \(R\) by \(r\) in \(E_z = kQh/(h^2+R^2)^{3/2}\).

    \(\displaystyle dE\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k\,(2\pi\sigma r\,dr)\,h}{(h^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\)

  3. Add all the rings

    Why\(r\) from 0 (center) to \(a\) (edge). Constants out front.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \pi k\sigma h\displaystyle\int_0^a \frac{2r\,dr}{(h^2+r^2)^{3/2}}\)

  4. Substitute u = h² + r²

    Why\(du = 2r\,dr\) is exactly the top. Limits: \(u = h^2\) to \(u = h^2 + a^2\).

    \(\displaystyle \int u^{-3/2}\,du\) \(\displaystyle = -2u^{-1/2}\)
    \(\displaystyle \Big[-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt u}\Big]_{h^2}^{h^2+a^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac2h - \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{h^2+a^2}}\)

  5. Multiply out

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \pi k\sigma h\left(\dfrac2h - \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{h^2+a^2}}\right)\) \(\displaystyle = 2\pi k\sigma\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+a^2}}\right)\)

  6. Rewrite with ε₀

    Why\(2\pi k = 2\pi/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\) \(= 1/(2\varepsilon_0)\).

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+a^2}}\right)\)

  7. Let the disk become infinite

    WhyAs \(a \to \infty\) (or close to the disk, \(h \ll a\)), the fraction \(h/\sqrt{h^2+a^2} \to 0\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansThe infinite-sheet field: the same at every distance, perpendicular to the sheet, away from positive \(\sigma\) on both sides. Parallel-plate capacitors (Chapter 8) and multi-sheet problems (Chapter 6) are built from this.

sheet: E = σ/2ε₀
What each letter means
\(\sigma\)
surface charge density: charge per unit area on a sheet or surface, in C/m² (\(\sigma = Q/A\) when uniform)
\(a\)
the outer radius of the disk, in m
\(r,\ dr\)
the radius of one thin ring inside the disk and its tiny width; \(2\pi r\,dr\) is the ring's area, so \(dq = \sigma\,2\pi r\,dr\)
\(h\)
the distance from the disk's center along its axis to the field point, in m
\(E\)
the field on the axis, in N/C, pointing away from a positive disk
\(u\)
the substitution \(u = h^2 + r^2\) that makes the integral doable
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

5.6 Electric field lines

Rules for reading and drawing field lines
  • Lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or at infinity). The number of lines leaving or entering a charge is proportional to \(|Q|\).
  • The tangent to a line gives the direction of \(\vec E\); lines never cross (the field has one direction at each point).
  • The density of lines (lines per unit area crossing perpendicular) is proportional to \(|E|\). For a point charge the lines spread over a sphere of area \(4\pi r^2\), so density and \(E\) both fall as \(1/r^2\).
  • Lines leave a conductor's surface perpendicular to it (Chapter 7).
Why field lines carry the information they do

A field line is a path that always follows the local direction of \(\vec E\). Since the field at each point has one direction, two lines can never cross (they would need two directions at the crossing point). Lines begin on positive charges because that is where \(\vec E\) points away from, and end on negative charges for the same reason.

The density rule comes from a choice plus the inverse square. Choose to draw a number of lines proportional to the charge. Around a lone point charge those lines spread radially; at distance \(r\) they pass through a sphere of area \(4\pi r^2\), so the number of lines per unit area falls as \(1/r^2\), exactly like \(E\). Because the field of many charges is the sum of point-charge fields, the same proportionality survives for any picture: crowded lines mean strong field, sparse lines mean weak field. This is also the intuition behind flux in Chapter 6, which is nothing but a count of lines through a surface.

Reading a field-line picture
Lecture 3 checkpoints
A picture shows field lines around two charges, points A and B, and a "red circle" drawn around part of the picture. Compare the charges, compare the field at A and B, and find the net charge inside the circle.

  1. Compare the charges by counting lines

    WhyThe number of lines touching a charge is proportional to its size.

    More lines on charge 1 than on charge 2, so \(\displaystyle |Q_1| \gt |Q_2|\).

  2. Find the signs from where lines go

    WhyLines leave positive charges and end on negative charges.

    Lines run from one charge into the other, so the signs are opposite. Like signs would have lines curving away from each other, never connecting.

  3. Compare field strengths by spacing

    WhyCrowded lines mean a strong field; sparse lines mean a weak one.

    A is next to a charge where lines bunch: \(\displaystyle |E_A| \gt |E_B|\).

  4. Net charge inside a closed curve

    WhyCount lines leaving minus lines entering. Net outward lines mean net positive charge inside.

    More leave the red circle than enter, so the net charge inside is positive. But some lines do enter and end inside, so a negative charge must also be inside. The matching choice is \(\displaystyle -Q\) and \(\displaystyle +2Q\).

Motion in a field. A charge released from rest in a field accelerates along the line (positive) or opposite to it (negative). If the lines are getting denser in the direction of motion, the force grows, so it is not constant acceleration (Lecture 3 clicker: "lines getting denser… force getting stronger!"). Only in a uniform field (parallel, evenly spaced lines) is the motion constant-acceleration kinematics: \(a = qE/m\).

An electron released in a uniform field
Lecture 3 clicker · the standard constant-acceleration problem
An electron starts from rest in a uniform field \(E = 2.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N/C}\) and moves \(1.0\ \mathrm{cm}\). Find its acceleration, its final speed, and how long it takes. (\(m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}\), \(e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\).)

  1. Force on the electron

    Why\(\vec F = q\vec E\) with \(q = -e\): the size is \(eE\), the direction opposite to \(\vec E\).

    \(\displaystyle F = eE\) \(\displaystyle = (1.60\times10^{-19})(2.0\times10^{3})\) \(\displaystyle = 3.2\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N}\)

  2. Is gravity worth including?

    WhyCompare with the weight \(mg\).

    \(\displaystyle mg = (9.11\times10^{-31})(9.8)\) \(\displaystyle = 8.9\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{N}\)

    MeansSmaller by a factor of about \(10^{13}\). Ignore it.

  3. Acceleration

    WhyNewton's second law, \(a = F/m\). The field is uniform, so \(a\) is constant.

    \(\displaystyle a = \dfrac{eE}{m}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{3.2\times10^{-16}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.51\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\)

  4. Final speed

    WhyConstant acceleration from rest over a distance \(d\): \(v^2 = 2ad\). Convert \(1.0\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.010\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle v = \sqrt{2ad}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{2(3.51\times10^{14})(0.010)}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.65\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}\)

  5. Time

    WhyFrom rest, \(v = at\).

    \(\displaystyle t = \dfrac{v}{a}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2.65\times10^{6}}{3.51\times10^{14}}\) \(\displaystyle = 7.5\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s}\)

    MeansTwo thousand kilometers per second in a few nanoseconds: why electron beams are easy to make.

a = 3.51×10¹⁴ m/s² v = 2.65×10⁶ m/s
What each letter means
\(a\)
acceleration of the charge, in m/s²
\(q\)
the charge of the particle, in C, with its sign
\(E\)
the field magnitude where the particle is, in N/C
\(m\)
the particle's mass, in kg (proton \(1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}\), electron \(9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}\))

5.7 Electric dipoles

Dipole moment, torque, and energy

Two charges \(\pm q\) separated by \(\vec d\): dipole moment \(\vec p = q\vec d\), pointing from \(-q\) to \(+q\) (Lecture 2: "points from negative to positive, opposite the electric field inside the dipole"). Units C·m. Water: \(6.2\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\,m}\).

\[ \vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E,\quad |\tau| = pE\sin\theta \qquad\qquad U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E = -pE\cos\theta \]
What each letter means
\(\vec p,\ p\)
the dipole moment vector and its magnitude \(qd\), in C·m, pointing from \(-q\) to \(+q\)
\(q\)
the size of each of the two charges, in C
\(\vec d\)
the displacement from \(-q\) to \(+q\), in m
\(\vec E,\ E\)
the external field the dipole sits in and its magnitude, N/C
\(\vec\tau,\ |\tau|\)
the torque on the dipole and its size, in N·m
\(\theta\)
the angle between \(\vec p\) and \(\vec E\)
\(U\)
the potential energy of the dipole, in J: lowest (\(-pE\)) when aligned, highest (\(+pE\)) when anti-aligned
\(\times,\ \cdot\)
cross product (magnitude \(pE\sin\theta\)) and dot product (\(pE\cos\theta\))

\(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec p\) and \(\vec E\). In a uniform field the net force on a dipole is zero (the \(+q\) and \(-q\) forces cancel); only the torque acts, and it rotates \(\vec p\) toward alignment with \(\vec E\).

Why a dipole turns but does not move, and where the energy formula comes from

In a uniform field the \(+q\) end is pushed along \(\vec E\) with force \(qE\) and the \(-q\) end is pushed against \(\vec E\) with the same \(qE\). Equal and opposite forces cancel, so the dipole as a whole is not accelerated anywhere. But the two forces act at different points, a distance \(d\) apart, so together they form a couple that twists the dipole. The lever arm of each force is \((d/2)\sin\theta\), so the torque is \(2\cdot qE\cdot(d/2)\sin\theta\) \(= pE\sin\theta\), largest when the dipole is broadside to the field and zero when it is lined up. The twist always acts to swing \(\vec p\) toward \(\vec E\).

Rotating the dipole against that torque takes work, and the work is stored as potential energy. Integrating \(\tau\,d\theta = pE\sin\theta\,d\theta\) gives \(U = -pE\cos\theta + \text{constant}\); choosing \(U = 0\) at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) drops the constant. Aligned (\(\theta = 0\)) is the bottom of the energy valley, \(-pE\); anti-aligned is the top, \(+pE\). A dipole released at any other angle swings toward alignment, just as a compass needle swings north.

In a non-uniform field the two ends sit in fields of different strength, the forces no longer cancel, and the dipole is pulled toward the stronger-field region. That net force is why neutral dust sticks to a charged comb and why the balloon sticks to the wall.

Orientation of \(\vec p\) relative to \(\vec E\)\(\theta\)Torque\(U\)Stability
aligned (\(+\) downstream of \(-\))00\(-pE\) (minimum)stable equilibrium
perpendicular90°\(pE\) (maximum)0 (smallest magnitude)not equilibrium
anti-aligned180°0\(+pE\) (maximum)unstable equilibrium

Lecture 2's four-orientation clickers use this table directly: orientations (a) and (b) are along the field (torque zero); the one with \(+\) on the downstream side has the lowest \(U\); the perpendicular ones (c) and (d) have the smallest \(|U|\) (zero) and the largest torque; the net force is zero in all four because the field is uniform.

Salt molecule in a field
Lecture 2, Example 2.6
An NaCl molecule has charges \(\pm e\) separated by \(500\ \mathrm{pm}\). It sits in a uniform field \(E = 10\ \mathrm{N/C}\) with its dipole moment at \(\theta = 20^\circ\) from \(\vec E\). Find \(p\), the torque, and the potential energy.

  1. Dipole moment

    Why\(p = qd\). "p" (pico) means \(10^{-12}\), so \(500\ \mathrm{pm}\) \(= 5.00\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle p\) \(\displaystyle = (1.60\times10^{-19})(5.00\times10^{-10})\) \(\displaystyle = 8.0\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{C\,m}\)

  2. Torque

    Why\(\tau = pE\sin\theta\): largest at 90°, zero when aligned.

    \(\displaystyle \tau\) \(\displaystyle = (8.0\times10^{-29})(10)\sin20^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = (8.0\times10^{-28})(0.342)\) \(\displaystyle = 2.7\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{N\,m}\)

    MeansIt turns \(\vec p\) toward \(\vec E\).

  3. Potential energy

    Why\(U = -pE\cos\theta\), with \(U = 0\) chosen at 90°.

    \(\displaystyle U\) \(\displaystyle = -(8.0\times10^{-29})(10)\cos20^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = -(8.0\times10^{-28})(0.940)\) \(\displaystyle = -7.5\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative because the dipole is mostly lined up with the field, near the bottom of its energy valley.

p = 8.0×10⁻²⁹ C·m τ = 2.7×10⁻²⁸ N·m U = −7.5×10⁻²⁸ J
N·m

Torque and energy versus orientation

The NaCl dipole from Lecture 2 (p = 8.0×10⁻²⁹ C·m) in E = 10 N/C. θ is the angle from p to E. Torque is largest at 90°, zero at 0° and 180°; energy is lowest when p points along E.

Chapter 6 · Lecture Units 3 and 4 · HW 3 and 4

Electric Flux and Gauss's Law

On Exam 1: electric flux (6.1), 2 of 28 · Gauss's law (6.2–6.5), 4 of 28.

OpenStax 6.1 Electric flux · 6.2 Explaining Gauss's law · 6.3 Applying Gauss's law · 6.4 Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium

Lecture 3 gives the whole motivation in one line: "What's the point of all this flux stuff? To introduce Gauss's law so we can find the E field without doing an integral." Gauss's law is always true; it is useful for finding \(E\) only when symmetry lets you pull \(E\) out of the integral. Exam questions test both halves: the "always true" half with flux-counting questions, the "useful" half with spheres, cylinders, and planes.

The chapter in plain words

Flux measures how much electric field passes through a surface, like the amount of rain passing through a hoop.

Gauss's law says: for any closed surface, the total outward flux equals the charge inside divided by \(\varepsilon_0\). Charges outside do not change the total.

The payoff: when the charge has a symmetric shape (a sphere, a long cylinder, a flat sheet), you can pick a surface on which \(E\) is the same everywhere. Then Gauss's law turns into "\(E\) times area \(=\) charge inside \(/\varepsilon_0\)", and you can solve for \(E\) with one division instead of an integral.

6.1 Electric flux

The picture to keep. Rain falls straight down. Hold a hoop flat and it catches the most rain; tilt it and it catches less; hold it vertical and none passes through, even though the rain is unchanged. The amount of rain through the hoop depends on the rain rate, the hoop's area, and the angle. Electric flux is the same idea with field lines instead of raindrops: it measures how much field "passes through" a surface. The angle enters through the surface's normal (the direction perpendicular to the surface), because a surface catches the component of the field along its normal and ignores the component sliding along it.

Flux = how much field passes through a surface
\[ \Phi_E = \int_S \vec E\cdot d\vec A \qquad\text{(uniform field, flat surface: } \Phi_E = EA\cos\theta) \]
What each letter means
\(\Phi_E\)
the electric flux through the surface, in N·m²/C: a count of how much field passes through
\(\int_S\)
add up over every patch of the surface \(S\)
\(\vec E\)
the electric field vector: the force per coulomb that a positive test charge would feel at that point, in N/C (= V/m)
\(d\vec A\)
a tiny patch of the surface, treated as a vector: its size is the patch area \(dA\) (m²) and it points along the patch's normal (perpendicular to the surface; outward for a closed surface)
\(E,\ A\)
for a uniform field and a flat surface: the field magnitude (N/C) and the total area (m²)
\(\theta\)
the angle between \(\vec E\) and the surface's normal (not the surface itself); \(\cos\theta = 1\) when the field pokes straight through, 0 when it skims along

\(d\vec A\) is a vector normal (perpendicular) to the surface element with magnitude \(dA\). \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec E\) and the normal, not the angle between \(\vec E\) and the surface. Units: N·m²/C. Picture: flux counts field lines crossing the surface. Tilting the surface reduces the count; a surface parallel to the field catches nothing.

Reading the flux formula one piece at a time

  1. Cut the surface into tiny patches

    WhyEach patch is small enough to be flat, and the field is the same all over it.

  2. Give each patch an arrow: the area vector

    WhyThe arrow \(d\vec A\) points straight out of the patch (along its normal). Its length is the patch area \(dA\). For a closed surface, it always points outward.

  3. Flux through one patch: a dot product

    WhyOnly the part of \(\vec E\) that goes straight through the patch counts. The dot product picks out exactly that part.

    \(\displaystyle d\Phi = \vec E\cdot d\vec A\) \(\displaystyle = E\,dA\cos\theta\)

    Means\(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec E\) and the patch's normal. Straight through: \(\theta = 0\), full flux. Skimming along: \(\theta = 90^\circ\), zero flux. Going in against the normal: \(\theta \gt 90^\circ\), negative flux.

  4. Add up every patch

    WhyThe integral sign just means "add the flux of every patch."

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_E = \int_S \vec E\cdot d\vec A\)

  5. The shortcut you will use most

    WhyIf \(\vec E\) is uniform and the surface is flat, every patch gives the same \(E\,dA\cos\theta\), so the sum is that times the total area.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_E = EA\cos\theta\)
Flux through a tilted plate
Lecture 3, Example 3.1
A uniform field \(E = 12\ \mathrm{N/C}\) points to the right. A square plate \(3\ \mathrm{cm}\) on a side is tilted so that the plate itself makes \(30^\circ\) with the field. Find the flux through the plate.

  1. Convert the side length to meters

    WhyFlux is in N·m²/C, so the area must be in m².

    \(\displaystyle 3\ \mathrm{cm}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.03\ \mathrm{m}\)

  2. Area of the plate

    WhyA square: side times side.

    \(\displaystyle A = (0.03)(0.03)\) \(\displaystyle = 9\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}\)

  3. Find the angle that goes into the formula

    WhyThe formula needs the angle between \(\vec E\) and the plate's normal. The normal is \(90^\circ\) away from the plate.

    \(\displaystyle \theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = 60^\circ\)

    MeansThis is the step most people get wrong.

  4. Cosine of that angle

    \(\displaystyle \cos60^\circ = 0.5\)

  5. Multiply

    Why\(\Phi = EA\cos\theta\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi = (12)(9\times10^{-4})(0.5)\) \(\displaystyle = 5.4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C}\)

The classic error: using \(\cos30^\circ\) gives \(0.0094\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C}\). If a problem gives the angle between the field and the plate itself, subtract it from \(90^\circ\) first.

Φ = 0.0054 N·m²/C
Explore · Flux
Flux through a tilted square

θ is the angle between the field and the surface's normal. At θ = 0 the square faces the field and catches the most lines; at 90° it is edge-on and catches none.

Sign of flux on a closed surface

For a closed surface, \(d\vec A\) always points outward.

  • Field leaving the surface: \(\theta \lt 90^\circ\), positive flux.
  • Field entering the surface: \(\theta \gt 90^\circ\), negative flux.
  • Field skimming along a face: \(\theta = 90^\circ\), zero flux.

In a uniform field, every line that enters a closed surface also leaves it, so the net flux through any closed surface in a uniform field is zero. The wedge below checks this face by face.

Flux through every face of a closed wedge
Lecture 3, wedge example (sizes chosen to make the arithmetic visible)
A closed wedge sits in a uniform field \(\vec E = E\,\hat x\). Its left face (1) is at \(x = 0\) with height \(a\); its top face (2) is flat; its right face (3) is at \(x = a\) with height \(2a\); its bottom face (4) is slanted at \(45^\circ\). Every face has depth \(w\) into the page. Find the flux through each face and the total.

  1. Face 1 (left, at x = 0)

    WhyIts outward normal points in \(-x\), exactly opposite to \(\vec E\): \(\theta = 180^\circ\), \(\cos\theta = -1\). Its area is height times depth.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_1 = E\,(a w)\cos180^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = -Eaw\)

    MeansNegative: the field goes in here.

  2. Face 2 (top)

    WhyIts normal points up (\(+z\)), perpendicular to \(\vec E\): \(\cos90^\circ = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_2 = 0\)

    MeansThe field skims along the top.

  3. Face 3 (right, at x = a)

    WhyIts normal points in \(+x\), along \(\vec E\): \(\cos0 = 1\). This face is \(2a\) tall.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_3 = E\,(2a\,w)(1)\) \(\displaystyle = +2Eaw\)

    MeansPositive: the field comes out here.

  4. Face 4 (slanted)

    WhyIts area is (slant length)\(\times w\). The slant runs \(a\) across and \(a\) down, so its length is \(a\sqrt2\). Its outward normal points down and to the left, \(135^\circ\) from \(+x\): \(\cos135^\circ = -1/\sqrt2\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_4\) \(\displaystyle = E\,(a\sqrt2\,w)\left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\) \(\displaystyle = -Eaw\)

    MeansThe \(\sqrt2\) in the area and the \(1/\sqrt2\) in the cosine cancel. A tilted face catches the same flux as its shadow seen along the field, which is \(a\) tall.

  5. Front and back faces

    WhyTheir normals point along \(\pm y\), perpendicular to \(\vec E\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{front}}\) \(\displaystyle = \Phi_{\text{back}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

  6. Add them all

    WhyThe net flux is the sum over every face of the closed surface.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{net}}\) \(\displaystyle = -Eaw + 0 + 2Eaw - Eaw + 0 + 0\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

    MeansZero, as it must be: the wedge holds no charge. What enters through faces 1 and 4 leaves through face 3.

Φ₁ = −Eaw Φ₂ = 0 Φ₃ = +2Eaw Φ₄ = −Eaw net = 0
Flux through a cylinder around a charged rod
Lecture 3 checkpoint · Homework 3, Problem 1
An infinite rod with charge per length \(\lambda\) runs along the axis of a closed cylinder of radius \(s\) and length \(L\). On the curved side, the rod's field has size \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 s)\) and points straight out. Find the total flux through the closed cylinder.

  1. Split the closed surface into its three pieces

    WhyA closed cylinder = curved side + top cap + bottom cap. Find the flux of each, then add.

  2. The two flat caps

    WhyTheir normals point along the axis. The field points away from the axis, so it lies along the caps: \(\theta = 90^\circ\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{caps}} = 0\)

  3. The curved side: the angle

    WhyOn the side, the normal points straight out from the axis, the same direction as \(\vec E\): \(\theta = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle \vec E\cdot d\vec A\) \(\displaystyle = E\,dA\)

  4. The curved side: E is the same everywhere on it

    WhyEvery point of the side is the same distance \(s\) from the rod, so \(E\) has the same value all over it and comes out of the sum.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{side}}\) \(\displaystyle = E\cdot(\text{side area})\) \(\displaystyle = E\,(2\pi sL)\)

    MeansThe side, unrolled, is a rectangle: height \(L\), width equal to the circumference \(2\pi s\).

  5. Put in the field of the rod

    \(\displaystyle \Phi\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 s}\cdot 2\pi sL\)

  6. Cancel

    WhyThe \(2\pi\) cancels and the radius \(s\) cancels.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0}\)

    Means\(\lambda L\) is exactly the charge inside the cylinder. The flux depends only on the enclosed charge: this is Gauss's law, found by hand.

Two cylinders. Cylinder 1 has radius \(s\), length \(L\); cylinder 2 has radius \(2s\), length \(L/2\). The radius does not matter, and cylinder 2 encloses half as much rod, so \(\Phi_1 = 2\Phi_2\).

Φ = λL/ε₀
What each letter means
\(\Phi\)
the flux through the closed cylinder, N·m²/C
\(E\)
magnitude of the electric field, in N/C (the same unit as V/m)
\(s\)
the radius of the cylinder (the perpendicular distance from the rod), in m; it cancels
\(L\)
the length of the cylinder, in m; \(2\pi sL\) is the area of its curved side
\(\lambda\)
linear charge density: charge per unit length along a line, rod, or ring, in C/m (\(\lambda = Q/L\) when uniform)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

6.2 Gauss's law

Gauss's law
\[ \oint_S \vec E\cdot d\vec A = \frac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0} \]
What each letter means
\(\oint\)
integral over a closed surface (one with an inside and an outside, like a balloon); the circle on the sign is what marks it as closed
\(S\)
the closed surface you chose (the "Gaussian surface"); it is imaginary, not a physical object
\(\vec E\)
the electric field vector: the force per coulomb that a positive test charge would feel at that point, in N/C (= V/m)
\(d\vec A\)
a tiny patch of the surface, treated as a vector: its size is the patch area \(dA\) (m²) and it points along the patch's normal (perpendicular to the surface; outward for a closed surface)
\(\vec E\cdot d\vec A\)
the flux through one patch: field magnitude × patch area × cosine of the angle between them
\(Q_{\text{enc}}\)
the net charge enclosed inside the Gaussian surface, in C (count signs; charge outside the surface does not count)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

The net flux through any closed surface equals the total charge inside divided by \(\varepsilon_0\). Charges outside the surface contribute field on the surface but zero net flux (their lines enter and leave). Where the charge sits inside does not matter, and the surface's shape does not matter.

Check with a point charge and a sphere: \(E = kq/R^2\) everywhere on the sphere, \(A = 4\pi R^2\), so \(\Phi\) \(= \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2}\,4\pi R^2\) \(= q/\varepsilon_0\). Doubling the sphere's radius changes \(E\) by \(1/4\) and \(A\) by \(4\): flux unchanged (Lecture 3 clicker).

In plain words

Charges are the sources and sinks of field lines. Every positive charge sprouts a fixed number of lines (proportional to its charge) and every negative charge swallows a fixed number. Any closed surface, whatever its shape, is crossed by a line once for each line that starts inside it and does not end inside it. Lines from outside charges pass through in one side and out the other and contribute nothing on net. So counting the net lines crossing a closed surface is the same as counting the charge inside. Gauss's law is that counting rule written with an integral, and the \(1/\varepsilon_0\) is just the conversion between "number of lines" and coulombs. The next paragraphs make this exact.

Why the flux depends only on the enclosed charge

The sphere check above is a special case. The general statement needs three ideas. Exam questions test each one separately, so each gets its own step.

  1. Idea 1: flux through one patch, for a charge inside

    WhyTake a small patch at distance \(r\) from a point charge \(q\), tilted by \(\theta\). The field there is \(kq/r^2\), radial.

    \(\displaystyle d\Phi = E\,dA\cos\theta\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}\,dA\cos\theta\) \(\displaystyle = kq\cdot\dfrac{dA\cos\theta}{r^2}\)

  2. Recognize the solid angle

    Why\(dA\cos\theta\) is the patch's shadow on a sphere of radius \(r\) (figure). Dividing by \(r^2\) gives the patch's share of all directions, called the solid angle \(d\Omega\).

    \(\displaystyle d\Omega\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{dA\cos\theta}{r^2} \quad\Rightarrow\) \(\displaystyle d\Phi\) \(\displaystyle = kq\,d\Omega\)

    MeansFar patches are bigger but weaker in field; tilted patches catch less. Both effects are inside dΩ.

  3. Add up the whole closed surface

    WhyA closed surface around the charge covers every direction exactly once. All directions together make \(4\pi\) (the area of a sphere of radius 1).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi = kq\oint d\Omega\) \(\displaystyle = kq\cdot4\pi\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot4\pi\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansThis works for a sphere, a blob, a cube, anything, and wherever the charge sits inside.

  4. Idea 2: a charge outside the surface

    WhyNow each narrow cone of directions from the charge either misses the surface or crosses it twice: once going in, once coming out. Both crossings cover the same \(d\Omega\).

    \(\displaystyle d\Phi_{\text{in}}\) \(\displaystyle = -kq\,d\Omega,\) \(\displaystyle d\Phi_{\text{out}}\) \(\displaystyle = +kq\,d\Omega\)

    MeansThey cancel in pairs. The net flux from an outside charge is zero. The field on the surface is not zero; only its net flux is.

  5. Idea 3: many charges, by superposition

    WhyThe field of many charges is the sum of their fields, so the flux is the sum of their fluxes: \(q_i/\varepsilon_0\) for each one inside, \(0\) for each one outside.

    \(\displaystyle \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q_1 + q_2 + \cdots\ (\text{inside only})}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansThat is Gauss's law.

What each letter means
\(d\Phi\)
the tiny flux through one patch, N·m²/C
\(dA\)
the area of the patch, m²
\(r\)
the distance from the charge to the patch, m
\(\theta\)
the angle between the patch's normal and the line from the charge (the radial direction)
\(d\Omega\)
the solid angle of the patch as seen from the charge: the "cone of directions" it fills; all directions together make \(4\pi\)
\(q\)
the enclosed point charge, C
Trap · flux vs. field

Gauss's law constrains the total flux, not the field at a point. In Spring 2014 Q8–9 the outside charge \(q_1\) changes the line density on the near and far patches (\(n_1 \gt n_2\)) while leaving the net flux at \(q_2/\varepsilon_0\). "The flux is the same" never means "the field is the same."

Flux-counting questions (always true, no symmetry needed)

Moving a charge inside a closed surface
Lecture 3 checkpoint
A charge \(+Q\) sits inside a closed spherical shell. It is moved to the left, closer to patch A and farther from patch B. What happens to (a) the flux through A, (b) the flux through B, (c) the total flux, (d) the flux through the right half of the surface?

  1. Total flux: count the charge inside

    WhyThe charge is still inside, and nothing else is. Gauss's law does not care where inside it sits.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{total}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\quad\text{(unchanged)}\)

  2. Patch A (now closer)

    WhyThe field at A is \(kQ/r^2\) with a smaller \(r\): stronger. More lines cross A.

    \(\displaystyle d\Phi_A\) increases.

  3. Patch B (now farther)

    WhyLarger \(r\), weaker field, fewer lines.

    \(\displaystyle d\Phi_B\) decreases.

  4. Right half of the surface

    WhyThe total number of lines is fixed at \(Q/\varepsilon_0\). If more of them now go through the left half, fewer go through the right half.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{right}}\) decreases.
A: up B: down total: unchanged right half: down
A charge outside the surface: net flux vs. field
Spring 2014, Questions 8–9
A spherical Gaussian surface surrounds \(q_2 = -6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). A second charge \(q_1 = +3\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) sits outside it, to the left. (Q8) What is the net flux through the sphere? (Q9) Compare the density of field lines \(n_1\) at the patch nearest \(q_1\) with \(n_2\) at the far patch.

  1. Which charges are enclosed?

    WhyOnly \(q_2\) is inside the sphere. \(q_1\) is outside, and an outside charge adds zero net flux.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = q_2\) \(\displaystyle = -6\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\)

  2. Divide by ε₀

    \(\displaystyle \Phi\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-6\times10^{-6}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}\) \(\displaystyle = -6.8\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C}\)

    MeansNegative: the field of a negative charge points inward, so more flux goes in than out.

  3. Field at the near patch (left side)

    Why\(q_1\) is to the left and positive: its field points away from it, to the right (\(+x\)). \(q_2\) is negative: its field points toward it, which from the left side is also to the right.

    Both fields point \(\displaystyle +x\): they add.

  4. Field at the far patch (right side)

    Why\(q_1\)'s field still points right. \(q_2\)'s field points toward \(q_2\), which from the right side is to the left.

    The two fields oppose: they partly cancel.

  5. Compare the line densities

    WhyLine density is proportional to the field strength.

    \(\displaystyle n_1 \gt n_2\)

    MeansThe net flux is fixed by \(q_2\) alone, but where the lines cross the surface depends on every charge nearby.

Φ = −6.8×10⁵ N·m²/C n₁ > n₂
A negative charge off-center in a cylinder
Fall 2018, Questions 5–6
A charge \(-q\) sits off-center inside a closed cylinder of length \(L\) and radius \(R\), close to end A. (Q5) What is the net flux? (Q6) What is the sign of the flux through end A?

  1. Net flux

    WhyOnly \(-q\) is inside. Its position, \(L\), and \(R\) do not matter.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{net}}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  2. Direction of the field at end A

    WhyThe field of a negative charge points toward the charge. At end A the outward normal points away from the cylinder, but the field points back in, toward \(-q\).

    \(\displaystyle \theta \gt 90^\circ\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \vec E\cdot d\vec A \lt 0\)

  3. Sign of the flux through A

    WhyEvery patch of end A has negative flux, so the sum is negative.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_A \lt 0\)

    MeansThe same is true for every piece of this surface: a lone negative charge inside gives negative flux everywhere.

Φnet = −q/ε₀ ΦA < 0
Sphere, blob, and cube
Fall 2015, Question 26
A sphere, an irregular blob, and a cube each enclose the same charge \(Q\). Rank the fluxes through them.

  1. Apply Gauss's law to each

    WhyEach closed surface encloses \(Q\). The shape never enters Gauss's law.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{sphere}}\) \(\displaystyle = \Phi_{\text{blob}}\) \(\displaystyle = \Phi_{\text{cube}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansSee the sixteen-line figure above: the same lines cross all three shapes.

all equal: Q/ε₀
A box around a neutral conducting slab
Fall 2015, Question 21
A Gaussian box encloses a whole neutral conducting slab. A second, identical box encloses a piece of a charged sheet. Which box has more flux?

  1. Charge inside the first box

    WhyThe slab is neutral: its two faces carry equal and opposite charge, \(\sigma_L = -\sigma_R\).

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = (\sigma_L + \sigma_R)A\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \Phi\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

  2. Charge inside the second box

    WhyIt encloses \(\sigma A\) of the sheet.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  3. Compare

    The box around the neutral slab has the smaller flux (zero).
slab box: 0, smaller
Why Gauss's law can find \(E\) only when there is symmetry, and how to think about symmetry

Gauss's law is one equation. It says the total flux through a surface equals \(Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\). But a surface has infinitely many points, and \(E\) can differ at each one; one equation cannot determine infinitely many unknowns. Unless, that is, you already know that \(E\) is the same at every point of the surface and points straight through it. Then the integral collapses to (one unknown number) × (known area), and one equation is enough.

How do you know \(E\) is the same everywhere on the surface without computing it? By symmetry, which is a way of reasoning that beginners often find slippery, so here it is spelled out. Suppose a charge distribution is unchanged when you rotate it about some axis. Then the field it produces must also be unchanged by that rotation, because the field is determined entirely by the charges, and after the rotation the charges are exactly where they were. So any two points that the rotation carries into each other must have fields of equal magnitude, related by the same rotation. For a sphere of charge, every point at radius \(r\) can be rotated into every other point at radius \(r\), so \(|E|\) is the same over the whole Gaussian sphere. And if \(\vec E\) had a sideways component at some point, a reflection through the plane containing the axis and that point would flip the sideways component while leaving the charges unchanged, a contradiction; so \(\vec E\) is radial. The same two moves (rotate to compare magnitudes, reflect to kill components) handle the cylinder and the plane.

A cube of charge has no such symmetry: no rotation maps every point of a surrounding sphere onto every other point, so \(|E|\) varies over the sphere and Gauss's law, though still true, cannot be solved for \(E\). That is the meaning of Lecture 3's "always true, sometimes not useful."

When Gauss's law gives you \(E\)

Choose a closed surface on which either (1) \(E\) is constant in magnitude and perpendicular to the surface, so \(\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec A = EA\); or (2) \(\vec E\) is parallel to the surface, so the piece contributes zero. Then \(E = Q_{\text{enc}}/(\varepsilon_0 A)\). Only three symmetries allow this:

SymmetryGaussian surfaceArea that countsResult
Spherical (point charge, spheres, shells)concentric sphere of radius \(r\)\(4\pi r^2\)\(E\) \(= \dfrac{Q_{\text{enc}}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\) \(= \dfrac{kQ_{\text{enc}}}{r^2}\)
Cylindrical (infinite lines, rods, tubes)coaxial cylinder, radius \(r\), length \(L\)\(2\pi rL\) (ends give 0)\(E\) \(= \dfrac{\lambda_{\text{enc}}}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\) \(= \dfrac{2k\lambda_{\text{enc}}}{r}\)
Planar (infinite sheets, slabs)pillbox through the sheet, end area \(A\)\(2A\) (both ends; side gives 0)\(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) each side
What each letter means
\(E\)
magnitude of the electric field, in N/C (the same unit as V/m)
\(Q_{\text{enc}}\)
the net charge enclosed inside the Gaussian surface, in C (count signs; charge outside the surface does not count)
\(\lambda_{\text{enc}}\)
the charge per unit length enclosed by the Gaussian cylinder, in C/m
\(\sigma\)
the surface density of the sheet, C/m²
\(r\)
the radius of the Gaussian sphere or cylinder: put it through the point where you want \(E\)
\(4\pi r^2\)
surface area of the Gaussian sphere
\(L,\ 2\pi rL\)
the length of the Gaussian cylinder and the area of its curved side; the two flat ends contribute nothing because \(\vec E\) skims along them
\(A,\ 2A\)

\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
