Lecture 3's checkpoint: for a charged cube, none of the listed surfaces works (a sphere around a cube does not have constant \(E\) on it). Gauss's law is still true there; it just cannot be solved for \(E\).

The three Gaussian surfaces, in three dimensions

Each standard surface is chosen so that the surface integral falls apart into pieces that are either "\(E\) times area" or zero. The figures show each surface as a solid in space, with the field arrows (green) piercing it and a few area vectors \(d\vec A\) (gold). Every derivation has the same four moves: state the symmetry, choose the surface, split the integral, solve for \(E\).

Derivation: the field of a point charge
Lecture 3

  1. Symmetry

    WhyRotate the charge about any axis through it: nothing changes. So the field cannot have a sideways part (which way would it point?), and its size cannot depend on direction.

    \(\displaystyle \vec E = E(r)\,\hat r\)

    MeansThe field points straight out and depends only on the distance r.

  2. Choose the surface

    WhyA sphere of radius \(r\) centered on the charge, passing through the point where you want \(E\).

    MeansEvery point on it is the same distance \(r\) away, so \(E\) is the same all over it.

  3. Evaluate the flux

    WhyOn the sphere \(d\vec A\) points straight out, along \(\vec E\), so \(\vec E\cdot d\vec A = E\,dA\). \(E\) is constant on the sphere, so it comes out of the integral.

    \(\displaystyle \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A\) \(\displaystyle = E\oint dA\) \(\displaystyle = E\cdot4\pi r^2\)

  4. Charge inside

    WhyJust the point charge.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}} = q\)

  5. Set them equal (Gauss's law)

    \(\displaystyle E\cdot4\pi r^2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  6. Solve for E

    WhyDivide both sides by \(4\pi r^2\). Recall \(k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}\)

    MeansCoulomb's law, recovered from Gauss's law.

What each letter means
\(E(r)\)
the field magnitude at radius \(r\); the notation says it depends only on \(r\)
\(\hat r\)
unit vector (length exactly 1, no units) pointing from the source charge toward the point you care about; it only supplies a direction
\(d\vec A\)
a tiny patch of the surface, treated as a vector: its size is the patch area \(dA\) (m²) and it points along the patch's normal (perpendicular to the surface; outward for a closed surface)
\(E\,4\pi r^2\)
constant field times the sphere's area: the whole surface integral collapses to this
\(Q_{\text{enc}}\)
the net charge enclosed inside the Gaussian surface, in C (count signs; charge outside the surface does not count)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
Derivation: the field of an infinite line
Lecture 3

  1. Symmetry

    WhySlide along the line, rotate about it, or flip it end for end: nothing changes. A part of \(\vec E\) along the axis would flip under the end-for-end flip, so it is zero. A part circling the axis would reverse in a mirror through the axis, so it is zero too.

    \(\displaystyle \vec E = E(r)\,\hat r\)

    MeansHere \(r\) is the perpendicular distance from the line.

  2. Choose the surface

    WhyA closed cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(L\), with the line on its axis.

  3. Flux through the two caps

    WhyThe caps' normals point along the axis; \(\vec E\) points away from the axis, along the cap surface.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{caps}} = 0\)

  4. Flux through the side wall

    Why\(d\vec A\) points straight out, along \(\vec E\), and \(E\) is the same everywhere on the wall (same distance \(r\)).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{side}}\) \(\displaystyle = E\cdot2\pi rL\)

  5. Charge inside

    WhyThe cylinder holds a length \(L\) of the line.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = \lambda L\)

  6. Gauss's law

    \(\displaystyle E\cdot2\pi rL\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  7. Solve for E

    WhyDivide by \(2\pi rL\). \(L\) cancels, as it must: nothing about an infinite line can depend on the length you happened to pick.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}\)

    MeansFalls like \(1/r\), not \(1/r^2\). The same recipe works for a rod, a tube, or a hollow cylinder: only \(\lambda_{\text{enc}}\) changes.

What each letter means
\(E(r)\)
the field magnitude at perpendicular distance \(r\) from the axis
\(L\)
the length of the Gaussian cylinder, in m; it appears on both sides and cancels
\(2\pi rL\)
the area of the cylinder's curved side
\(\lambda,\ \lambda_{\text{enc}}\)
charge per unit length on the line; for thick objects, only the part inside radius \(r\)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
Derivation: the field of an infinite sheet
Lecture 4

  1. Symmetry

    WhySliding along the sheet changes nothing, so \(\vec E\) cannot have a part along the sheet and cannot depend on where along the sheet you are. Flipping the sheet over swaps its two sides, so the field has the same size on both sides.

    MeansE points straight away from a positive sheet on both sides.

  2. Choose the surface

    WhyA short cylinder (pillbox) through the sheet, caps of area \(A\) parallel to the sheet, one on each side.

  3. Flux through the side wall

    WhyIts normal is parallel to the sheet; \(\vec E\) is perpendicular to the sheet.

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{side}} = 0\)

  4. Flux through the two caps

    WhyOn each cap \(\vec E\) points outward, along \(d\vec A\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi_{\text{caps}}\) \(\displaystyle = EA + EA\) \(\displaystyle = 2EA\)

  5. Charge inside

    WhyThe pillbox cuts out a patch of the sheet of area \(A\).

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}} = \sigma A\)

  6. Gauss's law, then solve

    WhyDivide both sides by 2A.

    \(\displaystyle 2EA\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansThe height of the pillbox never appeared: E does not depend on the distance from an infinite sheet.

Derivation: the field just outside a conductor
Lecture 4

  1. What is different from a sheet

    WhyInside a conductor in equilibrium \(\vec E = 0\) (Section 6.4). Just outside, \(\vec E\) is perpendicular to the surface, because a parallel part would push the surface charges along.

  2. Flux through the pieces

    WhyInner cap: \(E = 0\), so zero. Side wall: \(\vec E\) is along it (outside) or zero (inside), so zero. Outer cap: \(\vec E\) along \(d\vec A\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi = 0 + 0 + EA = EA\)

  3. Charge inside

    Why\(\sigma\) is the charge density on the surface right under the cap.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}} = \sigma A\)

  4. Gauss's law, then solve

    WhyDivide both sides by A.

    \(\displaystyle EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansTwice the free-sheet value for the same \(\sigma\). \(E\) here is the total field, made by every charge on the conductor, not just the patch under the cap. The other charges supply the other half.

permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

Derivation cards for the catalog

Open any card to see the Gaussian surface, the enclosed charge, and the algebra, one step at a time.

CardSolid insulating sphere, uniform \(\rho\): field inside and outside

  1. Total charge

    WhyCharge = density times volume of a ball of radius \(R\).

    \(\displaystyle Q = \rho\cdot\tfrac43\pi R^3\)

  2. Surface and flux

    WhyGaussian sphere of radius \(r\), centered on the ball. By symmetry \(E\) is radial and the same all over it.

    \(\displaystyle \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A\) \(\displaystyle = E\cdot4\pi r^2\)

  3. Inside (r < R): the enclosed charge

    WhyOnly the charge in the smaller ball of radius \(r\) is enclosed.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = \rho\cdot\tfrac43\pi r^3\) \(\displaystyle = Q\,\dfrac{r^3}{R^3}\)

    MeansDividing the two volumes: \(\tfrac43\pi r^3 / \tfrac43\pi R^3\) \(= r^3/R^3\).

  4. Inside: solve for E

    WhySet the flux equal to \(Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\), then divide by \(4\pi r^2\).

    \(\displaystyle E\cdot4\pi r^2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho\tfrac43\pi r^3}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQr}{R^3}\)

    MeansA straight line through the origin: zero at the center, largest at the surface.

  5. Outside (r > R)

    WhyAll the charge is enclosed.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\)

  6. Check at the surface

    WhyBoth formulas must agree at \(r = R\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{kQR}{R^3}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{R^2}\ \checkmark\)

    MeansThe graph is continuous, with a peak at the surface.

CardThick insulating shell, \(a \lt r \lt b\), uniform \(\rho\) (Lecture 4, Example 4.3)

  1. Hole (r < a)

    WhyA Gaussian sphere in the hole encloses no charge.

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

    MeansThe common wrong answer, \(\rho(b^3-a^3)/(3\varepsilon_0 r^2)\), is the outside formula used inside.

  2. In the material (a < r < b): enclosed charge

    WhyOnly the material between \(a\) and \(r\) is enclosed: a big ball minus the hole.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = \rho\cdot\tfrac43\pi(r^3 - a^3)\)

  3. In the material: solve for E

    WhyDivide by \(4\pi r^2\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho(r^3 - a^3)}{3\varepsilon_0 r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\left(r - \dfrac{a^3}{r^2}\right)\)

    MeansAt \(r = a\) this is zero, and it grows from there, but not in a straight line.

  4. Outside (r > b)

    WhyAll the material is enclosed.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho(b^3 - a^3)}{3\varepsilon_0 r^2}\)
CardNon-uniform density \(\rho(r)\), for example \(\rho = Ar\) (Homework 4, Problem 1)

  1. Why an integral now

    WhyWhen \(\rho\) changes with radius, "density times volume" no longer works. Cut the material into thin shells, each thin enough that \(\rho\) is constant on it.

  2. Charge of one thin shell

    WhyA shell of radius \(r'\) and thickness \(dr'\) has volume (area)\(\times\)(thickness).

    \(\displaystyle dq = \rho(r')\cdot4\pi r'^2\,dr'\)

  3. Add the shells from the inner edge out to r

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}(r)\) \(\displaystyle = \int_{r_{\text{in}}}^{r}\rho(r')\,4\pi r'^2\,dr'\)

  4. With ρ = Ar and the material starting at R₁

    WhyPull out the constants, then use \(\int r^3dr = r^4/4\).

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = 4\pi A\int_{R_1}^{r} r'^3\,dr'\) \(\displaystyle = 4\pi A\cdot\dfrac{r^4 - R_1^4}{4}\) \(\displaystyle = \pi A(r^4 - R_1^4)\)

  5. Then E as usual

    WhyAdd any point charge at the center, then divide by the sphere area.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{kQ_{\text{enc}}}{r^2}\)

    MeansFor cylinders, the thin pieces are rings of area \(2\pi r'\,dr'\) per unit length: \(\lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(= \int\rho(r')\,2\pi r'\,dr'\).

What each letter means
\(\rho(r)\)
a density that changes with radius, C/m³
\(A\)
here a given constant (units C/m⁴ for \(\rho = Ar\)), not an area
\(r\prime\)
the "dummy" radius you integrate over, from the inner edge of the charge out to \(r\)
\(4\pi r\prime^2\,dr\prime\)
the volume of a thin spherical shell of radius \(r\prime\) and thickness \(dr\prime\)
\(2\pi r\prime\,dr\prime\)
the area of a thin ring, giving charge per unit length for cylinders
\(R_1,\ r_{\text{in}}\)
the inner radius where the charged material begins
\(Q_{\text{enc}}(r),\ \lambda_{\text{enc}}(r)\)
the enclosed charge (per length) as a function of the Gaussian radius
CardSolid insulating cylinder, uniform \(\rho\): inside and outside

  1. Surface and flux

    WhyGaussian cylinder of radius \(r\), length \(L\). Caps: zero. Side: \(E\cdot2\pi rL\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi = E\cdot2\pi rL\)

  2. Inside (r < R)

    WhyEnclosed: a cylinder of radius \(r\), volume \(\pi r^2L\).

    \(\displaystyle E\cdot2\pi rL\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho\pi r^2L}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho r}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

  3. Outside (r > R)

    WhyEnclosed: the whole cross-section, \(\pi R^2L\). Call \(\lambda = \rho\pi R^2\) the charge per length.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho R^2}{2\varepsilon_0 r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)

    MeansOutside, the cylinder acts like a line of charge. Homework 3 P3 runs this formula backward to find R.

CardHollow insulating cylinder, \(a \lt r \lt b\) (Fall 2015 Q22–25)

  1. Hole (r < a)

    WhyNothing enclosed.

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

  2. In the material

    WhyEnclosed per length: the ring from \(a\) to \(r\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = \rho\pi(r^2 - a^2)\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho(r^2 - a^2)}{2\varepsilon_0 r}\)

  3. Outside (r > b)

    WhyThe whole ring.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = \rho\pi(b^2 - a^2)\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho(b^2 - a^2)}{2\varepsilon_0 r}\)

  4. Add a neutral metal tube around it

    WhyIts inner surface takes \(-\lambda\), its outer surface \(+\lambda\). The field is zero in the metal and unchanged outside.

CardSheet, plate, and conductor: keeping \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) and \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) straight

  1. Free sheet with density σ

    WhyThe pillbox catches flux through both caps.

    \(\displaystyle 2EA\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\ \text{on each side}\)

  2. Conductor surface with local density σ

    WhyOne cap is inside the metal, where \(E = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\ \text{just outside}\)

  3. Isolated conducting plate with total charge Q on area A

    WhyThe charge splits evenly onto the two faces.

    \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\text{face}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2A}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma_{\text{face}}}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0A}\)

    MeansThe same answer as a free sheet carrying all of \(Q\): \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) with \(\sigma = Q/A\).

  4. Parallel-plate capacitor

    WhyAll of \(+Q\) moves to the inner face, facing the other plate.

    \(\displaystyle \sigma = \dfrac{Q}{A}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}\ \text{in the gap, 0 outside}\)
The shell theorem: why only the charge inside \(r\) counts

  1. Split the ball into shells

    WhyThink of the ball as an inner ball of radius \(r\) plus many thin shells outside \(r\).

  2. One outer shell, alone: no field inside it

    WhyPut a Gaussian sphere inside that shell. It encloses nothing, and by symmetry \(E\) is the same all over it.

    \(\displaystyle E\cdot4\pi r^2\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

    MeansA uniform shell makes no field anywhere inside itself. The near side is closer but smaller, the far side farther but larger, and the 1/r² law makes the two cancel exactly.

  3. The inner ball: like a point charge

    WhySeen from its surface or beyond, the inner ball acts like a point charge at the center holding its charge \(Q(r/R)^3\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{k\,Q(r/R)^3}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQr}{R^3}\)

    MeansThat is why Gauss's law only "sees" the charge inside r.

Trap · \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) vs. \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\)

A free-standing sheet of charge makes \(\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)\) on each side. The field just outside a conductor's surface is \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) because the other end of the pillbox sits inside the conductor where \(E = 0\); all the flux exits through one end. The two are consistent: a conducting plate with \(\sigma\) on each face is two sheets whose fields add outside (\(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\)) and cancel inside (0).

What the field graphs look like

Deriving the four sphere results in one pass
Spring 2015 Q10–12 · Lecture 4 · Homework 6, Problem 1
An insulating sphere of radius \(R\) carries charge spread uniformly through it, density \(\rho\). Find \(E\) outside and inside, and pick the graph of \(E(r)\).

  1. Surface

    WhyGaussian sphere of radius \(r\). By symmetry \(\vec E\) is radial and depends only on \(r\).

    \(\displaystyle \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A\) \(\displaystyle = E\cdot4\pi r^2\)

  2. Outside (r > R): enclosed charge

    WhyThe whole ball.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = Q\) \(\displaystyle = \rho\cdot\tfrac43\pi R^3\)

  3. Outside: E

    WhyDivide by \(4\pi r^2\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho R^3}{3\varepsilon_0 r^2}\)

  4. Inside (r < R): enclosed charge

    WhyOnly the ball of radius \(r\).

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = \rho\cdot\tfrac43\pi r^3\)

  5. Inside: E

    \(\displaystyle E\cdot4\pi r^2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho\tfrac43\pi r^3}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQr}{R^3}\)

  6. Join them at r = R

    WhyBoth give \(\rho R/3\varepsilon_0\). The graph is continuous, with a corner at \(R\).

    MeansGraph (a) in Spring 2015 Q12: a straight line up to R, then a 1/r² fall.

outside: ρR³/(3ε₀r²) inside: ρr/(3ε₀)
Field inside an insulating sphere, with a shell around it
Spring 2014, Question 10
An insulating sphere of radius \(a = 6\ \mathrm{cm}\) carries \(Q = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) spread through its volume. It sits inside an uncharged conducting shell. Find \(E\) at \(r = 4\ \mathrm{cm}\).

  1. Which region is P in?

    Why\(r = 4\ \mathrm{cm} \lt a\) \(= 6\ \mathrm{cm}\): inside the insulator.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{kQr}{a^3}\)

  2. What about the shell?

    WhyThe shell is outside the Gaussian sphere through P. Its charges (inner \(-8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), outer \(+8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)) are not enclosed.

    MeansThe shell changes nothing inside it.

  3. Convert to SI

    \(\displaystyle Q = 8\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C},\) \(\displaystyle r\) \(\displaystyle = 0.04\ \mathrm{m},\) \(\displaystyle a\) \(\displaystyle = 0.06\ \mathrm{m}\)

  4. Cube the radius

    \(\displaystyle a^3 = (0.06)^3\) \(\displaystyle = 2.16\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}\)

  5. Plug in

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(8\times10^{-6})(0.04)}{2.16\times10^{-4}}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.33\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
E = 1.33×10⁷ N/C, outward
Find λ from a measured field
Homework 3, Problem 2
A long copper rod (all its charge sits on its surface) produces \(E = 4.6\ \mathrm{N/C}\) at \(r = 4.25\ \mathrm{cm}\) from its axis. Find \(\lambda\). Then find the flux through a cube of edge \(L = 6.5\ \mathrm{cm}\) that the rod passes straight through.

  1. Which formula?

    WhyOutside a long charged rod (conductor or not), it acts like a line of charge.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)

  2. Solve for λ

    WhyMultiply both sides by \(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = 2\pi\varepsilon_0 rE\)

  3. Plug in

    Why\(r = 0.0425\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda\) \(\displaystyle = 2\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.0425)(4.6)\) \(\displaystyle = 1.09\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{C/m}\)

  4. Flux through the cube: what is inside?

    WhyThe rod crosses the whole cube, so a length \(L\) of rod is inside. The cube's shape does not matter.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = \lambda L\)

  5. Gauss's law

    Why\(L = 0.065\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle \Phi\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(1.09\times10^{-11})(0.065)}{8.85\times10^{-12}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.080\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C}\)
λ = 1.09×10⁻¹¹ C/m Φ = 0.080 N·m²/C
C/m
Find R from an outside field
Homework 3, Problem 3
A long solid insulating cylinder has \(\rho = 1.44\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^3}\). Outside it, at \(r = 0.752\ \mathrm{m}\) from the axis, \(E = 3130\ \mathrm{N/C}\). Find its radius \(R\).

  1. Which formula?

    WhyOutside a solid cylinder (from the card above):

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\rho R^2}{2\varepsilon_0 r}\)

  2. Isolate R²

    WhyMultiply both sides by \(2\varepsilon_0 r\), then divide by \(\rho\).

    \(\displaystyle R^2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2\varepsilon_0 rE}{\rho}\)

  3. Plug in

    Why\(\rho\) \(= 1.44\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C/m^3}\).

    \(\displaystyle R^2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.752)(3130)}{1.44\times10^{-6}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.0289\ \mathrm{m^2}\)

  4. Square root

    \(\displaystyle R = \sqrt{0.0289}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.170\ \mathrm{m}\)
R = 0.170 m

Wire inside a thin charged cylinder
Homework 4, Problem 3
A wire on the axis carries \(\lambda_1 = -227\ \mathrm{pC/m}\). A thin cylindrical shell of radius \(4.89\ \mathrm{cm}\) around it carries \(\lambda_2 = +586\ \mathrm{pC/m}\). Find \(E\) at \(r = 2.73\ \mathrm{cm}\) and at \(r = 7.56\ \mathrm{cm}\).

  1. Inside the shell: what is enclosed?

    WhyA Gaussian cylinder of radius \(2.73\ \mathrm{cm}\) is inside the shell. It encloses the wire only.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = -227\ \mathrm{pC/m}\)

  2. Inside the shell: the size of E

    Why\(E = 2k|\lambda_{\text{enc}}|/r\) with \(r = 0.0273\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(227\times10^{-12})}{0.0273}\) \(\displaystyle = 150\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  3. Inside the shell: direction

    Why\(\lambda_{\text{enc}} \lt 0\), so the field points toward the axis.

    \(\displaystyle E = 150\ \mathrm{N/C}\), inward

  4. Outside the shell: what is enclosed?

    WhyNow both the wire and the shell are inside.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = -227 + 586\) \(\displaystyle = +359\ \mathrm{pC/m}\)

  5. Outside the shell: E

    Why\(r = 0.0756\ \mathrm{m}\). Positive, so outward.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(359\times10^{-12})}{0.0756}\) \(\displaystyle = 85\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
2.73 cm: 150 N/C inward 7.56 cm: 85 N/C outward
Conducting rod inside a conducting pipe
Homework 4, Problem 4
A conducting rod of radius \(2\ \mathrm{cm}\) carries \(\lambda = +6.5\ \mathrm{pC/m}\). A neutral conducting pipe (inner radius \(4\ \mathrm{cm}\), outer \(6\ \mathrm{cm}\)) surrounds it. Find \(E\) at \(r = 0.45\), \(2.7\), \(4.8\), \(6.5\), and \(8.8\ \mathrm{cm}\).

  1. Charges on the pipe

    WhyA Gaussian cylinder inside the pipe wall has \(E = 0\) on it, so it encloses zero. The inner surface must cancel the rod. The pipe is neutral, so its outer surface takes the opposite.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{inner}}\) \(\displaystyle = -6.5,\) \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{outer}}\) \(\displaystyle = +6.5\ \mathrm{pC/m}\)

  2. A shortcut number

    WhyEvery nonzero answer is \(2k\lambda_{\text{enc}}/r\) with the same \(\lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(= 6.5\ \mathrm{pC/m}\).

    \(\displaystyle 2k\lambda\) \(\displaystyle = 2(8.99\times10^{9})(6.5\times10^{-12})\) \(\displaystyle = 0.1169\ \mathrm{N\,m/C}\)

  3. r = 0.45 cm: inside the rod

    WhyInside a conductor, E = 0.

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

  4. r = 2.7 cm: in the gap

    WhyEncloses the rod only.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{0.1169}{0.027}\) \(\displaystyle = 4.3\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  5. r = 4.8 cm: in the pipe wall

    WhyInside a conductor again.

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

  6. r = 6.5 cm: just outside

    WhyEncloses rod + inner + outer surfaces: \(6.5 - 6.5 + 6.5 = 6.5\ \mathrm{pC/m}\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{0.1169}{0.065}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.8\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  7. r = 8.8 cm

    WhySame enclosed charge, larger r.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{0.1169}{0.088}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.3\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
0 4.3 N/C 0 1.8 N/C 1.3 N/C
Non-uniform charge density: integrate to get \(Q_{\text{enc}}\)
Homework 4, Problem 1
A non-conducting shell from \(R_1 = 7\ \mathrm{cm}\) to \(R_2 = 12\ \mathrm{cm}\) has density \(\rho = Ar\) with \(A = 21\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^4}\). A point charge \(Q = -35\ \mathrm{nC}\) sits at the center. Find \(E\) at \(r = 0.5R_1\), \(r = 0.5(R_1 + R_2)\), and \(r = 2R_2\).

  1. ① r = 3.5 cm (in the hole): enclosed charge

    WhyOnly the point charge; no shell material yet.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = -35\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\)

  2. ① E

    WhyNegative means inward.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(-35\times10^{-9})}{(0.035)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = -2.57\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  3. ② r = 9.5 cm: shell charge inside r

    WhyUse the card above: \(Q_{\text{shell}}(r)\) \(= \pi A(r^4 - R_1^4)\). Raise each radius to the 4th power first.

    \(\displaystyle (0.095)^4 = 8.145\times10^{-5},\) \(\displaystyle (0.07)^4\) \(\displaystyle = 2.401\times10^{-5}\)
    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{shell}}\) \(\displaystyle = \pi(21\times10^{-6})(5.744\times10^{-5})\) \(\displaystyle = 3.79\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\)

  4. ② total enclosed

    WhyAdd the point charge (with its sign).

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = -35 + 3.79\) \(\displaystyle = -31.2\ \mathrm{nC}\)

  5. ② E

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(-31.2\times10^{-9})}{(0.095)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = -3.11\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  6. ③ r = 24 cm: all of the shell is inside

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{shell}}\) \(\displaystyle = \pi(21\times10^{-6})\big((0.12)^4 - (0.07)^4\big)\) \(\displaystyle = 1.21\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{C}\)
    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = -35 + 12.1\) \(\displaystyle = -22.9\ \mathrm{nC}\)

  7. ③ E

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(-22.9\times10^{-9})}{(0.24)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = -3.57\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

    MeansStill negative: the shell's positive charge is not enough to cancel the −35 nC, so the field points inward everywhere.

① −2.57×10⁵ N/C ② −3.11×10⁴ N/C ③ −3.57×10³ N/C
N/C

6.4 Conductors in equilibrium and layered problems

Four properties of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium
  1. \(\vec E = 0\) everywhere inside the conducting material. (If it were not, free charges would move; "equilibrium" means they have stopped.)
  2. All excess charge sits on surfaces. Proof: a Gaussian surface just inside the metal has \(E = 0\) on it, so \(Q_{\text{enc}} = 0\).
  3. Just outside, \(\vec E\) is perpendicular to the surface with magnitude \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\). (A parallel component would push surface charges along the surface.)
  4. The whole conductor, surface and interior, is at one potential (Chapter 7).

Cavity rule. If a conductor has a cavity containing charge \(q\), a Gaussian surface inside the metal surrounding the cavity must enclose zero: the inner surface acquires exactly \(-q\). Charge conservation then puts \(Q_{\text{conductor}} + q\) on the outer surface. The outside world sees only the total \(Q_{\text{conductor}} + q\), arranged with the conductor's own symmetry.

What each letter means
\(\vec E\)
the electric field vector: the force per coulomb that a positive test charge would feel at that point, in N/C (= V/m)
\(\sigma\)
the local surface charge density on the conductor, C/m²; \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) is the field just outside
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
\(q\)
a charge placed inside the cavity, C
\(-q\)
the charge induced on the cavity wall (inner surface)
\(Q_{\text{conductor}}\)
the conductor's own net charge, C; \(Q_{\text{conductor}} + q\) ends up on the outer surface
The mechanism behind the four conductor properties

Why \(E = 0\) inside. Put a metal object in an electric field. The field pushes the free electrons; they move; wherever they pile up (one side) the metal becomes negative and wherever they leave (the other side) it becomes positive. Those separated charges make their own field, pointing against the applied one inside the metal. Electrons keep moving until the field they create exactly cancels the applied field everywhere inside; then there is nothing left to push them and the motion stops. In a good conductor this takes about \(10^{-19}\) seconds, so for any static problem the interior field is zero. "Electrostatic equilibrium" means this settling has finished.

Why the charge is on the surface. With \(E = 0\) throughout the metal, take any Gaussian surface drawn entirely inside the metal: zero field on it means zero flux means zero enclosed charge. Shrink and move that surface anywhere you like inside the material and it always encloses zero. So every bit of excess charge must be on the surfaces, where no interior Gaussian surface can enclose it.

Why \(E\) is perpendicular at the surface. A component of \(\vec E\) along the surface would drag the surface charges sideways along the surface. In equilibrium they are not moving, so that component is zero. Only the perpendicular component survives, and Gauss's pillbox gives its size, \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\).

Why a cavity's wall takes exactly \(-q\). A charge \(q\) sitting in a hollow inside the metal makes a field. That field would penetrate the metal, so electrons rush toward the cavity wall (if \(q \gt 0\)) until the wall charge cancels the field of \(q\) everywhere in the metal. Gauss's law quantifies "cancels": a surface inside the metal enclosing the cavity has zero flux, so \(q + q_{\text{wall}} = 0\). The electrons that moved to the wall came from the rest of the metal, which is left with \(+q\), and that \(+q\) sits on the outer surface. Because the outer surface does not "know" where inside the cavity \(q\) is (the metal has screened it), the \(+q\) arranges itself by the outer surface's own symmetry.

Why sharp points spray charge. Two connected conductors share one potential (Chapter 7), and a sphere at potential \(V\) holds \(Q = 4\pi\varepsilon_0RV\) with surface density \(\sigma = Q/4\pi R^2 = \varepsilon_0V/R\). Smaller radius means larger \(\sigma\) and, since \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0\), larger field. A sharp point is a tiny-radius region, so the field there is intense enough to ionize air. Lightning rods work on this principle.

What each letter means
\(V\)
the potential of the conductor, V
\(R\)
the sphere's radius, m
\(Q\)
the charge it holds at that potential, C
\(\sigma\)
its surface charge density, C/m²
\(E\)
magnitude of the electric field, in N/C (the same unit as V/m)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
Point charge inside a neutral conducting shell
Lecture 4, Example 4.4
A charge \(+3Q\) sits at the center of a neutral conducting shell with inner radius \(r_1\) and outer radius \(r_2\). Find \(E\) in each region and the charge on each surface of the shell.

  1. Region r < r₁ (the hole)

    WhyA Gaussian sphere here encloses only the point charge.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = +3Q\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{3kQ}{r^2}\ \text{outward}\)

  2. Region r₁ < r < r₂ (the metal)

    WhyInside a conductor, \(E = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

  3. Inner surface charge

    WhyA Gaussian sphere inside the metal has \(E = 0\) on it, so zero flux, so it encloses zero. It encloses the point charge plus the inner surface.

    \(\displaystyle 3Q + q_{\text{inner}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow q_{\text{inner}}\) \(\displaystyle = -3Q\)

  4. Outer surface charge

    WhyThe shell is neutral: its two surfaces add to zero.

    \(\displaystyle q_{\text{inner}} + q_{\text{outer}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow q_{\text{outer}}\) \(\displaystyle = +3Q\)

  5. Region r > r₂ (outside)

    WhyEverything is enclosed.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = 3Q - 3Q + 3Q\) \(\displaystyle = +3Q\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{3kQ}{r^2}\)

    MeansOutside, the neutral shell is invisible: the field is the same as with no shell.

  6. Surface densities

    WhySame size of charge on each surface, but the inner surface is smaller.

    \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\text{in}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-3Q}{4\pi r_1^2},\) \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\text{out}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{+3Q}{4\pi r_2^2}\)

    Means\(r_1 \lt r_2\), so \(|\sigma_{\text{in}}| \gt |\sigma_{\text{out}}|\) (Lecture 4's last clicker).

inner: −3Q outer: +3Q E = 3kQ/r² outside and in the hole E = 0 in the metal
Algorithm for any layered sphere or cylinder problem
  1. List the layers from the inside out, marking each as conductor or insulator, with its charge (total, or \(\rho\), \(\lambda\), \(\sigma\)).
  2. Assign conductor surface charges. Work outward: the inner surface of each conductor gets minus the total charge enclosed inside it; the outer surface gets (its net charge) minus (its inner-surface charge).
  3. For each region, write \(Q_{\text{enc}}(r)\) for a Gaussian sphere/cylinder of radius \(r\) in that region. Inside a conductor: skip, \(E = 0\).
  4. \(E(r) = kQ_{\text{enc}}/r^2\) (sphere) or \(2k\lambda_{\text{enc}}/r\) (cylinder). Sign of \(Q_{\text{enc}}\) gives direction: positive means outward.
  5. Sanity check: \(E\) is continuous except at surface charges; it is zero throughout every conductor; far away it looks like a point charge (or line) with the total charge.
What each letter means
\(Q_{\text{enc}}(r)\)
enclosed charge as a function of the Gaussian radius \(r\): everything inside \(r\), including induced surface charges
\(\lambda_{\text{enc}}\)
the charge per unit length enclosed by the Gaussian cylinder, in C/m
\(E(r)\)
the field magnitude at radius \(r\); positive means outward
\(\rho\)
volume charge density: charge per unit volume inside an insulator, in C/m³ (\(\rho = Q/V\) when uniform)
\(\lambda\)
linear charge density: charge per unit length along a line, rod, or ring, in C/m (\(\lambda = Q/L\) when uniform)
\(\sigma\)
surface charge density: charge per unit area on a sheet or surface, in C/m² (\(\sigma = Q/A\) when uniform)
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)

Walking a Gaussian sphere through the layers

The four cutaways below show the same object, an insulating sphere of radius \(a\) carrying \(+Q\) inside a conducting shell (inner radius \(b\), outer radius \(c\)) carrying net charge \(Q_{\text{shell}}\), with a Gaussian sphere placed in each of the four regions. The shell's inner surface carries \(-Q\) (forced by \(E = 0\) in the metal) and its outer surface carries \(Q_{\text{shell}} + Q\) (forced by charge conservation).

Fall 2018 Q7–10, Spring 2014 Q10–12, and Homework 6 P1 are exactly this object. The explorer below draws the same cutaway live for any charges and radii you choose.

What each letter means
\(Q\)
the charge of the insulating sphere, spread through its volume, C
\(a\)
the insulator's radius, m
\(b,\ c\)
the conducting shell's inner and outer radii, m
\(Q_{\text{shell}}\)
the shell's net charge, C
\(q_{\text{inner}}\)
the charge that collects on the shell's inner surface (\(-Q\)); the outer surface then carries \(Q_{\text{shell}} + Q\)
\(r\)
the radius of the Gaussian sphere, m
\(E\)
magnitude of the electric field, in N/C (the same unit as V/m)
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
A charge inside a hollow conductor, step by step

  1. Gaussian sphere inside the metal

    Why\(E = 0\) everywhere on it, so its flux is zero, so it encloses zero net charge.

    \(\displaystyle q + q_{\text{wall}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow q_{\text{wall}}\) \(\displaystyle = -q\)

    MeansIf \(q\) is off-center, the \(-q\) on the wall is spread unevenly, but it still totals \(-q\).

  2. Outer surface

    WhyThe conductor is neutral, so the outer surface carries the opposite of the wall.

    \(\displaystyle q_{\text{outer}} = +q\)

  3. How the outer charge spreads

    WhyThe metal screens the cavity completely, so the outer surface "cannot tell" where \(q\) is. On a spherical outer surface, \(+q\) spreads uniformly.

    MeansThe outside world sees a uniform +q, exactly like a point charge at the center.

  4. Two exam consequences

    The field outside depends only on the total enclosed charge, not its position (Lecture 3 checkpoint).
    Removing a neutral shell from around a charge leaves the field outside unchanged (Fall 2015 Q25).
Explore · Gauss's law, layer by layer
Insulator inside a conducting shell

A uniformly charged insulating sphere (or long cylinder) of radius a sits inside a conducting shell with inner radius b and outer radius c. Set the charges, then slide the Gaussian surface radius r through the four regions and read E and V. The cutaway drawing shows the layers in three dimensions, the dashed Gaussian surface with its field arrows, and the induced surface charges, all updating live.

In the gap, \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\), radial, with no flux through the flat caps. The tube's inner surface carries \(-\lambda\) per length and its outer surface \(+\lambda\). Inside the tube wall \(E = 0\); outside, \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\) again. This is Fall 2015 Q22–25 and Homework 4 P4.

Line of charge inside a conducting tube
Lecture 4, Example 4.1
A line with \(\lambda_1 = -5.1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\) runs along the axis of a neutral conducting tube, inner radius \(a = 2.7\ \mathrm{cm}\), outer radius \(b = 5.0\ \mathrm{cm}\). Find the charge per length on each surface of the tube, and the field at point R, \(0.9\ \mathrm{cm}\) from the axis at \(30^\circ\) from the \(y\)-axis.

  1. Inner surface

    WhyA Gaussian cylinder inside the metal has \(E = 0\) on it, so it encloses zero. It encloses the line plus the inner surface.

    \(\displaystyle -5.1 + \lambda_a\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \lambda_a\) \(\displaystyle = +5.1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\)

  2. Outer surface

    WhyThe tube is neutral.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_a + \lambda_b\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \lambda_b\) \(\displaystyle = -5.1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\)

  3. What does R see?

    WhyA Gaussian cylinder through R (radius \(0.9\ \mathrm{cm} \lt a\)) encloses only the line. The tube's charges are all outside it and add nothing.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = -5.1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\)

  4. Size of E at R

    Why\(r = 0.009\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{2k|\lambda_1|}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(5.1\times10^{-6})}{0.009}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.02\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  5. Direction at R

    WhyNegative line: \(\vec E\) points toward the axis.

  6. x-component

    WhyR sits at \(30^\circ\) from the \(y\)-axis, so the radial direction has an \(x\)-part of \(\sin30^\circ\).

    \(\displaystyle |E_x| = E\sin30^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = (1.02\times10^{7})(0.5)\) \(\displaystyle = 5.1\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

    MeansThe sign of Eₓ comes from which side of the y-axis R is on in the figure: the field points back toward the axis.

λa = +5.1 μC/m λb = −5.1 μC/m E = 1.02×10⁷ N/C |Eₓ| = 5.1×10⁶ N/C
Give the tube a net charge
Lecture 4, Example 4.2
Same line and tube, but the tube now carries net \(\lambda_2 = +2.0\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\). Find the surface charges and the field at \(r = 7\ \mathrm{cm}\) (outside), along the same \(30^\circ\) direction.

  1. Inner surface

    WhyUnchanged: it must still cancel the line inside the metal.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_a = +5.1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\)

  2. Outer surface

    WhyThe two surfaces must add to the tube's net charge.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_b = \lambda_2 - \lambda_a\) \(\displaystyle = 2.0 - 5.1\) \(\displaystyle = -3.1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\)

  3. Enclosed at r = 7 cm

    WhyEverything: the line plus the whole tube.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = -5.1 + 2.0\) \(\displaystyle = -3.1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\)

  4. Size of E

    Why\(r = 0.07\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(3.1\times10^{-6})}{0.07}\) \(\displaystyle = 8.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

    MeansNegative enclosed charge: inward.

  5. x-component

    \(\displaystyle |E_x| = E\sin30^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = 4.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
λb = −3.1 μC/m E = 8.0×10⁵ N/C inward |Eₓ| = 4.0×10⁵ N/C
Ranking the field in three regions
Fall 2018, Questions 11–12
A line \(+\lambda\) runs along the axis of a conducting tube with net charge \(-\lambda/3\). Point A is in the hole, B in the metal, C outside. Rank \(|E_A|\), \(|E_B|\), \(|E_C|\). Then find \(|E_C|\) for \(\lambda = 1.3\ \mathrm{C/m}\), \(r_C = 0.35\ \mathrm{m}\).

  1. At A (in the hole)

    WhyEncloses only the line.

    \(\displaystyle |E_A| = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r_A}\)

  2. At B (in the metal)

    WhyInside a conductor.

    \(\displaystyle E_B = 0\)

  3. At C (outside)

    WhyEncloses the line and the whole tube.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = \lambda - \tfrac13\lambda\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac23\lambda\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow |E_C|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2k(2\lambda/3)}{r_C}\)

  4. Rank

    WhyA has more enclosed charge (\(\lambda \gt 2\lambda/3\)) and a smaller distance (\(r_A \lt r_C\)): both make \(E_A\) bigger.

    \(\displaystyle |E_A| \gt |E_C| \gt |E_B|\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

  5. The number

    \(\displaystyle |E_C|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(0.8667)}{0.35}\) \(\displaystyle = 4.5\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
|EA| > |EC| > |EB| = 0 |EC| = 4.5×10¹⁰ N/C
Insulating sphere inside a charged conducting shell
Fall 2018 Q7–10 · Spring 2014 Q10–12 · Homework 6, Problem 1
An insulating sphere of radius \(a\) carries \(Q_{\text{sphere}}\) spread through its volume. A conducting shell from \(b\) to \(c\) around it carries net \(Q_{\text{shell}}\). Find \(E\) in every region.
Region\(Q_{\text{enc}}\)\(E(r)\)
\(r \lt a\)\(Q_{\text{sphere}}\,r^3/a^3\)\(kQ_{\text{sphere}}\,r/a^3\)
\(a \lt r \lt b\)\(Q_{\text{sphere}}\)\(kQ_{\text{sphere}}/r^2\)
\(b \lt r \lt c\) (metal)0 (inner surface holds \(-Q_{\text{sphere}}\))0
\(r \gt c\)\(Q_{\text{sphere}} + Q_{\text{shell}}\) (outer surface holds \(Q_{\text{shell}} + Q_{\text{sphere}}\))\(k(Q_{\text{sphere}}+Q_{\text{shell}})/r^2\)

  1. r < a

    WhyOnly the part of the insulator inside \(r\): a fraction \(r^3/a^3\) of it.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ_{\text{sphere}}\,r}{a^3}\)

  2. a < r < b

    WhyThe whole insulator, none of the shell.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{kQ_{\text{sphere}}}{r^2}\)

  3. b < r < c (the metal)

    Why\(E = 0\). A Gaussian sphere here encloses zero, so the inner surface holds \(-Q_{\text{sphere}}\).

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

  4. r > c

    WhyEverything. The outer surface holds \(Q_{\text{shell}} + Q_{\text{sphere}}\).

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k(Q_{\text{sphere}} + Q_{\text{shell}})}{r^2}\)
Charge density on the inner wall
Spring 2014, Question 11
\(Q = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) is spread through an insulating sphere inside an uncharged conducting shell of inner radius \(b = 10\ \mathrm{cm}\). Find the charge density on the shell's inner surface.

  1. Charge on the inner surface

    WhyIt must cancel the enclosed \(+8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) so that \(E = 0\) in the metal.

    \(\displaystyle q_{\text{inner}}\) \(\displaystyle = -8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

  2. Area of the inner surface

    WhyA sphere of radius \(0.1\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle A = 4\pi(0.1)^2\) \(\displaystyle = 0.1257\ \mathrm{m^2}\)

  3. Divide

    \(\displaystyle \sigma\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-8\times10^{-6}}{0.1257}\) \(\displaystyle = -6.4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\)

Charge on a shell from the field outside it
Homework 4, Problem 2
A point charge \(q = -5.75\ \mathrm{pC}\) sits at the center of a conducting shell (inner radius \(2.9\ \mathrm{cm}\), outer \(3.7\ \mathrm{cm}\)). Just outside the shell the field is \(5.4\ \mathrm{N/C}\), pointing outward. Find the charge density on each surface and the net charge of the shell.

  1. Inner surface charge

    WhyIt must cancel \(q\) so that \(E = 0\) in the metal.

    \(\displaystyle q_{\text{in}} = +5.75\ \mathrm{pC}\)

  2. Inner surface density

    WhyArea \(4\pi(0.029)^2\) \(= 1.06\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}\).

    \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\text{in}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{5.75\times10^{-12}}{1.06\times10^{-2}}\) \(\displaystyle = 5.4\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\)

  3. Outer surface density, from the field

    WhyJust outside a conductor, \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0\). Outward field means positive \(\sigma\).

    \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\text{out}}\) \(\displaystyle = \varepsilon_0E\) \(\displaystyle = (8.85\times10^{-12})(5.4)\) \(\displaystyle = 4.8\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\)

  4. Outer surface charge

    WhyDensity times area, \(4\pi(0.037)^2\) \(= 1.72\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}\).

    \(\displaystyle q_{\text{out}}\) \(\displaystyle = (4.78\times10^{-11})(1.72\times10^{-2})\) \(\displaystyle = 8.2\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{C}\)

  5. Net charge of the shell

    WhyAdd its two surfaces.

    \(\displaystyle Q_{\text{shell}}\) \(\displaystyle = 5.75 + 0.82\) \(\displaystyle = 6.6\ \mathrm{pC}\)
σin = 5.4×10⁻¹⁰ C/m² σout = 4.8×10⁻¹¹ C/m² Qshell = 6.6 pC
Hollow insulating cylinder inside a neutral metal tube
Fall 2015, Questions 22–25
An insulating cylinder from \(a = 0.45\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(b = 0.675\ \mathrm{m}\) has \(\rho = 3\ \mathrm{C/m^3}\). A neutral metal tube runs from \(c = 0.9\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(d = 1.125\ \mathrm{m}\). Find \(E\) at \(r = 0.743\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(0.99\ \mathrm{m}\), the charge on the tube's inner surface, and what happens at \(1.69\ \mathrm{m}\) if the tube is removed.

  1. Charge per length of the insulator

    WhyArea of the ring times \(\rho\). Square the radii first: \(0.675^2 = 0.4556\), \(0.45^2 = 0.2025\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = \rho\pi(b^2 - a^2)\) \(\displaystyle = 3\pi(0.4556 - 0.2025)\) \(\displaystyle = 2.39\ \mathrm{C/m}\)

  2. E at r = 0.743 m (the gap)

    WhyEncloses the whole insulator.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2.39}{2\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.743)}\) \(\displaystyle = 5.77\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  3. E at r = 0.99 m (in the metal)

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

  4. Tube's inner surface

    WhyIt cancels the insulator's \(\lambda\) so that \(E = 0\) in the metal; the neutral tube's outer surface then carries \(+\lambda\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_c = -2.39\ \mathrm{C/m},\) \(\displaystyle \lambda_d\) \(\displaystyle = +2.39\ \mathrm{C/m}\)

  5. Remove the tube: E at 1.69 m

    WhyThe tube was neutral, so the enclosed charge at \(1.69\ \mathrm{m}\) is \(\lambda\) either way.

    MeansE is unchanged.

E(0.743 m) = 5.78×10¹⁰ N/C E(0.99 m) = 0 λc = −2.39 C/m
N/C

6.5 Infinite sheets, conducting slabs, and superposition

Sheet bookkeeping

Each infinite sheet makes a uniform field \(|\sigma|/(2\varepsilon_0)\) on both sides, pointing away from it if \(\sigma \gt 0\) and toward it if \(\sigma \lt 0\), independent of distance. The net field in any region is the sum of these constants. Procedure: for the region of interest, list each sheet, decide "away or toward," convert to \(\pm\), add. A neutral conducting slab placed among sheets contributes zero net field outside itself (its two faces carry \(\pm\sigma_{\text{ind}}\), whose fields cancel outside); inside the slab the total field must be zero, which fixes \(\sigma_{\text{ind}}\).

What each letter means
\(\sigma\)
the sheet's charge per unit area, C/m², with its sign
\(|\sigma|/(2\varepsilon_0)\)
the size of the field one sheet makes on either side, N/C; the same at every distance
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
\(\pm\)
the sign you assign to each contribution: + if it points along your chosen positive axis, − if against
\(\sigma_{\text{ind}}\)
the induced charge density on each face of a neutral conducting slab (equal and opposite on the two faces), C/m²
Why sheet problems are pure addition, and what the slab really does

Each infinite sheet makes a field of constant magnitude \(|\sigma|/2\varepsilon_0\) that does not depend on distance (Section 5.5). Superposition says the field at a point is the sum of every sheet's field there. Since each sheet contributes one of only two values (\(\pm|\sigma|/2\varepsilon_0\), depending on which side of that sheet the point is on), the field in any region is a short signed sum. Moving the point around inside a region changes nothing; crossing a sheet flips that sheet's sign and jumps the field by \(|\sigma|/\varepsilon_0\).

A conducting slab dropped into this field responds as in the mechanism box above: free electrons shift to one face until the field inside the slab is zero. Its two faces therefore carry opposite densities \(\pm\sigma_{\text{ind}}\), and from outside the slab their two contributions cancel (one face's field and the other's are equal and opposite everywhere outside the slab). That is why, for points outside a neutral slab, you can pretend the slab is not there; and why, for points inside it, you can set the total field to zero and solve for \(\sigma_{\text{ind}}\).

Three planes, ratio of fields
Spring 2014, Question 2
Three parallel planes carry \(+\sigma\), \(-2\sigma\), \(-2\sigma\) from left to right. Point A is between the first two; point B is between the last two. Find \(E_A/E_B\).

  1. Set up units and signs

    WhyEvery plane contributes \(|\sigma_i|/2\varepsilon_0\). Measure in units of \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\). Call right \(+\).

  2. At A: the +σ plane

    WhyIt is to the left of A and positive: it pushes A away, to the right.

    \(\displaystyle +1\)

  3. At A: the near −2σ plane

    WhyIt is to the right of A and negative: it pulls toward itself, to the right.

    \(\displaystyle +2\)

  4. At A: the far −2σ plane

    WhyAlso to the right, also negative: pulls right.

    \(\displaystyle +2\)

  5. Total at A

    \(\displaystyle E_A = 1 + 2 + 2\) \(\displaystyle = 5\ \left(\times\tfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\right)\)

  6. At B: each plane

    WhyThe \(+\sigma\) plane is still to the left: \(+1\). The near \(-2\sigma\) plane is now to the left of B, so its pull points left: \(-2\). The far \(-2\sigma\) plane is to the right: \(+2\).

    \(\displaystyle E_B = 1 - 2 + 2\) \(\displaystyle = 1\ \left(\times\tfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\right)\)

  7. Ratio

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{E_A}{E_B}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{5}{1}\) \(\displaystyle = 5\)
EA/EB = 5
(ratio)
Three planes with a doubly charged center
Homework 4, Problem 5
Three horizontal planes: the center one carries \(+2\sigma_0\), the outer two carry \(-\sigma_0\) each, with \(\sigma_0 = 435\ \mathrm{pC/m^2}\). Find the field in every region.

  1. Above the stack

    WhyAll three planes are below the point. The center pushes up (\(2\) units of \(\sigma_0/2\varepsilon_0\)); each negative plane pulls down (\(1\) unit each).

    \(\displaystyle 2 - 1 - 1 = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

  2. Below the stack

    WhySame count, mirrored.

    \(\displaystyle E = 0\)

  3. In the upper gap

    WhyThe center plane (below) pushes up: \(2\). The top plane (above, negative) pulls up: \(1\). The bottom plane (below, negative) pulls down: \(-1\).

    \(\displaystyle 2 + 1 - 1 = 2\ \text{units}\) \(\displaystyle = 2\cdot\dfrac{\sigma_0}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma_0}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  4. The number

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{435\times10^{-12}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}\) \(\displaystyle = 49\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  5. Directions

    WhyIn each gap the field points from the positive center plane toward the negative plane.

    Upper gap: \(\displaystyle +\hat k\). Lower gap: \(\displaystyle -\hat k\).
outside: 0 gaps: 49 N/C, away from the center plane
Field between sheets, then the induced charge on a slab
Fall 2018, Questions 13–14
Sheet \(\sigma_1 = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at \(x = 0.6\ \mathrm{m}\); sheet \(\sigma_2 = -6.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at \(x = 0.8\ \mathrm{m}\); a neutral conducting slab from \(x = 0\) to \(0.2\ \mathrm{m}\). (Q13) Find \(E_x\) at C, \(x = 0.7\ \mathrm{m}\). (Q14) Find the charge densities on the slab's two faces.

  1. C: the σ₁ sheet

    WhyC is to the right of \(\sigma_1\), which is positive: it pushes C away, to the right.

    \(\displaystyle +8\)

  2. C: the σ₂ sheet

    WhyC is to the left of \(\sigma_2\), which is negative: it pulls C toward itself, to the right.

    \(\displaystyle +6.5\)

  3. C: the slab

    WhyThe neutral slab's two faces cancel everywhere outside it.

    \(\displaystyle 0\)

  4. C: add and convert

    WhyThe sum is in units of \(\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) divided by \(2\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8 + 6.5)\times10^{-6}}{2(8.85\times10^{-12})}\) \(\displaystyle = +8.19\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V/m}\)

  5. Inside the slab: the field from the sheets

    WhyThe slab is left of both sheets. \(\sigma_1\) pushes left: \(-8\). \(\sigma_2\) pulls right: \(+6.5\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{sheets}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-8 + 6.5}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-1.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansPointing left.

  6. Inside the slab: the field from its own faces

    WhyLeft face \(\sigma_L\) (to the left of the inside) pushes right: \(+\sigma_L/2\varepsilon_0\). Right face \(\sigma_R = -\sigma_L\) (to the right) contributes \(-\sigma_R/2\varepsilon_0\) \(= +\sigma_L/2\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{faces}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma_L}{2\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{\sigma_L}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma_L}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  7. Total inside the metal must be zero

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{\sigma_L}{\varepsilon_0} - \dfrac{1.5}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \sigma_L\) \(\displaystyle = +0.75\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\)

  8. The other face

    WhyThe slab is neutral.

    \(\displaystyle \sigma_R = -\sigma_L\) \(\displaystyle = -0.75\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\)

    MeansCheck the physics: the sheets' field inside points left, so electrons are pushed right and pile up on the right face (negative). \(\checkmark\)

General rule (from the last three steps): with \(x\) to the right and \(E_{\text{ext}}\) the sheets' field inside the slab, \(\sigma_L = -\varepsilon_0E_{\text{ext}}\) and \(\sigma_R = +\varepsilon_0E_{\text{ext}}\).

Ex(C) = +8.19×10⁵ V/m σL = +0.75 μC/m² σR = −0.75 μC/m²
What each letter means
\(\sigma_L,\ \sigma_R\)
the induced charge densities on the slab's left and right faces, C/m²; they are equal and opposite for a neutral slab
\(E_{\text{ext}}\)
the field the outside sheets make at the slab's location (with sign: positive if along \(+x\)), N/C
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
\(x\)
the axis, taken to point to the right
V/m
μC/m²
Same setup, different numbers
Spring 2015, Questions 5–6
\(\sigma_1 = +5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at \(x = 0\); \(\sigma_2 = -9.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at \(x = 0.8\ \mathrm{m}\); a neutral slab from \(0.2\) to \(0.4\ \mathrm{m}\). Find \(E_x\) at \(x = 0.9\ \mathrm{m}\) and the charge density on the slab's left face.

  1. At x = 0.9: the σ₁ sheet

    WhyPositive and to the left: pushes right.

    \(\displaystyle +5\)

  2. At x = 0.9: the σ₂ sheet

    WhyNegative and to the left: pulls left, toward itself.

    \(\displaystyle -9.5\)

  3. Add and convert

    Why\(2\varepsilon_0 = 1.77\times10^{-11}\).

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(5 - 9.5)\times10^{-6}}{1.77\times10^{-11}}\) \(\displaystyle = -2.54\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V/m}\)

  4. Inside the slab: the sheets

    Why\(\sigma_1\) (left, positive) pushes right: \(+5\). \(\sigma_2\) (right, negative) pulls right: \(+9.5\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{sheets}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{+14.5}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

  5. The faces must cancel it

    WhyFaces give \(\sigma_L/\varepsilon_0\) (previous example).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{\sigma_L}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{14.5}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \sigma_L\) \(\displaystyle = -7.25\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\)

    MeansAnd \(\sigma_R = +7.25\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\).

Ex = −2.54×10⁵ V/m σL = −7.25 μC/m²
Two positive planes beside a neutral slab
Fall 2015, Questions 19–20
Two planes, each with \(\sigma = +5\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\), sit to the right of a neutral conducting slab. (Q19) What does the right plane alone contribute at a point P to its left? (Q20) Find the charge density on the slab's left face.

  1. Right plane alone at P

    WhyP is to its left; a positive plane pushes away, so to the left (\(-x\)).

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{5}{2(8.85\times10^{-12})}\) \(\displaystyle = -2.82\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  2. Inside the slab: the planes

    WhyBoth are to the right and positive: both push left.

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{planes}}\) \(\displaystyle = -2\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  3. The faces must cancel it

    WhyFaces give \(\sigma_L/\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{\sigma_L}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = +\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \sigma_L\) \(\displaystyle = +5,\) \(\displaystyle \sigma_R\) \(\displaystyle = -5\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\)
Ex = −2.82×10¹¹ N/C σL = +5 C/m²
Trap

The induced charges on the slab are real charges: they matter if you are asked for the field between the slab and a sheet when the slab is not neutral, or for a Gaussian surface that cuts through only one face. For a neutral slab and a point outside it, they cancel and you may ignore the slab entirely.

Fields region by region, induced charges, and ΔV

Two infinite insulating sheets and a neutral conducting slab, the layout used in Spring 2015 Q5–6 and Fall 2018 Q13–15. Each sheet adds a constant |σ|/2ε₀ pointing away from positive and toward negative. The slab's faces take whatever charge makes the field inside it zero.

Sheet plus a line of charge: where is \(E = 0\)?
Spring 2015, Questions 7–9
A sheet \(\sigma\) lies in the plane \(x = 0\). A line \(\lambda\), parallel to \(z\), passes through \(x = d\). Where on the \(x\)-axis between them is \(E = 0\), and what must be true of the signs?

  1. The sheet's field at x = r

    WhyA constant \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\), pointing away from a positive sheet: to the right.

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{sheet}}\) \(\displaystyle = +\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

  2. The line's field at x = r

    WhyThe distance to the line is \(d - r\). A positive line pushes the point away, and the point is to its left: to the left.

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{line}}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(d - r)}\)

  3. When can they cancel?

    WhyOnly if they point in opposite directions. With the signs above, that happens when \(\lambda\) and \(\sigma\) have the same sign.

  4. Set the sizes equal

    WhyCancel \(\varepsilon_0\) and a factor of 2 from both sides.

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(d - r)}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \sigma\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi(d - r)}\)

  5. Solve for r

    WhyMultiply by \((d - r)\), divide by \(\sigma\), then subtract from \(d\).

    \(\displaystyle d - r = \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\sigma}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow r\) \(\displaystyle = d - \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\sigma}\)
same signs r = d − λ/(πσ)
What each letter means
\(\sigma\)
surface charge density: charge per unit area on a sheet or surface, in C/m² (\(\sigma = Q/A\) when uniform)
\(\lambda\)
linear charge density: charge per unit length along a line, rod, or ring, in C/m (\(\lambda = Q/L\) when uniform)
\(d\)
the distance from the sheet to the line, m
\(r\)
the position of the point on the \(x\)-axis, measured from the sheet, m; \(d - r\) is its distance from the line
\(E_x\)
the \(x\)-component of the field at that point, N/C, with sign
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
Line charge plus a sphere-and-shell system
Spring 2014, Question 12
An insulating sphere with \(Q = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) (radius \(6\ \mathrm{cm}\)) sits inside an uncharged conducting shell (radius \(10\ \mathrm{cm}\)), centered at the origin. A line \(\lambda = +1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\), parallel to \(z\), passes through \((-30\ \mathrm{cm}, 0)\). Find \(E_x\) at \(P = (-20\ \mathrm{cm}, 0)\).

  1. Field of the line at P

    WhyP is \(10\ \mathrm{cm}\) to the right of the positive line: pushed away, to \(+x\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{line}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2(8.99\times10^{9})(10^{-6})}{0.1}\) \(\displaystyle = +1.8\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  2. What the sphere system looks like from P

    WhyP is outside the shell, \(20\ \mathrm{cm}\) from the center. The enclosed charge is \(+8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) (the shell is neutral).

    MeansFrom outside, it acts like a point charge +8 μC at the origin.

  3. Field of the sphere system at P

    WhyP is to the left of the origin; a positive charge pushes it away, to \(-x\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{\text{sph}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(8\times10^{-6})}{(0.2)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = -1.8\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  4. Add

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = 1.8\times10^{5} - 1.8\times10^{6}\) \(\displaystyle = -1.6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)
Ex = −1.6×10⁶ N/C

Electric Potential Energy and Electric Potential

On Exam 1: electrical potential (7.2–7.5), 7 of 28 · work and energy (7.1), 2 of 28.

OpenStax 7.1 Electric potential energy · 7.2 Potential and potential difference · 7.3 Calculations of potential · 7.4 Determining field from potential · 7.5 Equipotential surfaces and conductors · 7.6 Applications

Lecture 5's roadmap: Physics 2111 went Force → Energy; Physics 2112 goes Force → Field, and now Energy → Potential. Potential energy \(U\) belongs to a system of charges; potential \(V\) is \(U\) per unit charge and belongs to space, the same way \(\vec E\) is force per unit charge. Because \(U\) and \(V\) are scalars, this chapter is mostly "no sines and cosines," which the lectures repeat three times.

7.1 Electric potential energy

In plain words

Potential energy \(U\) is energy stored in the arrangement of charges. Pull two opposite charges apart and you store energy (like stretching a spring); let two like charges fly apart and stored energy turns into motion. The field's work and the change in \(U\) are always opposite: \(\Delta U = -W_{\text{field}}\).

Work and potential energy (the 2111 connection)
\[ W = \int_{1}^{2}\vec F\cdot d\vec r, \qquad W_{\text{total}} = \Delta K, \qquad \Delta U = U_f - U_i = -W_{\text{field}} \]
What each letter means
\(W\)
work done by a force as the object moves from point 1 to point 2, in J
\(\vec F\)
the force (here the electric force), N
\(d\vec r\)
a tiny step along the path, m; the dot product keeps only the part of the step along the force
\(W_{\text{total}}\)
the work of all forces added together
\(\Delta K\)
the change in kinetic energy, J
\(U,\ U_i,\ U_f\)
electric potential energy, and its initial and final values, J
\(\Delta U\)
final minus initial potential energy, J
\(W_{\text{field}}\)
the work done by the electric field's force (not by your hand), J

The Coulomb force is conservative, so it has a potential energy. Moving with the force: field does positive work, \(U\) decreases, kinetic energy can increase. Moving against the force: field does negative work, \(U\) increases (something else, like your hand, supplied the work). A charge released from rest moves in the direction that decreases \(U\) (Lecture 5 checkpoint: "Nature wants things to move in such a way that PE decreases").

Two charges brought from far apart to separation \(r\) (choosing \(U = 0\) at infinity):

\[ U = \frac{k\,q_1 q_2}{r} \]
What each letter means
\(U\)
the potential energy of the pair, J, taking \(U = 0\) when they are infinitely far apart
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(q_1,\ q_2\)
the two charges with their signs, C: like signs give \(U \gt 0\), opposite signs give \(U \lt 0\)
\(r\)
their separation, m (not squared, unlike the force)

Keep the signs. Like charges: \(U \gt 0\), and it grows as they get closer. Opposite charges: \(U \lt 0\), and it gets more negative (lower) as they get closer.

Why the Coulomb force has a potential energy, and where \(kq_1q_2/r\) comes from

Path independence. The force on \(q_2\) from a fixed \(q_1\) points along the line joining them and depends only on the distance \(r\). Move \(q_2\) along any path. On each tiny step, only the part of the step that changes \(r\) does work (the part perpendicular to the radial line is perpendicular to the force). So the total work depends only on the starting and ending distances, not on the route. That is the definition of a conservative force, and it is what allows a potential energy to exist. The same argument works for gravity, which is why the two theories look alike.

The formula, derived. Define \(U = 0\) when the charges are infinitely far apart (no interaction). Bring \(q_2\) in from infinity to distance \(d\) along a radial line. The field's force is \(kq_1q_2/r^2\) outward (for like charges); its work is \(W\) \(= \int_\infty^{d}\frac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}\,dr\), but the force and the inward motion oppose each other, so with \(dr\) negative this integral is \(kq_1q_2\left[-\frac1r\right]_\infty^{d}\) \(= -\frac{kq_1q_2}{d}\). Then \(U = -W = +\frac{kq_1q_2}{d}\). For opposite charges the force is inward, the work is positive, and \(U = -\frac{k|q_1q_2|}{d}\), which the same formula gives automatically once the signs of the charges are kept. So the one expression \(U = kq_1q_2/r\), signs included, covers both cases.

What each letter means
\(d\)
the final separation of the two charges, m
\(r,\ dr\)
the running separation during the trip in from infinity, and a tiny change in it (negative when moving inward)
\(W\)
the work done by the field's force during the trip, J
\(U\)
the potential energy at separation \(d\), J; equals \(-W\)

What the sign means physically. Positive \(U\) means the system holds energy it can release: let two like charges go and they fly apart, converting \(U\) into kinetic energy. Negative \(U\) means the system is bound: to separate two opposite charges you must supply \(|U|\) of work. "Higher \(U\)" always means "closer to being able to do something on its own."

Hand vs. field: who does the work?
Lecture 5 clicker · Lecture 6, Example 6.1
A charge \(q = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) sits in a uniform field \(E = 6\ \mathrm{N/C}\) pointing down. An outside force lifts it \(0.4\ \mathrm{m}\) straight up at constant velocity. Find (a) the work done by the field, (b) the work done by the outside force, (c) \(\Delta U\), and (d) \(\Delta V\).

  1. The electric force on the charge

    Why\(\vec F = q\vec E\). A positive charge is pushed along the field, so this force points down.

    \(\displaystyle F = qE\) \(\displaystyle = (8\times10^{-6})(6)\) \(\displaystyle = 4.8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N},\ \text{down}\)

  2. The outside force

    WhyConstant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero. The outside force must cancel the electric force exactly.

    Outside force: \(\displaystyle 4.8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N}\), up.

  3. (a) Work by the field

    WhyWork is force times displacement times \(\cos\) of the angle between them. The field pushes down, the charge moves up: \(180^\circ\), \(\cos180^\circ = -1\).

    \(\displaystyle W_E = Fd\cos180^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = -(4.8\times10^{-5})(0.4)\) \(\displaystyle = -1.92\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{J}\)

  4. (b) Work by the outside force

    WhyIt pushes up and the charge moves up: angle 0, \(\cos0 = 1\).

    \(\displaystyle W_{\text{out}}\) \(\displaystyle = +(4.8\times10^{-5})(0.4)\) \(\displaystyle = +1.92\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansCheck: total work \(W_E + W_{\text{out}} = 0 = \Delta K\), as it must be at constant speed. The lecture slide lists \(-1.92\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{J}\) under "work done moving the charge up"; that number is the field's work.

  5. (c) Change in potential energy

    Why\(\Delta U = -W_{\text{field}}\): only the conservative (electric) force has a potential energy. The outside force does not.

    \(\displaystyle \Delta U = -(-1.92\times10^{-5})\) \(\displaystyle = +1.92\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansYou pushed the charge against the field and stored that energy in the system.

  6. (d) Change in potential: two ways

    WhyDivide \(\Delta U\) by the charge, or use \(\Delta V = -\vec E\cdot\Delta\vec s\) directly. Both must agree.

    \(\displaystyle \Delta V = \dfrac{\Delta U}{q}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{1.92\times10^{-5}}{8\times10^{-6}}\) \(\displaystyle = +2.4\ \mathrm{V}\)
    \(\displaystyle \vec E\cdot\Delta\vec s\) \(\displaystyle = (6)(0.4)\cos180^\circ\) \(\displaystyle = -2.4\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \Delta V\) \(\displaystyle = +2.4\ \mathrm{V}\)

    MeansMoving against the field raises the potential, like climbing a hill.

What changes if \(q \to -8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)? The electric force flips (now up), both works flip sign, and \(\Delta U\) flips to \(-1.92\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{J}\). But \(\Delta V = +2.4\ \mathrm{V}\) is unchanged: a potential difference belongs to the field and the two points, not to the charge you move.

What if instead the field pointed up? Then every answer, (a) through (d), changes sign.

What is \(V\) at the starting point? It cannot be determined. Only differences are physical; you may put \(V = 0\) anywhere.

W_E = −1.92×10⁻⁵ J W_out = +1.92×10⁻⁵ J ΔU = +1.92×10⁻⁵ J ΔV = +2.4 V
What each letter means
\(F\)
the electric force on the charge, \(qE\), N
\(d\)
the distance moved, m
\(W_E,\ W_H\)
work done by the electric field, and by the hand (outside force), J
\(\Delta U\)
change in potential energy, J; equals \(-W_E\)
\(\Delta V\)
change in potential, V; equals \(\Delta U/q\)
\(\vec E\)
the field vector, N/C
\(\Delta\vec s\)
the displacement vector (where it ended minus where it started), m
\(q\)
the moved charge, C, with sign
V
