Change in \(U\) when one charge moves
Lecture 5 checkpoint · Homework 5, Problem 4
A charge \(q\) moves from distance \(r_1\) to \(r_2\) from a fixed charge \(Q\). The change in potential energy is the difference of the two pair energies:\[ \Delta U = U_2 - U_1 = kQq\left(\frac{1}{r_2} - \frac{1}{r_1}\right) \]
What each letter means
\(\Delta U\)
change in potential energy, final minus initial, J
\(Q\)
the fixed charge, C
\(q\)
the charge that moves, C
\(r_1,\ r_2\)
the initial and final distances between them, m; only these two numbers matter, not the route
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)

Homework 5, Problem 4: \(Q_1 = +5.7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) is fixed; \(Q_2 = +3.5\ \mathrm{nC}\) with mass \(6.4\ \mu\mathrm{g}\) is free. (a) Find \(U\) when \(Q_2\) is \(0.39\ \mathrm{m}\) from \(Q_1\). (b) Released from rest there, what is its speed at \(0.79\ \mathrm{m}\)?

  1. Read the setup

    WhyOnly the free charge can move, so only it can have kinetic energy. The fixed one never moves and never gets any.

    \(\displaystyle Q_1 = +5.7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\): fixed in place.
    \(\displaystyle Q_2 = +3.5\ \mathrm{nC}\), mass \(\displaystyle m = 6.4\ \mu\mathrm{g}\): free to move.
    It starts at \(\displaystyle r_i = 0.39\ \mathrm{m}\) from \(\displaystyle Q_1\) and we want its speed at \(\displaystyle r_f = 0.79\ \mathrm{m}\).

    MeansBoth charges are positive, so they repel. \(Q_2\) is pushed away from \(Q_1\) and speeds up as it goes outward.

  2. Convert to SI units

    Why\(k\) works in coulombs and meters, and \(K = \tfrac12mv^2\) needs kilograms to give joules.

    "μ" is \(\displaystyle 10^{-6}\): \(\displaystyle Q_1 = 5.7\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\).
    "n" (nano) is \(\displaystyle 10^{-9}\): \(\displaystyle Q_2 = 3.5\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\).
    A microgram is \(\displaystyle 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{g}\), and a gram is \(\displaystyle 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}\), so \(\displaystyle 1\ \mu\mathrm{g}\) \(\displaystyle = 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{kg}\): \(\displaystyle m = 6.4\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{kg}\).

    MeansGetting the mass wrong by a factor of 1000 is the most common way to lose this problem.

  3. Compute \(kQ_1Q_2\) once

    WhyThe top of \(U = kQ_1Q_2/r\) is the same at both distances. Work it out once and reuse it.

    Charges: \(\displaystyle (5.7)(3.5)\times10^{-6}\times10^{-9}\) \(\displaystyle = 19.95\times10^{-15}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.995\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    Times \(\displaystyle k\): \(\displaystyle (8.99\times10^{9})(1.995\times10^{-14})\) \(\displaystyle = 1.794\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,m}\)

  4. Part (a): \(U\) at the starting distance

    WhyUse \(U = kQ_1Q_2/r\) with \(r = r_i\). Divide by \(r\); do not square it.

    \(\displaystyle U_i\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{1.794\times10^{-4}}{0.39}\) \(\displaystyle = 4.60\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansPositive, as it must be for two like charges. This stored energy is what will turn into motion.

  5. Part (b): write down energy conservation

    WhyNo outside force acts, so the total energy \(K + U\) stays the same. That is \(K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f\). \(K\) is the moving charge's kinetic energy; \(U\) is the pair's potential energy.

    \(\displaystyle K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f\)

  6. "Released from rest" means \(K_i = 0\)

    WhyAt rest, \(v = 0\), so \(K = \tfrac12m(0)^2 = 0\). The problem gives you this number in words, not symbols.

    \(\displaystyle 0 + U_i = K_f + U_f\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow K_f\) \(\displaystyle = U_i - U_f\)

    MeansThe kinetic energy gained equals the potential energy lost.

  7. \(U\) at the final distance

    WhySame top, new distance \(r_f\).

    \(\displaystyle U_f\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{1.794\times10^{-4}}{0.79}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.27\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansSmaller than \(U_i\), because the charges are farther apart.

  8. Subtract to get the kinetic energy

    \(\displaystyle K_f\) \(\displaystyle = 4.60\times10^{-4} - 2.27\times10^{-4}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.33\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansPositive, so the outward motion really happens. A negative result would mean a sign slip.

  9. Solve \(K = \tfrac12mv^2\) for \(v\)

    WhyUndo each operation around \(v\) in reverse order: the ½, then the \(m\), then the square.

    \(\displaystyle K_f = \tfrac12mv^2\)
    Multiply both sides by 2: \(\displaystyle 2K_f = mv^2\)
    Divide by \(\displaystyle m\): \(\displaystyle v^2 = \dfrac{2K_f}{m}\)
    Square root: \(\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K_f}{m}}\)

  10. Plug in

    Top: \(\displaystyle 2K_f = 2(2.33\times10^{-4})\) \(\displaystyle = 4.66\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J}\)
    Divide by the mass: \(\displaystyle \dfrac{4.66\times10^{-4}}{6.4\times10^{-9}}\) \(\displaystyle = 7.28\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}\)
    Square root: \(\displaystyle v = \sqrt{7.28\times10^{4}}\) \(\displaystyle = 270\ \mathrm{m/s}\)

    MeansUnits check: J/kg is \(\mathrm{m^2/s^2}\), and its square root is m/s.

(a) U = 4.60×10⁻⁴ J (b) v = 270 m/s
m/s
Moving a charge toward a line of charge
Fall 2015, Questions 8–9
\(+Q\) is moved from distance \(a\) to a closer distance \(b\) from an infinite line with positive charge per length \(\lambda\). (Q8) What is the sign of the work done by the field? (Q9) What is \(|\Delta U|\)?

  1. Which way does the field push?

    WhyA positive charge near a positive line is repelled: pushed away from the line.

    The charge is moved from \(\displaystyle a\) to \(\displaystyle b \lt a\), toward the line: against the push.

    MeansMotion against the force: the field does negative work (Q8).

  2. Potential of a line

    WhyIntegrating the line field \(E = 2k\lambda/r\) gives a logarithm (Section 7.4).

    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = -2k\lambda\ln r + \text{const}\)

  3. Change in V from a to b

    WhyThe constant cancels in a difference. \(\ln b - \ln a = \ln(b/a)\).

    \(\displaystyle \Delta V = V(b) - V(a)\) \(\displaystyle = -2k\lambda\ln\dfrac{b}{a}\)

    MeansSince \(b \lt a\), \(\ln(b/a) \lt 0\), so \(\Delta V \gt 0\): closer to a positive line is higher potential.

  4. Change in U (Q9)

    Why\(\Delta U = Q\,\Delta V\).

    \(\displaystyle |\Delta U| = |2k\lambda Q\ln(b/a)|\)

    MeansThe distractor \(|2k\lambda Q(1/b - 1/a)|\) is the point-charge shape; \(|2k\lambda Q(a-b)|\) is the uniform-field shape.

Q8: negative Q9: |2kλQ ln(b/a)|
What each letter means
\(Q\)
the charge that is moved, C
\(\lambda\)
linear charge density: charge per unit length along a line, rod, or ring, in C/m (\(\lambda = Q/L\) when uniform)
\(a,\ b\)
the starting and ending distances from the line, m
\(\ln\)
natural logarithm; \(\ln(b/a)\) is negative when \(b \lt a\)
\(V(r)\)
the potential at distance \(r\) from the line; "const" is the arbitrary reference value
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
Two charges released: energy plus momentum
Lecture 5, Example 5.1
\(q_1 = +6\ \mathrm{nC}\) (mass \(m_1 = 5\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{kg}\)) and \(q_2 = +8\ \mathrm{nC}\) (mass \(m_2 = 7\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{kg}\)) are held \(10\ \mathrm{cm}\) apart and released. Find their speeds when they are far apart.

  1. Energy stored at the start

    WhyBoth at rest, so all the energy is the pair's potential energy.

    \(\displaystyle U_i = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{d}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(6\times10^{-9})(8\times10^{-9})}{0.10}\) \(\displaystyle = 4.32\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{J}\)

  2. Energy at the end

    Why"Far apart" means \(U_f = 0\). Every joule of \(U_i\) is now kinetic energy, shared by both charges.

    \(\displaystyle \tfrac12 m_1v_1^2 + \tfrac12 m_2v_2^2\) \(\displaystyle = 4.32\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{J}\)

  3. Momentum is conserved too

    WhyThe only forces are the two charges pushing on each other, internal to the system. Total momentum starts at zero and stays zero.

    \(\displaystyle m_1v_1 = m_2v_2\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow v_2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{m_1}{m_2}v_1\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac57 v_1\)

    MeansThey fly in opposite directions; the lighter one faster.

  4. Put the momentum result into the energy equation

    WhyReplace \(v_2\) so only \(v_1\) is unknown, then factor out \(\tfrac12 m_1v_1^2\).

    \(\displaystyle \tfrac12 m_1v_1^2 + \tfrac12 m_2\left(\tfrac{m_1}{m_2}\right)^2v_1^2\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12 m_1v_1^2\left(1 + \tfrac{m_1}{m_2}\right)\)
    \(\displaystyle 1 + \tfrac{m_1}{m_2}\) \(\displaystyle = 1 + \tfrac57\) \(\displaystyle = 1.714\)

  5. Solve for v₁

    WhyMultiply by 2, divide by everything that multiplies \(v_1^2\), take the square root.

    \(\displaystyle v_1\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{\dfrac{2U_i}{m_1(1 + m_1/m_2)}}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(4.32\times10^{-6})}{(5\times10^{-10})(1.714)}}\) \(\displaystyle = 100\ \mathrm{m/s}\)

  6. Then v₂

    \(\displaystyle v_2 = \tfrac57(100.3)\) \(\displaystyle = 71.7\ \mathrm{m/s}\)

  7. Check the energy

    WhyPut both speeds back in.

    \(\displaystyle \tfrac12(5\times10^{-10})(100.3)^2 + \tfrac12(7\times10^{-10})(71.67)^2\) \(\displaystyle = 4.32\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{J}\ \checkmark\)
v₁ = 100 m/s v₂ = 71.7 m/s
What each letter means
\(q_1,\ q_2\)
the two charges, C
\(m_1,\ m_2\)
their masses, kg
\(v_1,\ v_2\)
their final speeds when far apart, m/s
\(d\)
the initial separation, m
\(U_i\)
the initial potential energy, \(kq_1q_2/d\), J; it all becomes kinetic energy
\(m_1v_1 = m_2v_2\)
momentum conservation: equal and opposite momenta because they started at rest
m/s

If one charge is fixed (Homework 5 P4 and P6), skip the momentum step: all the released energy goes to the free charge.

One charge released between two fixed charges
Homework 5, Problem 6
Two \(5.22\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) charges are fixed at \(x = \pm3.01\ \mathrm{cm}\). A \(3.08\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), \(7.64\ \mathrm{mg}\) particle is released from rest on the \(y\)-axis at \(y = 1.99\ \mathrm{cm}\). What is its speed at \(y = 5.35\ \mathrm{cm}\)?

  1. Read the figure

    WhyThe two fixed charges are mirror images across the \(y\)-axis. Their sideways pushes on the particle cancel, so it slides straight up the \(y\)-axis.

    Fixed: \(\displaystyle Q = +5.22\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at \(\displaystyle x = +3.01\ \mathrm{cm}\) and at \(\displaystyle x = -3.01\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    Moving: \(\displaystyle q = +3.08\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), mass \(\displaystyle 7.64\ \mathrm{mg}\), released from rest at \(\displaystyle y = 1.99\ \mathrm{cm}\), asked about at \(\displaystyle y = 5.35\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    MeansAll positive, so the particle is repelled by both fixed charges and speeds up as it moves away.

  2. Convert to SI units

    Why\(k\) needs C and m; \(K = \tfrac12mv^2\) needs kg.

    \(\displaystyle Q = 5.22\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\), \(\displaystyle q = 3.08\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\)
    A milligram is \(\displaystyle 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}\) \(\displaystyle = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{kg}\): \(\displaystyle m = 7.64\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{kg}\)
    Positions: divide centimeters by 100 at the end, once each distance is found.

  3. Distance from the particle to one fixed charge

    WhyThe height \(y\) is not that distance. The particle, the origin, and a fixed charge form a right triangle with legs \(3.01\ \mathrm{cm}\) (sideways) and \(y\) (up). The distance is the hypotenuse.

    Start: \(\displaystyle r_i = \sqrt{3.01^2 + 1.99^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{9.060 + 3.960}\) \(\displaystyle = 3.608\ \mathrm{cm}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.03608\ \mathrm{m}\)
    End: \(\displaystyle r_f = \sqrt{3.01^2 + 5.35^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{9.060 + 28.62}\) \(\displaystyle = 6.139\ \mathrm{cm}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.06139\ \mathrm{m}\)

    MeansBoth fixed charges are at this same distance, by symmetry.

  4. Which energies change?

    WhyThere are three pairs. The pair of fixed charges never moves, so its energy is the same before and after and cancels out. The two pairs that include the particle are identical (same charges, same distance), so together they give twice one pair.

    \(\displaystyle U_{\text{moving}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQq}{r} + \dfrac{kQq}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2kQq}{r}\)

  5. Compute \(2kQq\) once

    Charges: \(\displaystyle (5.22)(3.08)\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.608\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    Times \(\displaystyle k\): \(\displaystyle 0.1445\ \mathrm{J\,m}\); times 2: \(\displaystyle 0.2891\ \mathrm{J\,m}\)

  6. Potential energy at the start and at the end

    WhyDivide the same top by each distance in meters.

    \(\displaystyle U_i = \dfrac{0.2891}{0.03608}\) \(\displaystyle = 8.01\ \mathrm{J}\)
    \(\displaystyle U_f = \dfrac{0.2891}{0.06139}\) \(\displaystyle = 4.71\ \mathrm{J}\)

  7. Energy conservation

    Why\(K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f\). Released from rest means \(K_i = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle K_f = U_i - U_f\) \(\displaystyle = 8.01 - 4.71\) \(\displaystyle = 3.30\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansPositive, so moving away is what happens.

  8. Speed from \(K = \tfrac12mv^2\)

    WhyMultiply by 2, divide by \(m\), take the square root: \(v = \sqrt{2K_f/m}\).

    \(\displaystyle 2K_f = 6.60\ \mathrm{J}\)
    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{6.60}{7.64\times10^{-6}}\) \(\displaystyle = 8.64\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle v = \sqrt{8.64\times10^{5}}\) \(\displaystyle = 930\ \mathrm{m/s}\)
v = 930 m/s
Potential energy of a collection of charges
\[ U_{\text{total}} = \sum_{\text{all pairs } i \lt j}\frac{k\,q_i q_j}{r_{ij}} \]
What each letter means
\(U_{\text{total}}\)
the energy stored in the whole arrangement, J
\(\sum_{i \lt j}\)
add one term for every pair of charges, counting each pair once (\(i \lt j\) is the bookkeeping that prevents double counting)
\(q_i,\ q_j\)
the two charges in that pair, with signs, C
\(r_{ij}\)
the distance between charge \(i\) and charge \(j\), m
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(\Delta U = qV\)
energy change when one more charge \(q\) is brought to a point where the others make potential \(V\)
  • One term per pair: 3 charges have 3 pairs, 4 charges have 6 pairs. Do not double count (Lecture 5: "don't double count, no sines and cosines").
  • \(U_{\text{total}}\) = the work an outside agent must do to assemble the configuration from infinity = minus the work done by the field during assembly.
  • Bringing in one more charge \(q\) to a point where the existing charges make potential \(V\): \(\Delta U = qV\) = work you do (Section 7.2).
Equilateral triangles and the sign of "work"
Lecture 5 clickers
Three identical charges \(Q\) are brought from far away to the corners of an equilateral triangle of side \(d\). How much work does the outside agent do, and how much does the field do? Then: what changes if one charge is \(-Q\)?

  1. Count the pairs

    WhyThree charges make \(3\times2/2 = 3\) pairs, all at the same distance \(d\).

    pairs: (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)

  2. Write the total

    WhyOne \(kq_iq_j/r_{ij}\) per pair, signs in.

    \(\displaystyle U\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ^2}{d} + \dfrac{kQ^2}{d} + \dfrac{kQ^2}{d}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{3kQ^2}{d}\)

  3. The same total, built one charge at a time

    WhyThe first charge costs nothing (nothing else is there). The second creates one pair. The third creates two new pairs.

    \(\displaystyle W_1 = 0,\) \(\displaystyle W_2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ^2}{d},\) \(\displaystyle W_3\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2kQ^2}{d}\)
    \(\displaystyle W_1 + W_2 + W_3\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{3kQ^2}{d}\) \(\displaystyle = U\)

    MeansThe order does not matter; the sum of pair terms is the same.

  4. Who did the work?

    WhyThe outside agent assembled the charges: its work equals \(U\). The field's work is the opposite.

    \(\displaystyle W_{\text{agent}}\) \(\displaystyle = +\dfrac{3kQ^2}{d},\) \(\displaystyle W_{\text{field}}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{3kQ^2}{d}\)

  5. One charge flipped to −Q

    WhyTwo pairs now have opposite signs; one pair (the two \(+Q\)) is still like-signed.

    \(\displaystyle U\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k}{d}\left(-Q^2 - Q^2 + Q^2\right)\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{kQ^2}{d}\)

    MeansNegative: the field did \(+kQ^2/d\) of work pulling the charges together; the agent had to hold them back.

Checkpoint: a third charge at a point equidistant from \(+Q\) and \(-Q\). The two new pair terms are \(+kQq/r\) and \(-kQq/r\); they cancel for either sign of \(q\), so \(U\) does not change.

Checkpoint: \(+Q\) and \(-2Q\). A third charge can be added without changing \(U\) anywhere the existing charges make \(V = 0\): \(kQ/r_1 - 2kQ/r_2 = 0\), so \(r_2 = 2r_1\). On the axis with \(Q\) at 0 and \(-2Q\) at \(d\): at \(x = -d\) (distances \(d\) and \(2d\)) and at \(x = d/3\) (distances \(d/3\) and \(2d/3\)). The sign of the third charge does not matter.

U = 3kQ²/d with one −Q: U = −kQ²/d
Work to assemble a square of charges
Spring 2014, Question 13
Charges \(q\) at \((0, 0)\), \(q\) at \((0, a)\), \(q\) at \((a, 0)\), and \(2q\) at \((a, a)\). How much work does it take to assemble them from infinity?

  1. Count the pairs

    WhyFour charges make \(4\times3/2 = 6\) pairs.

    4 sides + 2 diagonals = 6

  2. The four sides (distance a)

    WhyList each pair by its two charges.

    \(\displaystyle (q)(q) + (q)(q) + (q)(2q) + (q)(2q)\) \(\displaystyle = q^2 + q^2 + 2q^2 + 2q^2\) \(\displaystyle = 6q^2\)
    \(\displaystyle \text{sides: } \dfrac{6kq^2}{a}\)

  3. The two diagonals (distance a√2)

    WhyOne diagonal joins \((0,0)\) to the \(2q\); the other joins \((0,a)\) to \((a,0)\).

    \(\displaystyle (q)(2q) + (q)(q) = 3q^2\)
    \(\displaystyle \text{diagonals: } \dfrac{3kq^2}{a\sqrt2}\)

  4. Add and factor

    WhyPull out \(kq^2/a\) so only numbers remain. Write \(k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\) as the answer choices do.

    \(\displaystyle U\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kq^2}{a}\left(6 + \dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}\right)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\left(6 + \dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}\right)\) \(\displaystyle = 8.12\,\dfrac{kq^2}{a}\)
U = (q²/4πε₀a)(6 + 3/√2)
Energy of a three-charge square corner
Fall 2018, Question 2
\(+2Q\) at \((0, a)\), \(-Q\) at \((0, 0)\), \(+Q\) at \((a, 0)\), with \(Q = 7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) and \(a = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}\). How much work is required to create this configuration from infinity?

  1. Count the pairs

    WhyThree charges, three pairs: two along sides, one along the diagonal.

  2. Write each pair with its sign

    WhyThe \(+2Q\) and \(-Q\) share a side (distance \(a\)); so do \(-Q\) and \(+Q\). The \(+2Q\) and \(+Q\) are across the diagonal \(a\sqrt2\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{k(2Q)(-Q)}{a}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{2kQ^2}{a},\) \(\displaystyle \dfrac{k(-Q)(Q)}{a}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{kQ^2}{a},\) \(\displaystyle \dfrac{k(2Q)(Q)}{a\sqrt2}\) \(\displaystyle = +\dfrac{\sqrt2\,kQ^2}{a}\)

  3. Add

    \(\displaystyle U\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ^2}{a}\left(-2 - 1 + \sqrt2\right)\) \(\displaystyle = -1.586\,\dfrac{kQ^2}{a}\)

  4. The common factor

    Why\(Q^2 = (7\times10^{-6})^2\) \(= 49\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2}\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{kQ^2}{a}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(49\times10^{-12})}{0.5}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.8810\ \mathrm{J}\)

  5. Multiply

    \(\displaystyle U = (0.8810)(-1.586)\) \(\displaystyle = -1.40\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative: the attractions win. The charges pull themselves together; the assembler does negative work, and the field does +1.40 J.

U = −1.40 J
J
Three charges on a right triangle
Homework 5, Problem 1
\(q_1 = 9.5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), \(q_2 = 58\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) (drawn negative), \(q_3 = 25\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) on a right triangle with the right angle at \(q_2\); \(q_1\)–\(q_2\) is \(26\ \mathrm{cm}\) and \(q_2\)–\(q_3\) is \(65\ \mathrm{cm}\). (a) Find \(U\). (b) Find \(\Delta U\) when \(q_3\) is brought in from infinity with the others fixed.

  1. Read the figure: signs and sides

    WhyThe problem prints only the sizes of the charges. The ⊕ and ⊖ drawn in the figure carry the signs, and the labels on the sides tell you which distance belongs to which pair.

    \(\displaystyle q_1 = +9.5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) (left corner), \(\displaystyle q_2 = -58\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) (the right-angle corner, drawn ⊖), \(\displaystyle q_3 = +25\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) (top corner).
    Side \(\displaystyle a = 26\ \mathrm{cm}\) joins \(\displaystyle q_1\) and \(\displaystyle q_2\). Side \(\displaystyle b = 65\ \mathrm{cm}\) joins \(\displaystyle q_2\) and \(\displaystyle q_3\). The right angle is at \(\displaystyle q_2\).

    MeansTwo pairs have opposite signs (1–2 and 2–3), so they will give negative terms. One pair has like signs (1–3), so it will give a positive term. Knowing this in advance lets you catch a sign slip later.

  2. Convert everything to SI units

    Why\(k\) \(= 8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\) is built from coulombs and meters. If the charges are not in coulombs and the distances not in meters, the answer is off by powers of ten.

    "μ" means micro, \(\displaystyle \times10^{-6}\): \(\displaystyle q_1 = 9.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\), \(\displaystyle q_2 = -58\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\), \(\displaystyle q_3 = 25\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\).
    "c" means centi, \(\displaystyle \times10^{-2}\): \(\displaystyle a = 26\ \mathrm{cm}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.26\ \mathrm{m}\), \(\displaystyle b = 65\ \mathrm{cm}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.65\ \mathrm{m}\).

  3. Count the pairs

    WhyPotential energy belongs to pairs of charges, not to single charges. Each pair is counted once: "1 with 2" and "2 with 1" are the same pair.

    Three charges make \(\displaystyle \dfrac{3\times2}{2} = 3\) pairs: \(\displaystyle (1,2)\), \(\displaystyle (2,3)\), \(\displaystyle (1,3)\).

    MeansPart (a) will be a sum of exactly three terms.

  4. Find the distance that is not printed

    Why\(q_1\) and \(q_3\) sit at the two ends of the hypotenuse. The right angle is at \(q_2\), so the Pythagorean theorem gives the hypotenuse from the two legs.

    \(\displaystyle r_{13} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{(0.26)^2 + (0.65)^2}\)
    \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{0.0676 + 0.423}\) \(\displaystyle = \sqrt{0.4901}\)
    \(\displaystyle = 0.700\ \mathrm{m}\)

    MeansIt is longer than either leg but shorter than \(a + b = 0.910\ \mathrm{m}\). Adding the legs is a common mistake.

  5. Pair 1–2: \(U_{12} = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{a}\)

    WhyThis is \(U = kq_1q_2/r\) with the signs kept inside the charges. The distance between \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) is side \(a\). The distance is not squared: \(r^2\) belongs to the force law, not to the energy.

    Multiply the charges, plain numbers first, then powers of ten: \(\displaystyle (9.5)(-58)\times10^{-6}\times10^{-6}\) \(\displaystyle = -551\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = -5.510\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    Multiply by \(\displaystyle k\): \(\displaystyle (8.99\times10^{9})(-5.510\times10^{-10})\) \(\displaystyle = -4.953\ \mathrm{J\,m}\)
    Divide by the distance \(\displaystyle a = 0.260\ \mathrm{m}\): \(\displaystyle -4.953 \div 0.260\) \(\displaystyle = -19.05\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative, because a positive and a negative charge attract.

  6. Pair 2–3: \(U_{23} = \dfrac{kq_2q_3}{b}\)

    WhySame equation, now with \(q_2\) and \(q_3\). The distance between them is side \(b\).

    Multiply the charges, plain numbers first, then powers of ten: \(\displaystyle (-58)(25)\times10^{-6}\times10^{-6}\) \(\displaystyle = -1450\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = -1.450\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    Multiply by \(\displaystyle k\): \(\displaystyle (8.99\times10^{9})(-1.450\times10^{-9})\) \(\displaystyle = -13.04\ \mathrm{J\,m}\)
    Divide by the distance \(\displaystyle b = 0.650\ \mathrm{m}\): \(\displaystyle -13.04 \div 0.650\) \(\displaystyle = -20.05\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative again: another attracting pair.

  7. Pair 1–3: \(U_{13} = \dfrac{kq_1q_3}{r_{13}}\)

    Why\(q_1\) and \(q_3\) are joined by the hypotenuse, so the distance is \(r_{13}\) from the Pythagoras step.

    Multiply the charges, plain numbers first, then powers of ten: \(\displaystyle (9.5)(25)\times10^{-6}\times10^{-6}\) \(\displaystyle = 237.5\times10^{-12}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.375\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)
    Multiply by \(\displaystyle k\): \(\displaystyle (8.99\times10^{9})(2.375\times10^{-10})\) \(\displaystyle = 2.135\ \mathrm{J\,m}\)
    Divide by the distance \(\displaystyle r_{13} = 0.700\ \mathrm{m}\): \(\displaystyle 2.135 \div 0.700\) \(\displaystyle = 3.050\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansPositive: two like charges repel, and energy is stored in pushing them together.

  8. Add the three terms: this is part (a)

    WhyEnergy is a plain number with no direction. The total is just the sum of the pair terms, with their signs.

    \(\displaystyle U = U_{12} + U_{23} + U_{13}\)
    \(\displaystyle = (-19.05) + (-20.05) + (3.050)\)
    \(\displaystyle = -36.1\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative: the attractions outweigh the repulsion. It would take \(36.1\ \mathrm{J}\) of outside work to pull all three charges apart to infinity.

  9. Part (b): decide which pairs are new

    WhyBefore \(q_3\) arrives, \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) are already sitting there, so their pair energy \(U_{12}\) already exists. \(q_3\) starts at infinity, where every pair it belongs to has zero energy. Bringing it in creates exactly the pairs that contain \(q_3\).

    \(\displaystyle \Delta U\) \(\displaystyle = U_{\text{after}} - U_{\text{before}}\)
    \(\displaystyle = (U_{12} + U_{23} + U_{13}) - U_{12}\)
    \(\displaystyle = U_{23} + U_{13}\)

    Means\(U_{12}\) cancels. Leaving it in is the most common mistake on part (b).

  10. Add the two new terms: this is part (b)

    \(\displaystyle \Delta U = (-20.05) + (3.050)\) \(\displaystyle = -17.0\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative: \(q_2\) pulls \(q_3\) in harder than \(q_1\) pushes it away, so the field itself does positive work bringing \(q_3\) in.

If your version of the figure shows all three charges positive, \(U_{12}\) and \(U_{23}\) flip to positive and every step stays the same: (a) \(+42.2\ \mathrm{J}\), (b) \(+23.1\ \mathrm{J}\).

(a) U = −36.1 J (b) ΔU = −17.0 J
Two charges from their energy
Homework 5, Problem 2
Two charges have total potential energy \(-33\ \mathrm{J}\), are \(16\ \mathrm{cm}\) apart, and have total charge \(45\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). Find the positive and the negative charge.

  1. Read what each number is

    WhyTwo unknowns need two facts. The energy gives one fact (the product of the charges) and the total gives the other (their sum).

    \(\displaystyle U = -33\ \mathrm{J}\): the potential energy of the pair.
    \(\displaystyle r = 16\ \mathrm{cm}\): how far apart they are.
    \(\displaystyle q_+ + q_- = 45\ \mu\mathrm{C}\): the sum with signs, so the negative charge subtracts.

    MeansThe unknowns are \(q_+\) and \(q_-\).

  2. Read the sign of U

    WhyIn \(U = kq_1q_2/r\), \(k\) and \(r\) are always positive. So \(U\) has the same sign as the product \(q_1q_2\).

    \(\displaystyle U \lt 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow q_+q_- \lt 0\)
    So one charge is positive and the other is negative.

    MeansThat is why the problem calls them \(q_+\) and \(q_-\). It also tells you the product you are about to compute must come out negative.

  3. Convert the distance

    Why\(k\) is in \(\mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\), so \(r\) must be in meters. \(U\) is already in joules.

    \(\displaystyle r = 16\ \mathrm{cm}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.16\ \mathrm{m}\)

  4. Solve equation for the product

    WhyTreat \(q_+q_-\) as one unknown. It is multiplied by \(k\) and divided by \(r\), so undo both: multiply both sides by \(r\), then divide both sides by \(k\).

    \(\displaystyle U = \dfrac{k\,q_+q_-}{r}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow q_+q_-\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{U\,r}{k}\)

  5. Plug in

    Top: \(\displaystyle U r = (-33)(0.16)\) \(\displaystyle = -5.28\ \mathrm{J\,m}\)
    Divide by \(\displaystyle k\): \(\displaystyle q_+q_-\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-5.28}{8.99\times10^{9}}\) \(\displaystyle = -5.873\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C^2}\)

    MeansNegative, as the sign of U predicted.

  6. Switch the product to microcoulombs

    WhyThe sum is given in μC and the answers are asked in μC. Since \(1\ \mathrm{C} = 10^{6}\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), one \(\mathrm{C^2}\) is \(10^{12}\ (\mu\mathrm{C})^2\). Working in μC keeps the numbers readable.

    \(\displaystyle q_+q_-\) \(\displaystyle = (-5.873\times10^{-10})(10^{12})\) \(\displaystyle = -587.3\ (\mu\mathrm{C})^2\)

  7. Turn "sum" and "product" into one equation

    WhyCall the positive charge \(x\) (in μC). The sum says the negative one is whatever is left: \(45 - x\). Put both into the product.

    \(\displaystyle q_+ = x,\) \(\displaystyle q_-\) \(\displaystyle = 45 - x\)
    \(\displaystyle x(45 - x) = -587.3\)
    \(\displaystyle 45x - x^2 = -587.3\)
    \(\displaystyle x^2 - 45x - 587.3 = 0\)

    MeansA quadratic \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) with \(a = 1\), \(b = -45\), \(c = -587.3\).

  8. Apply the quadratic formula

    Why\(x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). With \(a = 1\), \(b = -45\), \(c = -587.3\), the \(-4ac\) becomes \(+4(587.3)\).

    \(\displaystyle b^2 = 45^2 = 2025\)
    \(\displaystyle -4ac = 4(587.3) = 2349\)
    Under the root: \(\displaystyle 2025 + 2349 = 4374\), and \(\displaystyle \sqrt{4374} = 66.14\)
    Plus sign: \(\displaystyle x = \dfrac{45 + 66.14}{2}\) \(\displaystyle = 55.57\)
    Minus sign: \(\displaystyle x = \dfrac{45 - 66.14}{2}\) \(\displaystyle = -10.57\)

  9. Pick the root: this is part (a)

    Why\(x\) was defined as the positive charge, so it must be the positive root. The negative root is not wasted: it is the other charge.

    \(\displaystyle q_+ = 55.6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

  10. Find the negative charge and check: part (b)

    WhyUse the sum, then confirm both facts. A check costs ten seconds and catches a wrong root.

    \(\displaystyle q_- = 45 - 55.57\) \(\displaystyle = -10.6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)
    Sum: \(\displaystyle 55.57 + (-10.57) = 45\) ✓
    Product: \(\displaystyle (55.57)(-10.57)\) \(\displaystyle = -587.3\ (\mu\mathrm{C})^2\) ✓
q₊ = 55.6 μC q₋ = −10.6 μC
Water molecule
Spring 2015, Questions 24–25
Model water as three point charges: O carries \(-2e\); each H carries \(+e\) at \(1.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\) from the O; the two H are \(1.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\) apart. (Q24) Find \(U\). (Q25) If the H–O–H angle opens to \(180^\circ\) with the O–H distances fixed, does \(U\) increase, decrease, or stay the same?

  1. List the three pairs

    O–H (left), O–H (right), H–H

  2. Each O–H pair

    WhyCharges \((-2e)(+e) = -2e^2\), distance \(1.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{k(-2e)(e)}{1.0\times10^{-10}}\) \(\displaystyle = ke^2\left(\dfrac{-2}{1.0\times10^{-10}}\right)\)

  3. The H–H pair

    Why\((+e)(+e) = +e^2\), distance \(1.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{k(e)(e)}{1.6\times10^{-10}}\) \(\displaystyle = ke^2\left(\dfrac{1}{1.6\times10^{-10}}\right)\)

  4. Add the brackets

    WhyFactor out \(ke^2\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{-2}{10^{-10}} + \dfrac{-2}{10^{-10}} + \dfrac{1}{1.6\times10^{-10}}\) \(\displaystyle = (-2 - 2 + 0.625)\times10^{10}\) \(\displaystyle = -3.375\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\)

  5. The factor ke²

    \(\displaystyle ke^2\) \(\displaystyle = (8.99\times10^{9})(1.60\times10^{-19})^2\) \(\displaystyle = (8.99\times10^{9})(2.56\times10^{-38})\) \(\displaystyle = 2.301\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{J\,m}\)

  6. Multiply (Q24)

    \(\displaystyle U\) \(\displaystyle = (2.301\times10^{-28})(-3.375\times10^{10})\) \(\displaystyle = -7.77\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative: the molecule is bound.

  7. Open the angle (Q25)

    WhyAt \(180^\circ\) the two H sit on opposite sides of the O, \(2.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\) apart. The O–H terms are unchanged; only the positive H–H term changes, and it gets smaller.

    \(\displaystyle U_{180^\circ}\) \(\displaystyle = ke^2(-4 + 0.5)\times10^{10}\) \(\displaystyle = -8.06\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansMore negative: \(U\) decreases.

Q24: U = −7.77×10⁻¹⁸ J Q25: decreases
J

7.2 Electric potential

Definition
\[ V \equiv \frac{U}{q}, \qquad \Delta V = V_b - V_a = \frac{\Delta U}{q} = -\frac{W_{\text{field}}}{q} = -\int_a^b\vec E\cdot d\vec l \]
What each letter means
\(V\)
electric potential at a point, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C): the potential energy per coulomb a charge would have there
\(U\)
the potential energy a charge \(q\) has at that point, J
\(q\)
the charge used to probe the potential, C; it divides out, so \(V\) does not depend on it
\(V_a,\ V_b\)
the potential at the starting point \(a\) and the ending point \(b\)
\(\Delta V\)
potential difference (voltage) between two points, in volts; \(\Delta\) always means "final minus initial"
\(W_{\text{field}}\)
work the field does on \(q\) going from \(a\) to \(b\), J
\(\int_a^b\vec E\cdot d\vec l\)
add up (field) × (step along the path) from \(a\) to \(b\); \(d\vec l\) is a tiny step of the path in m; the minus sign means moving with the field lowers \(V\)

Units: 1 V = 1 J/C. Also \(1\ \mathrm{eV}\) \(= 1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\) (energy of charge \(e\) moved through 1 V) and N/C = V/m. Point charge, with \(V = 0\) at infinity:

\[ V = \frac{kq}{r}, \qquad V_{\text{total}} = \sum_i\frac{kq_i}{r_i}\quad\text{(scalar sum: signs, no components)} \]
What each letter means
\(V\)
the potential a point charge makes at distance \(r\), V, with \(V = 0\) at infinity
\(q\)
the source charge with its sign, C: negative charges make negative potential
\(r\)
distance from the charge to the point, m
\(V_{\text{total}},\ \sum_i,\ q_i,\ r_i\)
for several charges, simply add the numbers \(kq_i/r_i\) (each charge's value with its own distance); no directions, no components
\(W_{\text{you}} = qV\)
work an outside agent does to bring charge \(q\) from infinity to a point at potential \(V\), J
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)

Work you must do to bring a charge \(q\) from infinity (where \(V=0\)) to a point at potential \(V\), at constant speed: \(W_{\text{you}} = qV\). Work the field does: \(-qV\).

In plain words

Potential is "electrical height." A point at \(100\ \mathrm{V}\) gives every coulomb placed there \(100\ \mathrm{J}\) of potential energy: \(U = qV\). Positive charges roll downhill to lower \(V\); negative charges roll "uphill" to higher \(V\). Because \(V\) is a plain number with a sign, adding up the potentials of many charges needs no components at all.

Why divide by the charge again, and what a volt is

Chapter 5 divided force by charge to get a field that describes the space. Chapter 7 divides potential energy by charge for the same reason: \(U = qV\) means "\(V\) is what the space offers; \(q\) is how much of it a particular charge collects." A point at 100 V will give any charge \(q\) placed there \(100q\) joules of potential energy. The volt is one joule per coulomb, an energy per unit charge, exactly as \(gh\) in \(mgh\) is an energy per unit mass. Think of \(V\) as electrical height. Positive charges "fall" toward lower \(V\); negative charges "fall" toward higher \(V\) (because \(U = qV\) with \(q \lt 0\) is lowest where \(V\) is highest).

Two practical consequences. First, \(V\) is a scalar, so the potential of many charges is a plain sum with signs and no components; this is what makes potential so much easier than field. Second, because only differences in \(U\) ever matter physically (only \(\Delta U\) appears in energy conservation), only differences in \(V\) matter. You may set \(V = 0\) wherever is convenient; "at infinity" is convenient for finite objects because \(kq/r\) goes to zero there on its own.

Potential from two point charges
Lecture 6, Examples 6.2 and 6.3
On one line, left to right: point A, then \(+5\ \mathrm{nC}\) 10 cm away, then \(-5\ \mathrm{nC}\) 10 cm further, then point B 10 cm beyond. Point C is 10 cm directly above A. Find \(V_A\), \(V_B\), and \(V_C\) with \(V = 0\) at infinity.

  1. The rule

    WhyPotential is a scalar: add \(kq/r\) for each charge, with the sign of the charge, no directions.

    \(\displaystyle V = \sum_i \dfrac{kq_i}{r_i}\)

  2. The common factor

    \(\displaystyle kQ\) \(\displaystyle = (8.99\times10^{9})(5\times10^{-9})\) \(\displaystyle = 44.95\ \mathrm{V\,m}\)

  3. Point A

    WhyA is 0.10 m from \(+Q\) and 0.20 m from \(-Q\).

    \(\displaystyle V_A\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{44.95}{0.10} - \dfrac{44.95}{0.20}\) \(\displaystyle = 449.5 - 224.8\) \(\displaystyle = +225\ \mathrm{V}\)

    MeansPositive: A is closer to the positive charge.

  4. Point B

    WhyB is 0.20 m from \(+Q\) and 0.10 m from \(-Q\): the mirror image.

    \(\displaystyle V_B = 224.8 - 449.5\) \(\displaystyle = -225\ \mathrm{V}\)

  5. Point C: the distances

    WhyC is 10 cm straight above A. To \(+Q\): 10 cm up and 10 cm across. To \(-Q\): 10 cm up and 20 cm across. Pythagoras for each.

    \(\displaystyle r_{+} = \sqrt{0.10^2 + 0.10^2}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.141\ \mathrm{m}\)
    \(\displaystyle r_{-} = \sqrt{0.10^2 + 0.20^2}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.224\ \mathrm{m}\)

  6. Point C: the potential

    \(\displaystyle V_C\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{44.95}{0.1414} - \dfrac{44.95}{0.2236}\) \(\displaystyle = 317.8 - 201.0\) \(\displaystyle = +117\ \mathrm{V}\)
V_A = +225 V V_B = −225 V V_C = +117 V

Potential at the empty corner, and the work to bring a charge there
Fall 2018, Questions 3–4
The square from Fall 2018: \(+2Q\), \(-Q\), \(+Q\) on three corners, \(Q = 7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), side \(a = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}\). \(P\) is the empty corner: \(a\) from \(+2Q\), \(a\) from \(+Q\), \(a\sqrt2\) from \(-Q\). (Q3) Find \(V_P\). (Q4) Is the work you do to bring \(-2Q\) from infinity to \(P\) positive, negative, or zero?

  1. Add the three potentials

    WhySigns in, distances from the picture.

    \(\displaystyle V_P\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k(2Q)}{a} + \dfrac{kQ}{a} + \dfrac{k(-Q)}{a\sqrt2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{a}\left(2 + 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\)

  2. Numbers

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{kQ}{a}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(7\times10^{-6})}{0.5}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.259\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\)
    \(\displaystyle V_P = (1.259\times10^{5})(2.293)\) \(\displaystyle = 2.89\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\)

  3. Work you do (Q4)

    WhyBringing a charge from infinity (\(V = 0\)) to \(P\) at constant speed: \(W_{\text{you}} = q\,V_P\).

    \(\displaystyle W_{\text{you}}\) \(\displaystyle = (-2Q)(V_P)\) \(\displaystyle = (-14\times10^{-6})(2.89\times10^{5})\) \(\displaystyle = -4.04\ \mathrm{J}\)

    MeansNegative: the negative charge is attracted toward the high-potential point, so you hold it back rather than push it.

V_P = 2.89×10⁵ V W_you < 0
Potential in a uniform field, and the "zero field" checkpoint

In a uniform field, moving a distance \(d\) along \(\vec E\) lowers the potential: \(\Delta V = -Ed\). Moving perpendicular to \(\vec E\) changes nothing. Lecture 6's three points A, B, C in a constant field: choose any path (A→D→C, with A→D perpendicular to \(\vec E\) and D→C along it), so \(V_C - V_A = -E\,\Delta x \lt 0\).

What each letter means
\(E\)
the magnitude of the uniform field, N/C
\(d,\ \Delta x\)
the distance moved along the field direction, m
\(\Delta V,\ V_C - V_A\)
the potential difference, V; negative when moving with the field

If \(\vec E = 0\) throughout a region, then \(\Delta V = 0\) between any two points: \(V\) is constant, not necessarily zero (Lecture 6 checkpoint). This is why a conductor's interior is all at the surface potential.

Two charged conducting spheres, far apart
Lecture 7 checkpoints · Spring 2015 Q3–4
Sphere 1: radius \(20\ \mathrm{mm}\), charge \(0.4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). Sphere 2: radius \(5\ \mathrm{mm}\), charge \(0.12\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). They are far apart. (Q3) Find the potential difference between their surfaces. (Q4) If they are joined by a thin wire, which way does positive charge flow?

  1. Potential of one isolated sphere

    WhyOutside a charged sphere the potential is that of a point charge at the center. At the surface, \(r = R\).

    \(\displaystyle V = \dfrac{kQ}{R}\)

  2. Sphere 1

    Why\(20\ \mathrm{mm} = 0.020\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle V_1\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(0.4\times10^{-6})}{0.020}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.80\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\)

  3. Sphere 2

    Why\(5\ \mathrm{mm} = 0.005\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle V_2\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.99\times10^{9})(0.12\times10^{-6})}{0.005}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.16\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\)

    MeansLess charge but a much smaller radius: higher potential.

  4. Difference (Q3)

    \(\displaystyle V_2 - V_1\) \(\displaystyle = 3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\)

  5. Direction of flow (Q4)

    WhyPositive charge moves from high \(V\) to low \(V\), like water running downhill.

    From sphere 2 to sphere 1.

  6. Where it stops

    WhyFlow stops when the potentials are equal. Equal \(kq/r\) means charge proportional to radius. Total charge stays \(0.52\ \mu\mathrm{C}\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{q_1'}{r_1}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q_2'}{r_2}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \dfrac{q_1'}{q_2'}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{20}{5}\) \(\displaystyle = 4\)
    \(\displaystyle q_1' = 0.416\ \mu\mathrm{C},\) \(\displaystyle q_2'\) \(\displaystyle = 0.104\ \mu\mathrm{C},\) \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = 1.87\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\)

    MeansThe bigger sphere holds more charge, but the smaller one has the larger surface density (\(\sigma = q/4\pi r^2 \propto 1/r\)) and the stronger surface field. That is why charge leaks from sharp points.

Q3: 3.6×10⁴ V Q4: from 2 to 1
What each letter means
\(V\)
the potential at the sphere's surface (and everywhere inside it), V
\(Q,\ q_1,\ q_2\)
the charge on a sphere, C
\(R,\ r_1,\ r_2\)
the sphere radii, m
\(q_1\prime,\ q_2\prime\)
the charges after the spheres are connected by a wire and share one potential
\(\sigma\)
surface charge density, C/m²; \(\propto 1/r\) for connected spheres
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)

7.3 \(V\) from \(\vec E\), and \(\vec E\) from \(V\)

The two directions
\[ V_b - V_a = -\int_a^b \vec E\cdot d\vec l \qquad\qquad \vec E = -\nabla V,\quad E_x = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial x},\ E_y = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial y},\ E_z = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial z} \]
What each letter means
\(V_a,\ V_b\)
potential at the start and end points, V
\(\vec E\)
the electric field vector: the force per coulomb that a positive test charge would feel at that point, in N/C (= V/m)
\(d\vec l\)
a tiny step along any path from \(a\) to \(b\), m
\(\nabla V\)
the gradient of \(V\): a vector whose components are the slopes of \(V\) along \(x\), \(y\), \(z\); it points uphill
\(\partial V/\partial x\)
the partial derivative: the slope of \(V\) in the \(x\)-direction with \(y\) and \(z\) held fixed, V/m
\(E_x,\ E_y,\ E_z\)
the field components, N/C; each is minus the slope in its own direction

\(\vec E\) points from high \(V\) to low \(V\) ("downhill"), and its magnitude is the steepness of \(V\). On a graph of \(V(x)\): \(E_x\) is minus the slope. Steepest slope = strongest field; positive slope = field pointing in \(-x\); flat = zero field.

In plain words

The field points downhill on the potential landscape, and its strength is how steep the hill is. Walk along the field and \(V\) drops; walk against it and \(V\) rises; walk across it and \(V\) stays the same.

Why there is a minus sign in \(\Delta V = -\int E\,dl\) and in \(E = -dV/dx\)

Start from work. Move a charge \(q\) a small step \(d\vec l\); the field's force \(q\vec E\) does work \(q\vec E\cdot d\vec l\), and potential energy changes by the negative of that: \(dU = -q\vec E\cdot d\vec l\). Divide by \(q\): \(dV = -\vec E\cdot d\vec l\). Add up the steps: \(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec l\). The minus sign is inherited from \(\Delta U = -W\): moving with the field lowers the potential, the way moving with gravity lowers your height.

Read the same equation backward for a step along \(x\): \(dV = -E_x\,dx\), so \(E_x = -dV/dx\). The field is minus the slope of the potential. On a graph of \(V\) versus \(x\), where the curve goes downhill to the right (negative slope) the field points right; where it climbs to the right the field points left; where it is flat the field is zero. A steep curve means a strong field. This is the electrical version of "a ball on a hill rolls the way the ground slopes, faster where it is steeper."

It also explains why a region of zero field has constant potential (flat ground is level, but level at whatever height it happens to be, not necessarily sea level), and why \(V\) is constant throughout a conductor.

Potential difference between two points in a sheet configuration
Fall 2018, Question 15
Sheets \(\sigma_1 = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at \(x = 0.6\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(\sigma_2 = -6.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at \(x = 0.8\ \mathrm{m}\), with a neutral conducting slab from 0 to 0.2 m (Chapter 6 figure). Find \(V_B - V_A\) for A at \(x = 0.2\ \mathrm{m}\) and B at \(x = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}\).

  1. Which region are A and B in?

    WhyBoth lie between the slab (ends at 0.2) and the first sheet (at 0.6).

    region \(\displaystyle 0.2 \lt x \lt 0.6\)

  2. Field from σ₁ there

    WhyPositive sheet: field points away from it. The points are to its left, so away is \(-x\). Size \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{1x}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{8\times10^{-6}}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

  3. Field from σ₂ there

    WhyNegative sheet: field points toward it, to the right, \(+x\).

    \(\displaystyle E_{2x}\) \(\displaystyle = +\dfrac{6.5\times10^{-6}}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

  4. What about the slab?

    WhyA neutral conductor's two faces carry equal and opposite charge. Outside the slab their fields cancel, so it adds nothing here.

  5. Total field in the region

    Why\(2\varepsilon_0 = 1.77\times10^{-11}\).

    \(\displaystyle E_x\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(-8 + 6.5)\times10^{-6}}{1.77\times10^{-11}}\) \(\displaystyle = -8.47\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/m}\)

    MeansUniform and pointing left.

  6. Integrate from A to B

    WhyUniform field: \(\Delta V = -E_x\,\Delta x\), with \(\Delta x = 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle V_B - V_A\) \(\displaystyle = -(-8.47\times10^{4})(0.3)\) \(\displaystyle = +2.54\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\)

    MeansPositive: moving right, against a leftward field, raises the potential.

V_B − V_A = +2.54×10⁴ V
V
Two charged plates: field and potential in three regions
Homework 6, Problem 5
Plate \(-\sigma\) at \(y = 0\) (defined as \(V = 0\)) and plate \(+\sigma\) at \(y = d\). Find \(\vec E\) and \(V\) for \(y \lt 0\), \(0 \lt y \lt d\), and \(y \gt d\).

  1. Read the setup

    WhyEvery answer depends on which region you are in, so first fix where the plates are and which one is the zero.

    Plate at \(\displaystyle y = 0\): \(\displaystyle -\sigma\). The problem declares \(\displaystyle V = 0\) there.
    Plate at \(\displaystyle y = d\): \(\displaystyle +\sigma\).
    Three regions: below both (\(\displaystyle y \lt 0\)), between (\(\displaystyle 0 \lt y \lt d\)), above both (\(\displaystyle y \gt d\)).

    Means\(\sigma\) is charge per square meter; "very large" means each plate acts like an infinite sheet.

  2. The field of one plate by itself

    WhyThis is \(E_{\text{sheet}}\) \(= \sigma/2\varepsilon_0\). It does not weaken with distance, it is the same on both sides, and it points away from a positive sheet and toward a negative one.

    \(\displaystyle |\vec E_{\text{one plate}}|\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

  3. (a) Region \(y \lt 0\), below both plates

    WhyBoth plates are above this point. The \(-\sigma\) plate pulls toward itself: up, \(+\hat j\). The \(+\sigma\) plate pushes away from itself: down, \(-\hat j\).

    \(\displaystyle \vec E\) \(\displaystyle = +\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat j - \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat j\) \(\displaystyle = 0\)

    MeansEqual sizes, opposite directions: they cancel.

  4. (b) Region \(0 \lt y \lt d\), between the plates

    WhyThe \(-\sigma\) plate is below: it pulls down, \(-\hat j\). The \(+\sigma\) plate is above: it pushes down, \(-\hat j\). Same direction, so they add.

    \(\displaystyle \vec E\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat j - \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat j\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\hat j\)

    MeansThe field runs from the positive plate to the negative plate, as field lines always do.

  5. (c) Region \(y \gt d\), above both plates

    WhyBoth plates are below. \(-\sigma\) pulls down (\(-\hat j\)); \(+\sigma\) pushes up (\(+\hat j\)).

    \(\displaystyle \vec E = 0\)

  6. (d) Potential for \(y \lt 0\)

    WhyStart at the plate where \(V = 0\) and walk down into this region. The given \(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec l\) with \(\vec E = 0\) gives \(\Delta V = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle V = 0\)

    MeansZero field means the potential stays flat. Here it happens to be flat at 0.

  7. (e) Potential for \(0 \lt y \lt d\)

    WhyWalk up from \(y = 0\) to a height \(y\). The step is \(d\vec l = dy'\,\hat j\), and \(\vec E\cdot d\vec l\) \(= (-\sigma/\varepsilon_0)\,dy'\). Walking against the field raises \(V\).

    \(\displaystyle V(y)\) \(\displaystyle = V(0) - \int_0^y\left(-\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\right)dy'\)
    \(\displaystyle = 0 + \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\,y\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma y}{\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansCheck: at \(y = 0\) it gives 0 ✓, and it grows linearly toward the positive plate ✓.

  8. (f) Potential for \(y \gt d\)

    WhyAt \(y = d\) the potential has reached \(\sigma d/\varepsilon_0\). Above that the field is zero, so it stays there.

    \(\displaystyle V = \dfrac{\sigma d}{\varepsilon_0}\)

    MeansConstant, and not zero: zero field never means zero potential.

E = 0, −(σ/ε₀)ĵ, 0 V = 0, σy/ε₀, σd/ε₀
What each letter means
\(\sigma\)
the surface charge density on each plate (\(+\sigma\) on one, \(-\sigma\) on the other), C/m²
\(y\)
the coordinate perpendicular to the plates, m; the \(-\sigma\) plate is at \(y = 0\)
\(d\)
the plate separation, m
\(\hat j\)
unit vector along \(+y\)
\(V(y)\)
the potential as a function of position, with \(V = 0\) chosen at the lower plate
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
Potential difference near a line of charge (the logarithm)
Lecture 6, Example 6.5 · Fall 2015 Q9 · Homework 6, Problems 2–4
Outside any cylindrically symmetric charge, \(E = 2k\lambda_{\text{enc}}/r\), radially. Integrating it gives a logarithm:\[ V(r_2) - V(r_1) = -\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\frac{2k\lambda}{r}\,dr = -2k\lambda\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1} = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\frac{r_1}{r_2} \]
What each letter means
\(V(r_1),\ V(r_2)\)
the potential at distance \(r_1\) and at \(r_2\) from the axis, V
\(\lambda,\ \lambda_{\text{enc}}\)
the charge per length enclosed by a cylinder through the point, C/m, with sign
\(r\)
perpendicular distance from the axis, m; the integration variable
\(\ln\)
natural logarithm; \(\ln(r_2/r_1) = -\ln(r_1/r_2)\)
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

You cannot put \(V = 0\) at infinity for an infinite line (the logarithm grows without limit). Problems always give a reference radius, or ask only for a difference.

Lecture 6, Example 6.5: a solid insulating cylinder (\(a = 4.1\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(\rho = 27\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^3}\)) inside a conducting shell (\(b = 19.9\), \(c = 21.9\ \mathrm{cm}\)) carrying \(\lambda_{\text{shell}}\) \(= -0.36\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\). Find \(V(P) - V(R)\) for \(P = (46, 46)\ \mathrm{cm}\) and \(R = (0, 46)\ \mathrm{cm}\), both outside everything.

  1. Charge per length of the insulator

    WhyCharge per length = density × cross-section area \(\pi a^2\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{ins}}\) \(\displaystyle = \rho\pi a^2\) \(\displaystyle = (27\times10^{-6})\pi(0.041)^2\) \(\displaystyle = 1.43\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{C/m}\)

  2. Total enclosed charge per length

    WhyOutside the shell, a Gaussian cylinder encloses the insulator and the shell.

    \(\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.43\times10^{-7} - 3.6\times10^{-7}\) \(\displaystyle = -2.17\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{C/m}\)

    MeansNegative: the shell wins.

  3. The field outside

    \(\displaystyle E_r\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2k\lambda_{\text{enc}}}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-3909}{r}\ \mathrm{V/m}\)

    MeansNegative \(E_r\): the field points inward.

  4. Distances from the axis

    WhyR is straight up: 0.46 m. P is at \((0.46, 0.46)\): \(0.46\sqrt2\).

    \(\displaystyle r_R = 0.46\ \mathrm{m},\) \(\displaystyle r_P\) \(\displaystyle = 0.6505\ \mathrm{m}\)

  5. Integrate outward from R to P

    Why\(\Delta V = -\int E_r\,dr\) and \(\int dr/r = \ln r\).

    \(\displaystyle V_P - V_R\) \(\displaystyle = -\int_{r_R}^{r_P}\dfrac{-3909}{r}\,dr\) \(\displaystyle = 3909\,\ln\dfrac{r_P}{r_R}\)
    \(\displaystyle \ln\dfrac{0.6505}{0.46}\) \(\displaystyle = \ln\sqrt2\) \(\displaystyle = 0.3466\)
    \(\displaystyle V_P - V_R = (3909)(0.3466)\) \(\displaystyle = +1355\ \mathrm{V}\)

  6. Sign check

    WhyThe net charge is negative, so \(V\) is lowest near the axis and rises outward. P is farther out than R, so \(V_P \gt V_R\). ✓

    MeansThe lecture warns "you get three minus signs": from \(\lambda_{\text{enc}} \lt 0\), from the \(-\int\), and from the direction. Track them one at a time.

V(P) − V(R) = +1.36×10³ V
V

7.4 Potential of extended objects: Gauss's law, then integrate

Lecture 6's two-step plan
  1. Use Gauss's law to get \(E(r)\) in every region (Chapter 6 catalog).
  2. Integrate inward from the reference point: \(V(r)\) \(= V(\text{ref}) - \int_{\text{ref}}^{r}E\,dr'\). With \(V(\infty) = 0\) for finite objects: \(V(r) = \int_r^{\infty}E(r')\,dr'\), adding up region by region. Inside a conductor \(E = 0\), so \(V\) does not change across it.
What each letter means
\(V(r)\)
the potential at radius \(r\), V
\(V(\text{ref}),\ \text{ref}\)
the value of \(V\) at the reference point, and the reference point itself (infinity for finite objects, a stated radius for lines)
\(E(r\prime),\ dr\prime\)
the field from Gauss's law and a tiny step in radius; \(r\prime\) is the dummy variable you integrate over
\(\infty\)
infinity: infinitely far away, where \(V = 0\) is usually chosen

Lecture 6: "Good news: they're going to be really, really simple. Sometimes so simple we can do them conceptually."

Why "integrate inward from the reference" works, and why infinity fails for a line

Once Gauss's law has given \(E(r)\) in every region, the potential at any radius is the running total of \(-E\,dr\) starting from wherever \(V\) is defined to be zero. Starting at infinity and walking inward, \(V\) rises while you walk against an outward field (positive enclosed charge) and falls while you walk with an inward one. Crossing a conductor adds nothing, because \(E = 0\) there, so \(V\) stays flat across the metal. Crossing the boundary of an insulator, \(E\) changes from one formula to another, so you switch integrands but keep adding. The result is continuous everywhere (there are no jumps in \(V\), because no finite field over a zero-thickness step can change it), which is a useful check on your algebra.

For an infinite line or cylinder, \(E \propto 1/r\), and \(\int^\infty dr/r\) grows without bound: an infinite line has infinite total charge, and infinitely far away is not "far from all of it." So there is no natural zero at infinity. The formula \(V = -2k\lambda\ln(r/r_0)\) needs a chosen reference radius \(r_0\), and problems always supply one or ask only for a difference. This is why Fall 2018 Q19 rejects the \(\int_\infty^r\) answer choice.

Object (\(V=0\) at ∞ unless noted)OutsideInsideWhere it appears
Conducting sphere, charge \(Q\), radius \(R\)\(kQ/r\)\(kQ/R\) (constant)Fall 2015 Q10–12
Insulating sphere, uniform, charge \(Q\)\(kQ/r\)\(\dfrac{kQ}{2R^3}\left(3R^2 - r^2\right)\); center \(= \tfrac32 kQ/R\)Lecture 6, Example 6.7
Point \(q\) + conducting shells (nested)\(k(q+Q)/r\)constant across each metal; \(kq/r + \) constants in gapsLecture 6, Example 6.6; Fall 2018 Q10; HW6 P1
Long cylinder / line, \(\lambda\), reference at \(r_0\)\(-2k\lambda\ln(r/r_0)\)conductor: constant \(= -2k\lambda\ln(R/r_0)\); insulator: \(V(R) + \dfrac{\rho}{4\varepsilon_0}(R^2 - r^2)\)HW6 P2–4; Fall 2018 Q19–20
Parallel plates \(\pm\sigma\), gap \(d\)constant on each sidelinear, \(\Delta V = Ed = \sigma d/\varepsilon_0\)HW6 P5; Chapter 8
What each letter means
\(Q,\ q\)
the charge on the object (or the point charge at the center), C
\(R\)
the object's radius, m
\(r\)
the distance from the center or axis to the point, m
\(r_0\)
the reference radius where \(V = 0\) is chosen for a line or cylinder, m
\(\lambda\)
linear charge density: charge per unit length along a line, rod, or ring, in C/m (\(\lambda = Q/L\) when uniform)
\(\rho\)
volume charge density: charge per unit volume inside an insulator, in C/m³ (\(\rho = Q/V\) when uniform)
\(\sigma\)
surface charge density: charge per unit area on a sheet or surface, in C/m² (\(\sigma = Q/A\) when uniform)
\(d\)
the plate separation, m
\(E\)
magnitude of the electric field, in N/C (the same unit as V/m)
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
Solid conducting sphere: field and potential inside and out
Fall 2015 Q10–12
A solid conducting sphere of radius \(R = 0.4\ \mathrm{m}\) carries \(Q = 5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}\). Find (Q10) \(|E|\) at \(r = 0.8\ \mathrm{m}\), (Q11) \(V\) at \(r = 0.8\ \mathrm{m}\), and (Q12) \(V\) at \(r = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}\), with \(V = 0\) at infinity.

  1. The common factor

    \(\displaystyle kQ\) \(\displaystyle = (8.99\times10^{9})(5\times10^{-6})\) \(\displaystyle = 4.495\times10^{4}\)

  2. Q10: field outside

    WhyOutside, the sphere acts like a point charge at its center.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{4.495\times10^{4}}{(0.8)^2}\) \(\displaystyle = 7.02\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\)

  3. Q11: potential outside

    WhySame point-charge form, one power of \(r\).

    \(\displaystyle V = \dfrac{kQ}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{4.495\times10^{4}}{0.8}\) \(\displaystyle = 5.62\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\)

  4. Q12: inside the metal, the field

    WhyIn a conductor in equilibrium \(E = 0\) everywhere inside.

    \(\displaystyle E(0.1\ \mathrm{m}) = 0\)

  5. Q12: inside the metal, the potential

    WhyZero field means \(V\) does not change as you move inward from the surface. So every interior point has the surface value.

    \(\displaystyle V = \dfrac{kQ}{R}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{4.495\times10^{4}}{0.4}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.12\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\)

    MeansNot zero. "\(E = 0\) so \(V = 0\)" is the distractor; zero field means constant potential.

Q10: 7.0×10⁴ N/C Q11: 5.6×10⁴ V Q12: 1.13×10⁵ V

Nested conducting shells around a point charge
Lecture 6, Example 6.6 · Fall 2018 Q10
A point charge \(+q\) at the center; an uncharged metal shell from \(a_1\) to \(a_2\); a metal shell from \(a_3\) to \(a_4\) carrying \(+Q\). Find \(V(r)\) everywhere, with \(V = 0\) at infinity.

  1. Fields first (Gauss)

    WhyEnclosed charge in each region; zero inside metal.

    \(\displaystyle r \lt a_1\): \(\displaystyle kq/r^2\). Metal 1: 0. \(\displaystyle a_2 \lt r \lt a_3\): \(\displaystyle kq/r^2\) (metal 1 is neutral: \(\displaystyle -q\) inside, \(\displaystyle +q\) outside). Metal 2: 0. \(\displaystyle r \gt a_4\): \(\displaystyle k(q+Q)/r^2\).

  2. Outside, r > a₄

    WhyLooks like a point charge \(q + Q\); already zero at infinity.

    \(\displaystyle V = \dfrac{k(q+Q)}{r}\)

  3. In metal 2

    WhyNo field, so \(V\) stays at its value at \(r = a_4\).

    \(\displaystyle V = \dfrac{k(q+Q)}{a_4}\)

    MeansFall 2018 Q10: \(k(Q_{\text{sphere}} + Q_{\text{shell}})/c\), with \(c\) the outer radius.

  4. In the gap, a₂ < r < a₃

    WhyStart at \(a_3\) and integrate inward. Walking inward against an outward field raises \(V\).

    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = V(a_3) - \int_{a_3}^{r}\dfrac{kq}{r'^2}\,dr'\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k(q+Q)}{a_4} + kq\left(\dfrac1r - \dfrac{1}{a_3}\right)\)

  5. In metal 1

    WhyFlat again, at the value reached at \(r = a_2\).

    \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k(q+Q)}{a_4} + kq\left(\dfrac{1}{a_2} - \dfrac{1}{a_3}\right)\)

  6. Inside, r < a₁

    WhyOne more \(1/r\) climb toward the point charge.

    \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{k(q+Q)}{a_4} + kq\left(\dfrac{1}{a_2} - \dfrac{1}{a_3}\right) + kq\left(\dfrac1r - \dfrac{1}{a_1}\right)\)
staircase of 1/r pieces and flat steps
What each letter means
\(q\)
the point charge at the center (or the inner sphere's charge), C
\(Q\)
the net charge on the outer shell, C
\(a_1,\ a_2,\ a_3,\ a_4\)
the radii of the four metal surfaces, inside to outside, m
\(a,\ b,\ c\)
in Homework 6 P1: the inner sphere's radius and the shell's inner and outer radii, m
\(E_r\)
the radial field component, N/C; negative means inward
\(V\)
the potential in each region, V, with \(V = 0\) at infinity
\(r\prime\)
the dummy radius in the integral
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)
Aluminum sphere inside a copper shell
Homework 6, Problem 1
A solid aluminum sphere of radius \(a\) with charge \(-q\) sits inside a concentric copper shell (inner radius \(b\), outer \(c\)) with charge \(+Q\), \(Q \gt q\). Find \(E_r\) and \(V\) in all four regions, \(V(\infty) = 0\).

  1. Read the setup

    WhyFour regions, each with its own field and potential. \(V = 0\) at infinity, so the potential is built from the outside in.

    Aluminum sphere: radius \(\displaystyle a\), charge \(\displaystyle -q\).
    Copper shell: inner radius \(\displaystyle b\), outer radius \(\displaystyle c\), charge \(\displaystyle +Q\), with \(\displaystyle Q \gt q\).
    Regions: \(\displaystyle r \gt c\) (outside), \(\displaystyle b \lt r \lt c\) (in the copper), \(\displaystyle a \lt r \lt b\) (the gap), \(\displaystyle r \lt a\) (in the aluminum).

  2. Where the aluminum's charge sits

    WhyIn a conductor, all excess charge moves to the outer surface.

    Aluminum surface: \(\displaystyle -q\).

  3. Charge on the copper's inner surface

    WhyPut a Gaussian sphere inside the copper metal. \(E = 0\) in metal, so the flux is zero, so the charge enclosed must be zero. It already contains the aluminum's \(-q\).

    \(\displaystyle -q + q_{\text{inner}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow q_{\text{inner}}\) \(\displaystyle = +q\)

  4. Charge on the copper's outer surface

    WhyThe copper holds \(+Q\) in total; what is not on the inner surface is on the outer one.

    \(\displaystyle q_{\text{outer}}\) \(\displaystyle = Q - q \;(\gt 0)\)

  5. (a) \(E_r\) for \(r \gt c\)

    WhyA Gaussian sphere of radius \(r\) encloses \(-q + Q\). Gauss: \(E_r(4\pi r^2) = (Q - q)/\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle E_r\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q - q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\)

    MeansPositive, so outward, because \(Q \gt q\).

  6. (b) \(E_r\) for \(b \lt r \lt c\)

    WhyInside the copper metal.

    \(\displaystyle E_r = 0\)

  7. (c) \(E_r\) for \(a \lt r \lt b\)

    WhyA Gaussian sphere in the gap encloses only \(-q\).

    \(\displaystyle E_r(4\pi r^2)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{-q}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E_r\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\)

    MeansNegative: the field points inward, toward the negative sphere.

  8. (d) \(E_r\) for \(r \lt a\)

    WhyInside the aluminum metal.

    \(\displaystyle E_r = 0\)

  9. (e) \(V\) for \(r \gt c\)

    WhyOutside a spherically symmetric set of charges, it all acts like one point charge at the center holding the total, \(Q - q\). Use point-charge \(V\), which is already zero at infinity.

    \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q - q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)

  10. (f) \(V\) for \(b \lt r \lt c\)

    WhyNo field in the copper, so \(V\) is frozen at its value at the outer surface, \(r = c\).

    \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q - q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 c}\)

  11. (g) \(V\) for \(a \lt r \lt b\): walk in from the copper

    WhyStart at \(r = b\), where \(V\) equals the copper's value, and apply \(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec l\) with the gap field. The integral of \(1/r^2\) is \(-1/r\).

    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = V(b) - \int_b^r\left(-\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r'^2}\right)dr'\)
    \(\displaystyle = V(b) + \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[-\dfrac{1}{r'}\right]_b^r\) \(\displaystyle = V(b) - \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac1r - \dfrac1b\right)\)
    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q - q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 c} - \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac1r - \dfrac1b\right)\)

    MeansCheck: at \(r = b\) the bracket is 0, so it matches the copper ✓. As \(r\) shrinks, \(V\) drops: walking toward a negative charge lowers the potential ✓.

  12. (h) \(V\) for \(r \lt a\)

    WhyNo field in the aluminum, so \(V\) is frozen at the value the gap formula gives at \(r = a\).

    \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q - q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 c} - \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac1a - \dfrac1b\right)\)
V in the copper: (Q−q)/(4πε₀c)
Potential inside an insulating sphere
Lecture 6, Example 6.7
An insulating sphere of radius \(a\) carries \(+Q\) spread uniformly through its volume. Find \(V(r)\) inside, with \(V = 0\) at infinity.

  1. The field inside

    WhyGauss's law: a sphere of radius \(r \lt a\) encloses the fraction \((r/a)^3\) of the charge.

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{kQ(r/a)^3}{r^2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQr}{a^3}\)

  2. Start at the surface

    WhyOutside, \(V = kQ/r\), so at the surface:

    \(\displaystyle V(a) = \dfrac{kQ}{a}\)

  3. Integrate inward

    Why\(V(r) = V(a) - \int_a^r E\,dr'\).

    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{a} - \int_a^r\dfrac{kQr'}{a^3}\,dr'\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{a} - \dfrac{kQ}{2a^3}\left(r^2 - a^2\right)\)

  4. Simplify

    WhyWrite \(kQ/a\) as \(kQ\cdot2a^2/(2a^3)\) and combine.

    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{2a^3}\left(2a^2 - r^2 + a^2\right)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{kQ}{2a^3}\left(3a^2 - r^2\right)\)

  5. Value at the center

    WhyPut \(r = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle V(0) = \dfrac{3kQ}{2a}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.5\,\dfrac{kQ}{a}\)

    Means50% more than at the surface, because the field inside keeps pushing a test charge outward.

V(r) = kQ(3a² − r²)/(2a³)
What each letter means
\(V(r)\)
the potential at radius \(r\) inside the insulator, V
\(V(a)\)
the potential at the surface, \(kQ/a\)
\(a\)
the insulator's radius, m
\(Q\)
its total charge, spread uniformly through the volume, C
\(r\prime,\ dr\prime\)
the dummy radius integrated from the surface \(a\) inward to \(r\), and its tiny step
\(kQr\prime/a^3\)
the field inside a uniform insulator (grows linearly with radius)
\(k\)
Coulomb's constant, \(8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}\); it converts "charges and a distance" into newtons. Same thing as \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\)

The equipotentials of an insulating sphere are concentric spheres that get closer together toward the surface (the field grows with \(r\) inside) and then spread apart outside (the field falls as \(1/r^2\)).

Charged cylinder with V = 0 at r = 2R
Homework 6, Problem 2
A long aluminum cylinder of radius \(R\) carries charge per length \(\lambda\). \(V = 0\) at \(r = 2R\). Find \(E_r\) and \(V\) inside and outside.

  1. Read the setup

    WhyFor an infinitely long charged line or cylinder, \(V\) cannot be set to zero at infinity (the logarithm grows without limit), so the problem picks a finite radius instead.

    Long aluminum (metal) cylinder, radius \(\displaystyle R\), charge per length \(\displaystyle \lambda\).
    Zero of potential: \(\displaystyle V = 0\) at \(\displaystyle r = 2R\).

  2. (a) Field outside, \(r \gt R\)

    WhyGaussian cylinder of radius \(r\), length \(L\). It encloses \(\lambda L\). The flux goes through the curved side, area \(2\pi rL\).

    \(\displaystyle E_r(2\pi rL)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E_r\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)

    Means\(L\) cancels, as it must: the field cannot depend on the size of an imaginary surface.

  3. (b) Field inside, \(r \lt R\)

    WhyAluminum is a conductor. In equilibrium the field inside metal is zero and all the charge sits on the outer surface.

    \(\displaystyle E_r = 0\)

  4. (c) Potential outside: start at the zero and walk to \(r\)

    WhyUse \(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec l\), from \(2R\) (where \(V = 0\)) out or in to \(r\). The integral of \(1/r\) is \(\ln r\), and \(\ln r - \ln 2R = \ln(r/2R)\).

    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = 0 - \int_{2R}^{r}\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r'}\,dr'\)
    \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{r}{2R}\)

  5. Check the sign in each zone

    WhyBetween \(R\) and \(2R\), \(r/2R \lt 1\) and its log is negative, so \(V \gt 0\). Beyond \(2R\), \(V \lt 0\). At \(2R\), \(\ln 1 = 0\).

    \(\displaystyle V(2R)\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln 1\) \(\displaystyle = 0\ ✓\)

    MeansCloser to a positive cylinder is higher potential, so this is the right shape.

  6. (d) Potential inside, \(r \lt R\)

    WhyWith no field inside, \(V\) does not change as you go in. It stays at the surface value, found by putting \(r = R\) into (c). Use \(\ln\frac12 = -\ln 2\).

    \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{R}{2R}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac12\) \(\displaystyle = +\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln 2\)

    MeansA positive constant. Not zero: the most common wrong answer.

  7. (e) and (f) Match the graphs

    WhyRead the shapes straight off the formulas.

    \(\displaystyle E_r\): zero up to \(\displaystyle R\), a jump to \(\displaystyle \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 R)\) at the surface, then a \(\displaystyle 1/r\) fall that never crosses zero.
    \(\displaystyle V\): a flat positive plateau up to \(\displaystyle R\), then a smooth log fall that crosses zero exactly at \(\displaystyle 2R\) and keeps going negative. \(\displaystyle V\) never jumps.

  8. Variable-list check

    WhyExpert TA only accepts the letters it lists. If \(k\) is not listed, write \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\), not \(2k\lambda\). They are equal.

V inside = (λ/2πε₀) ln 2
Charged pipe with V = 0 at 3a, then moving the zero
Homework 6, Problem 3
A long metal pipe of radius \(a\) carries surface density \(\sigma\); \(V = 0\) at \(3a\). Find \(E_r\), \(V\), and the constant that moves the zero to \(2a\).

  1. Read the setup

    WhyThe charge is given per unit area of pipe, but the cylinder field uses charge per unit length. Converting is step one.

    Long metal pipe, radius \(\displaystyle a\), surface charge density \(\displaystyle \sigma\).
    Zero of potential at \(\displaystyle r = 3a\). Later, move the zero to \(\displaystyle r = 2a\).

  2. Turn \(\sigma\) into \(\lambda\)

    WhyUnroll a length \(L\) of pipe: it is a rectangle \(2\pi a\) wide (the circumference) and \(L\) long, so its area is \(2\pi aL\) and its charge \(\sigma\,2\pi aL\). Divide by \(L\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = 2\pi a\sigma\)

  3. (a) Field outside, \(r \gt a\)

    WhyPut \(\lambda = 2\pi a\sigma\) into \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\). The \(2\pi\) cancels.

    \(\displaystyle E_r\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2\pi a\sigma}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0 r}\)

    MeansCheck at the surface, \(r = a\): \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\), the standard field just outside a conductor ✓.

  4. (b) Field inside, \(r \lt a\)

    WhyA Gaussian cylinder inside the hollow pipe encloses no charge.

    \(\displaystyle E_r = 0\)

  5. (c) Potential outside, from the zero at \(3a\)

    WhySame steps as any line of charge: start at \(3a\) where \(V = 0\), apply \(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec l\), and use \(\int dr/r = \ln r\).

    \(\displaystyle V(r)\) \(\displaystyle = -\int_{3a}^{r}\dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0 r'}\,dr'\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{r}{3a}\)

  6. (d) Potential inside, \(r \lt a\)

    WhyNo field inside, so \(V\) is frozen at its surface value. Put \(r = a\) into (c) and use \(\ln\frac13 = -\ln 3\).

    \(\displaystyle V\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{a}{3a}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln 3\)

  7. (e) Why adding a constant moves the zero

    WhyThe field comes from how \(V\) changes (\(E = -dV/dr\)), and a constant does not change. So \(V_{\text{new}}\) \(= V_{\text{old}} + V_{\text{shift}}\) has the same field everywhere.

    \(\displaystyle V_{\text{new}}(r)\) \(\displaystyle = V_{\text{old}}(r) + V_{\text{shift}}\)

  8. (e) Pick the constant so \(V_{\text{new}}(2a) = 0\)

    WhySet the new potential at \(2a\) equal to zero and solve for the constant.

    \(\displaystyle 0\) \(\displaystyle = V_{\text{old}}(2a) + V_{\text{shift}}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow V_{\text{shift}}\) \(\displaystyle = -V_{\text{old}}(2a)\)
    \(\displaystyle V_{\text{old}}(2a)\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac{2a}{3a}\) \(\displaystyle = -\dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac23\)
    \(\displaystyle V_{\text{shift}}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln\dfrac23\)

    Means\(\ln\frac23 = -0.405\), so the shift is negative. \(2a\) is closer to the positive pipe than \(3a\), so the old potential there was positive and must be pulled down to zero.

V_shift = (σa/ε₀) ln(2/3)
Coaxial cylinders: the potential difference
Homework 6, Problem 4
Inner conductor radius \(a\) with \(+Q\); shell from \(b\) to \(c\) with \(-Q\); length \(L\). Find \(|\Delta V|\) between the conductors.

  1. Read the setup

    WhyTwo conductors with opposite charges, one inside the other. The question is the voltage between them.

    Inner solid conductor: radius \(\displaystyle a\), charge \(\displaystyle +Q\).
    Outer shell: inner radius \(\displaystyle b\), outer radius \(\displaystyle c\), charge \(\displaystyle -Q\).
    Length \(\displaystyle L \gg c\): treat both as infinitely long, so the field is radial.

  2. Find where the field is

    WhyCheck each region with Gauss's law or the conductor rule.

    \(\displaystyle r \lt a\): inside metal, \(\displaystyle E = 0\).
    \(\displaystyle a \lt r \lt b\): a Gaussian cylinder encloses \(\displaystyle +Q\), so \(\displaystyle E \ne 0\).
    \(\displaystyle b \lt r \lt c\): inside metal, \(\displaystyle E = 0\).
    \(\displaystyle r \gt c\): encloses \(\displaystyle +Q - Q = 0\), so \(\displaystyle E = 0\).

    MeansOnly the gap between \(a\) and \(b\) has a field. That is why \(c\) will never appear in the answer.

  3. Gauss's law in the gap

    WhyChoose a Gaussian cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(L\), sharing the axis. The field is radial, so it passes through the curved side only (area \(2\pi rL\)) and skims along the flat ends.

    \(\displaystyle E\,(2\pi rL)\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\)
    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L\,r}\)

    MeansPointing outward, from \(+Q\) toward \(-Q\).

  4. Set up \(\Delta V\) from \(a\) to \(b\)

    WhyEach conductor is an equipotential, so any path from one to the other gives the same answer. The straight radial path is the easy one: \(\vec E\) and \(d\vec l\) are parallel, so \(\vec E\cdot d\vec l = E\,dr\).

    \(\displaystyle |\Delta V| = \int_a^b E\,dr\) \(\displaystyle = \int_a^b \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L\,r}\,dr\)

  5. Pull the constants out, then integrate

    WhyEverything except \(1/r\) is a constant. The integral of \(dr/r\) is \(\ln r\), and \(\ln b - \ln a = \ln(b/a)\).

    \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}\int_a^b\dfrac{dr}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}\left(\ln b - \ln a\right)\)
    \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}\ln\dfrac{b}{a}\)

  6. Which conductor is higher

    WhyWalking outward goes with the field, and \(V\) always drops along the field.

    The inner conductor (\(\displaystyle +Q\)) is at the higher potential by \(\displaystyle \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}\ln\dfrac{b}{a}\).

    MeansThe answer choices with \(\ln(c/a)\) or \(\ln(c/b)\) are distractors: \(c\) bounds a region with no field.

|ΔV| = (Q/2πε₀L) ln(b/a)
