7.5 Equipotential surfaces and conductors

Reading equipotential maps
  • An equipotential is a surface of constant \(V\). No work is done by the field moving a charge along it (\(\Delta U = q\Delta V = 0\)).
  • Equipotentials are always perpendicular to field lines. \(\vec E\) points from higher \(V\) toward lower \(V\).
  • Drawn at equal \(\Delta V\) steps, closer spacing means stronger field (like contour lines on a topographic map: closer lines, steeper hill).
  • Potential difference between two points = (number of equipotential lines crossed) × (step size), regardless of the path length.
  • Every conductor in equilibrium is one equipotential (surface and interior), and \(\vec E\) meets its surface at 90°.
What each letter means
\(V\)
the potential, V; an equipotential is a surface where it has one value
\(\Delta V\)
the potential difference between two points, or the step between adjacent drawn lines, V
\(q\)
a charge moved along the surface, C
\(\Delta U\)
its change in potential energy, \(q\Delta V\), J
\(\vec E\)
the electric field vector: the force per coulomb that a positive test charge would feel at that point, in N/C (= V/m)
Why equipotentials are perpendicular to the field, and why a conductor is one big equipotential

Move a charge a small step along an equipotential: \(\Delta V = 0\), so the field did no work, so the force had no component along the step. That is true for every direction lying within the equipotential surface, so \(\vec E\) has no component in the surface: it is perpendicular to it. The converse is just as useful: field lines cross equipotentials at right angles, so you can sketch one family from the other.

Inside a conductor in equilibrium \(E = 0\), so \(\Delta V = 0\) between any two interior points; at the surface \(\vec E\) is perpendicular, so moving along the surface also costs nothing. The entire conductor, inside and surface, sits at one potential. This is why "two spheres connected by a wire" means "two spheres at the same \(V\)," and why charge flows through the wire until that is true: charge moves from high \(V\) to low \(V\) (for positive charge) as long as a difference remains, exactly as water flows until the levels equalize.

Equal-step equipotentials are close together where \(V\) changes fast, that is, where \(E\) is large. That single fact answers every "where is the field strongest" map question and the "count the lines crossed" potential-difference questions.

Equipotential and field-line questions from the exams
Fall 2015 Q27 · Lecture 6 checkpoints · Spring 2015 Q18 · Homework 6
Five short questions that all use the same three facts: equipotentials are perpendicular to field lines, \(\vec E\) points toward lower \(V\), and equal-step equipotentials crowd together where the field is strong.

  1. Where is the field weakest? (Lecture 6)

    WhyWeak field means \(V\) changes slowly, so equal-step equipotentials are far apart.

    Point D, where both the field lines and the equipotentials are most spread out.

  2. Compare two potential differences (Fall 2015 Q27)

    Why\(\Delta V\) = (number of equal-step lines crossed) × (step). Path length does not matter.

    G to H crosses as many dashed lines as A to D, so \(\displaystyle V_{GH} = V_{AD}\), even though A to D is a much longer path through a weaker field.

  3. Match equipotentials to field lines (Lecture 6)

    WhyThe lines point left and bunch up on the left: \(V\) decreases toward the left, fastest on the left.

    Any labeling that increases to the right with the tightest spacing on the left works: (a) 10 V inside, 50 V outside, or (c) −50 V inside, −10 V outside. Only order and spacing matter.

  4. Move a charge with no work (Spring 2015 Q18)

    WhyZero work means moving along an equipotential. Between parallel plates those are planes parallel to the plates.

    Move parallel to the plates (the \(\displaystyle x\)-direction in that figure).

  5. Homework 6 "select all" statements

    WhyEquipotentials follow the symmetry; field lines are perpendicular to them.

    Sphere and shells: each conductor's whole volume and every concentric sphere; never radial lines.
    Long cylinder: coaxial cylinders and the conductor's interior; never planes containing the axis or perpendicular to it. Field lines are radial, never circles and never parallel to the axis.
Chapter 8 · Lecture Unit 7 · HW 7

Capacitance

On Exam 1: capacitance and capacitor circuits, 5 of 28 questions.

OpenStax 8.1 Capacitors and capacitance · 8.2 Series and parallel · 8.3 Energy stored · 8.4 Capacitor with a dielectric · 8.5 Molecular model of a dielectric

Lecture 7 opens with the conductor facts you need here: charges are free to move, \(E = 0\) inside, the surface is an equipotential, and \(\vec E\) at the surface is perpendicular to it. A capacitor is two conductors with equal and opposite charge; its capacitance is a fixed number set by geometry (and any dielectric), and the exam checks that you know which quantities stay fixed when something changes.

The chapter in plain words

A capacitor is two conductors that hold equal and opposite charge, \(+Q\) and \(-Q\). The voltage between them grows in proportion to the charge, and the ratio \(C = Q/\Delta V\) (the capacitance) depends only on the shape and spacing of the conductors and on what fills the gap.

Circuits: capacitors side by side (parallel) share a voltage and their capacitances add. Capacitors in a chain (series) share a charge and their reciprocals add.

Energy: a charged capacitor stores \(U = \tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2\), and that energy lives in the electric field in the gap.

Changes: before changing anything (a slab, a dielectric, the gap), ask one question: is the battery still connected? If not, \(Q\) is fixed. If so, \(\Delta V\) is fixed.

8.1 Capacitors and capacitance

Definition
\[ Q = C\,\Delta V \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad C = \frac{Q}{\Delta V} \]
What each letter means
\(Q\)
the magnitude of the charge on one plate, C (the other plate holds \(-Q\); the net charge of the whole capacitor is zero)
\(C\)
capacitance, in farads (1 F = 1 C/V): how much charge the device stores per volt
\(\Delta V\)
the potential difference between the two plates, V (often written just \(V\))
\(\Longleftrightarrow\)
"is the same statement as": both forms say charge and voltage are proportional

Units: farad, \(1\ \mathrm{F} = 1\ \mathrm{C/V}\). Practical values are pF to μF. \(Q\) is the magnitude of the charge on one plate (the plates hold \(+Q\) and \(-Q\)); \(\Delta V\) is the potential difference between them. Lecture 7's key points: \(+Q\) and \(-Q\) always have the same magnitude; charge does not jump across the gap, it is moved around the outside circuit; \(C\) is a positive number that depends only on geometry, "just like \(k\) for a spring."

Method for any geometry: put \(\pm Q\) on the conductors, find \(E\) between them with Gauss's law, integrate to get \(\Delta V\), and take the ratio \(Q/\Delta V\); the \(Q\) cancels.

What physically happens when a capacitor charges, and why \(Q\) is proportional to \(V\)

Connect two metal plates to a battery. The battery is a pump for charge: it pulls electrons off the plate attached to its positive terminal and pushes them onto the plate attached to its negative terminal, through the wires, never across the gap. As the plates acquire \(+Q\) and \(-Q\) a field grows in the gap, and with it a potential difference between the plates. The battery keeps pumping until that potential difference equals its own; then there is nothing driving further flow and charging stops. The plates hold equal and opposite charges because every electron that landed on one plate left from the other.

Now double the charge. Every field line in the gap comes from the plate charge, so the field doubles; the potential difference is the field times the gap, so it doubles too. \(Q\) and \(\Delta V\) rise together in fixed proportion, and the constant of proportionality, \(C = Q/\Delta V\), depends only on how the conductors are shaped and arranged. A big \(C\) means the plates can take a lot of charge before the voltage climbs: closer plates (smaller \(d\), so smaller \(\Delta V = Ed\) for the same \(E\)) or bigger plates (larger \(A\), so the same \(Q\) makes a smaller \(\sigma\) and a weaker field). The formula \(\varepsilon_0A/d\) is those two facts in one line.

A farad is a coulomb per volt. One farad is enormous (a coulomb is enormous); practical capacitors are picofarads to microfarads, which is why the exam's numbers carry those prefixes.

Derivation: capacitance of parallel plates
Lecture 7

  1. Put charge on the plates

    Why\(+Q\) on one plate, \(-Q\) on the other, each spread over area \(A\).

    \(\displaystyle \sigma = \dfrac{Q}{A}\)

  2. Field in the gap

    WhyEach plate is a sheet making \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\). Between the plates the two fields point the same way (from \(+\) toward \(-\)), so they add.

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A}\)

    MeansOutside the plates the two fields point opposite ways and cancel: E = 0 there.

  3. Voltage across the gap

    WhyThe field is uniform, so the voltage is field times distance.

    \(\displaystyle \Delta V = Ed\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0 A}\)

  4. Divide Q by ΔV

    WhyThe \(Q\) cancels, which is why \(C\) depends only on geometry.

    \(\displaystyle C = \dfrac{Q}{\Delta V}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{Qd/(\varepsilon_0A)}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\)

    MeansBigger plates or a smaller gap give a bigger capacitance. Edge effects are ignored (the "infinite plane approximation").

Lecture 7, Example 7.1
A parallel-plate capacitor has \(C = 10\ \mathrm{pF}\) and plate area \(A = 1\ \mathrm{cm^2}\). How far apart are the plates?

  1. Convert to SI

    Why\(1\ \mathrm{cm^2}\) \(= (10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m})^2\) \(= 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}\); \(10\ \mathrm{pF}\) \(= 10\times10^{-12}\) \(= 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\).

    \(\displaystyle A = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2},\) \(\displaystyle C\) \(\displaystyle = 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\)

  2. Solve C = ε₀A/d for d

    WhyMultiply both sides by \(d\), then divide by \(C\).

    \(\displaystyle d = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{C}\)

  3. Plug in

    \(\displaystyle d\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.85\times10^{-12})(10^{-4})}{10^{-11}}\) \(\displaystyle = 8.85\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}\)

    MeansAbout the thickness of a hair.

d = 8.85×10⁻⁵ m

Charge, voltage, and scaling the geometry
Homework 7, Problem 1
Plates of area \(A = 0.0247\ \mathrm{m^2}\) are \(d = 9.98\ \mathrm{cm}\) apart and carry \(Q = 28.7\ \mathrm{nC}\). Find \(C\) and \(\Delta V\). Then (a) double the charge; (b) instead double the area and cut the gap to \(d/4\), keeping the original charge.

  1. Capacitance

    Why\(d = 0.0998\ \mathrm{m}\).

    \(\displaystyle C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.0247)}{0.0998}\) \(\displaystyle = 2.19\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F}\)

  2. Voltage

    Why\(\Delta V = Q/C\).

    Why\(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\) has no \(Q\) in it.

    \(\displaystyle C\) \(\displaystyle = 2.19\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F}\ \text{(unchanged)}\)

    MeansCapacitance is geometry, not charge.

  4. (a) Double the charge: ΔV

    Why\(\Delta V = Q/C\) with \(C\) fixed.

    \(\displaystyle \Delta V\) doubles, to \(\displaystyle 2.62\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\).

  5. (b) New geometry: C

    WhyArea \(\times2\) and gap \(\div4\): \(C\) is multiplied by \(2\times4 = 8\).

    \(\displaystyle C' = 8C\) \(\displaystyle = 1.75\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\) \(\displaystyle = 17.5\ \mathrm{pF}\)

    WhyOriginal charge on the new capacitance.

    \(\displaystyle \Delta V'\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{28.7\times10^{-9}}{1.75\times10^{-11}}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.64\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{V}\)

Derivation: capacitance of a cylindrical capacitor
Lecture 7, Example 7.2 · Homework 6, Problem 4

  1. Put charge on the conductors

    Why\(+Q\) on the inner conductor, \(-Q\) on the inner surface of the outer tube, over length \(L\).

    \(\displaystyle \lambda = \dfrac{Q}{L}\)

  2. Field in the gap (Gauss)

    WhyA coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius \(r\) (between \(a\) and \(b\)) and length \(L\) encloses \(+Q\). Only its side wall catches flux.

    \(\displaystyle E\cdot2\pi rL\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 Lr}\)

  3. Voltage between the conductors

    WhyAdd up \(E\,dr\) across the gap. The \(1/r\) integrates to a logarithm.

    \(\displaystyle |\Delta V|\) \(\displaystyle = \int_a^b \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0L}\,\dfrac{dr}{r}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0L}\ln\dfrac{b}{a}\)

  4. Divide Q by ΔV

    Why\(Q\) cancels.

    \(\displaystyle C = \dfrac{Q}{|\Delta V|}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)}\)

  5. Sanity checks

    Longer \(\displaystyle L\): bigger \(\displaystyle C\).
    \(\displaystyle b \to a\): \(\displaystyle \ln(b/a) \to 0\), so \(\displaystyle C\) grows without limit (a tiny gap is a huge capacitor).
    The tube's outer radius never appears: only the two facing surfaces matter.

Lecture 7 · Section 8.1 table

  1. Field in the gap (Gauss)

    WhyA Gaussian sphere of radius \(r\) between \(a\) and \(b\) encloses \(+Q\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\)

  2. Voltage between the spheres

    WhyIntegrate \(E\,dr\) from \(a\) to \(b\). \(\int dr/r^2 = -1/r\).

    \(\displaystyle |\Delta V|\) \(\displaystyle = \int_a^b \dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\,dr\) \(\displaystyle = kQ\left(\dfrac1a - \dfrac1b\right)\) \(\displaystyle = kQ\,\dfrac{b - a}{ab}\)

    WhyMove the outer shell infinitely far away: \(b \to \infty\), so \(b - a \approx b\).

    \(\displaystyle C = \dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,ab}{b}\) \(\displaystyle = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\)

    MeansAn isolated sphere of radius a holds Q = 4πε₀aV at potential V.

8.2 Capacitors in series and in parallel

The two rules and how to tell them apart
ParallelSeries
Wiringboth leads of each capacitor connect to the same two nodes (side by side)end to end along one path, with nothing else attached at the junction between them
What is sharedsame \(\Delta V\) across eachsame \(Q\) on each (the inner plates are an isolated island, net charge zero)
What splits\(Q_i = C_i\,\Delta V\); total \(Q = \sum Q_i\)\(\Delta V_i = Q/C_i\); total \(\Delta V = \sum\Delta V_i\)
Equivalent\(C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots\) (bigger than any one)\(\dfrac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}}\) \(= \dfrac1{C_1} + \dfrac1{C_2} + \cdots\) (smaller than any one); two in series: \(\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}\)
Largest sharelargest \(C\) takes the most chargesmallest \(C\) takes the most voltage
What each letter means
\(C_1,\ C_2,\ C_i\)
the individual capacitances, F; \(i\) is a label for "any one of them"
\(Q_i,\ \Delta V_i\)
the charge on and the voltage across capacitor \(i\)
\(Q,\ \Delta V\)
the total charge supplied and the total voltage across the combination
\(C_{\text{eq}}\)
the equivalent capacitance: one capacitor that would take the same total charge at the same total voltage, F
\(\sum\)
add up over all the capacitors in the combination

Compare resistors (Chapter 10, not on this exam): capacitor rules are the reverse of resistor rules.

Why series capacitors share charge and parallel capacitors share voltage

Series. Two capacitors in a chain: battery, then \(C_1\), then \(C_2\), then back to the battery. Look at the conductor in the middle: the right plate of \(C_1\), the wire, and the left plate of \(C_2\). It is connected to nothing else. It started neutral, and charge can neither enter nor leave it (there is no path), so it stays neutral forever: if \(-Q\) collects on the right plate of \(C_1\), exactly \(+Q\) must appear on the left plate of \(C_2\). Every capacitor in the chain therefore carries the same \(Q\). Their voltages add along the chain to the battery's, so \(V = Q/C_1 + Q/C_2\), which is where \(1/C_{\text{eq}} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2\) comes from. Adding capacitors in series lowers the capacitance: the battery must push the same charge across more gaps in a row.

Parallel. Two capacitors whose left plates are joined by a wire and whose right plates are joined by another wire. A wire in equilibrium is an equipotential, so both left plates are at one potential and both right plates at another: the two capacitors see the same \(\Delta V\). Each takes the charge its own capacitance allows, \(Q_i = C_i\Delta V\), and the battery supplies the sum. So \(C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2\): parallel plates act like one bigger plate.

These two arguments are all you need to classify any pair in a circuit: "same isolated island between them" means series; "both ends on the same two wires" means parallel; anything else is neither.

Circuit algorithm
  1. Reduce. Find a pair that is purely series or purely parallel, replace it with one equivalent, redraw. Repeat until one \(C_{\text{eq}}\) faces the battery.
  2. Total charge: \(Q_{\text{tot}}\) \(= C_{\text{eq}}V_{\text{battery}}\).
  3. Unwind. Go back one step at a time. A series combination: each member gets the combination's \(Q\); then \(V_i = Q/C_i\). A parallel combination: each member gets the combination's \(V\); then \(Q_i = C_iV\).
  4. Check: voltages around any loop add up to the battery's; charges into a junction of a series string are equal; \(\sum \tfrac12 C_iV_i^2\) \(= \tfrac12C_{\text{eq}}V^2\).
What each letter means
\(C_{\text{eq}}\)
the single equivalent capacitance of the whole network, F
\(V_{\text{battery}},\ V\)
the battery's voltage, V
\(Q_{\text{tot}}\)
the total charge the battery moves onto the network, C
\(Q_i,\ V_i,\ C_i\)
the charge, voltage, and capacitance of capacitor number \(i\)
\(\tfrac12C_iV_i^2\)
the energy stored in capacitor \(i\), J; the sum over all of them equals the energy of the equivalent capacitor

If a problem gives you one capacitor's charge instead of the battery voltage (Spring 2014 Q16–19), start there and unwind outward: \(V\) of that capacitor gives \(V\) of its parallel partners, then \(Q\) of the series string it belongs to, and so on.

Circuit (a): given one capacitor's charge, find everything
Spring 2014, Questions 16–19
\(C_1 = 6\), \(C_2 = 8\), \(C_3 = 12\), \(C_4 = 10\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). The charge on \(C_1\) is \(5.83\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). (Q16) Are \(C_3\) and \(C_4\) in series, in parallel, or neither? (Q17) Find \(C_{1234}\). (Q18) Find \(V_3\). (Q19) Find the battery voltage.

  1. C₁ and C₂: parallel

    WhyBoth connect the same two wires: the left top wire and the bottom wire.

    \(\displaystyle C_{12} = C_1 + C_2\) \(\displaystyle = 6 + 8\) \(\displaystyle = 14\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)

  2. C₁₂ and C₃: series

    WhyThe wire between them connects to nothing else, so it is an isolated island.

    \(\displaystyle C_{123}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{C_{12}C_3}{C_{12} + C_3}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(14)(12)}{26}\) \(\displaystyle = 6.46\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)

  3. C₁₂₃ and C₄: parallel

    WhyThe whole left string and \(C_4\) both connect the right top wire to the bottom wire (the battery does too).

    \(\displaystyle C_{1234} = 6.46 + 10\) \(\displaystyle = 16.5\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)

    MeansQ17 answered.

  4. Q16: C₃ and C₄

    WhyNot series: the wire between them also leads to the battery. Not parallel: \(C_3\)'s left end goes to \(C_{12}\), not to \(C_4\)'s other end.

8.3 Energy stored in a capacitor

Three equivalent forms, and the energy density
\[ U = \int_0^Q V\,dq = \int_0^Q\frac{q}{C}\,dq = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac12C(\Delta V)^2 = \frac12Q\,\Delta V \]
What each letter means
\(U\)
the energy stored in the capacitor, J
\(Q\)
the final charge on a plate, C
\(q,\ dq\)
the charge already on the plate part-way through charging, and the next tiny bit moved, C
\(V = q/C\)
the voltage at that moment, which grows as charge accumulates
\(C\)
capacitance, in farads (1 F = 1 C/V): how much charge the device stores per volt
\(\Delta V\)
the final voltage, V
\(\tfrac12\)
the factor that appears because the average voltage during charging is half the final one

The factor \(\tfrac12\) is there because the voltage grows from 0 to \(\Delta V\) as the charge is moved (Lecture 7: "\(U\) is the work it took to put all the charge on the two plates"). Energy per unit volume stored in the field:

\[ u = \frac{U}{\text{volume}} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E^2 \]
What each letter means
\(u\)
energy density: energy stored per cubic meter of field, J/m³
\(U\)
the total stored energy, J
\(\text{volume}\)
the volume of the region where the field exists (for parallel plates, area × gap \(= Ad\)), m³
\(E\)
magnitude of the electric field, in N/C (the same unit as V/m)
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

Pick the form that uses what is held fixed: \(Q^2/2C\) when the charge is fixed (battery removed), \(\tfrac12CV^2\) when the voltage is fixed (battery connected).

Why the stored energy is half of \(QV\), and why it lives in the field

Charging a capacitor means carrying charge from one plate to the other against the potential difference that already exists. The first bit of charge moves when the plates are uncharged and \(\Delta V = 0\): it costs nothing. The last bit moves against the full voltage. On average the charge was moved through half the final voltage, so the total work is \(\tfrac12 Q\,\Delta V\), not \(Q\,\Delta V\). The integral in the key box, \(\int_0^Q (q/C)\,dq = Q^2/2C\), is that averaging done exactly. The battery, meanwhile, moved the same charge through its full voltage and supplied \(Q\,\Delta V\); the other half is dissipated in the wires as heat (or radiated). That is a famous puzzle and it is true; the capacitor only ever keeps half.

Where is the stored energy? Not in the charges themselves, which are the same electrons as before, but in the field between the plates. Divide \(U = \tfrac12 CV^2\) by the volume of the gap and everything about the geometry cancels except \(E\): \(u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\) joules per cubic meter. This formula holds for the field of anything, not just capacitors, and it is the first hint that the field is a physical thing (Chapter 16 will show it carrying energy across empty space as light).

Energy and energy density
Lecture 7, Example 7.3
A \(C = 8\ \mathrm{pF}\) parallel-plate capacitor with a \(1\ \mathrm{mm}\) gap is charged to \(\Delta V = 120\ \mathrm{V}\). Find the stored energy and the energy density in the gap.

  1. Stored energy

    WhyVoltage is given, so use \(\tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2\).

    \(\displaystyle U = \tfrac12(8\times10^{-12})(120)^2\) \(\displaystyle = 5.76\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{J}\)

  2. Check with the charge form

    Why\(Q = C\Delta V\), then \(Q^2/2C\).

    \(\displaystyle Q = (8\times10^{-12})(120)\) \(\displaystyle = 9.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{C}\)
    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(9.6\times10^{-10})^2}{2(8\times10^{-12})}\) \(\displaystyle = 5.76\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{J}\ \checkmark\)

  3. Field in the gap

    WhyUniform field: \(E = \Delta V/d\).

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{120}{10^{-3}}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V/m}\)

  4. Energy density

    \(\displaystyle u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12(8.85\times10^{-12})(1.2\times10^{5})^2\) \(\displaystyle = 0.0637\ \mathrm{J/m^3}\)

  5. Check: energy ÷ volume

    WhyPlate area from \(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\), then volume \(= Ad\).

    \(\displaystyle A = \dfrac{Cd}{\varepsilon_0}\) \(\displaystyle = 9.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2},\) \(\displaystyle Ad\) \(\displaystyle = 9.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^3}\)
    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{U}{Ad}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{5.76\times10^{-8}}{9.0\times10^{-7}}\) \(\displaystyle = 0.0637\ \mathrm{J/m^3}\ \checkmark\)
U = 5.76×10⁻⁸ J u = 0.064 J/m³
J
Deriving the energy density
Homework 7, Problem 2
Show that the energy stored in a parallel-plate capacitor, divided by the volume of its gap, is \(u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\).

  1. Write U with the capacitance formula

    \(\displaystyle U = \tfrac12 C_0V_0^2\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12\,\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\,V_0^2\)

  2. Replace the voltage with the field

    WhyUniform field: \(V_0 = Ed\).

    \(\displaystyle U\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12\,\dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\,(Ed)^2\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\,(Ad)\)

  3. Divide by the gap volume Ad

    \(\displaystyle u = \dfrac{U}{Ad}\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\)

    MeansEvery trace of the geometry cancels. This holds for any electric field, not just a capacitor's.

u = ½ε₀E²

Sliding an uncharged conducting slab into the gap
Lecture 7 clicker sequence
Plates carry \(\pm Q_0\), gap \(d\), battery removed. An uncharged conducting slab of thickness \(t\) is slid into the gap without touching either plate. What happens to the charge, the field, the voltage, and the capacitance?

  1. Plate charge

    WhyNothing is connected, so charge has nowhere to go.

  2. Charges on the slab

    WhyInside the metal \(E = 0\). Its electrons shift toward the \(+\) plate until the faces carry \(-Q_0\) (top) and \(+Q_0\) (bottom).

    MeansThe slab stays neutral overall.

    WhyA Gaussian pillbox around the top plate still encloses only \(+Q_0\), so the field in each air gap is unchanged.

    WhyAdd \(E\,dx\) across the gap: \(E_0\) over the two air gaps (total width \(d - t\)), zero across the slab.

    Why\(C = Q/\Delta V\).

    MeansOnly the thickness matters, not where the slab sits in the gap.

    WhyThen \(\Delta V\) is fixed and the battery pushes in more charge: \(Q_1 = C_1\Delta V \gt Q_0\).

    MeansC₁ is the same either way: "C depends only on geometry!"

Same setup with \(t = d/2\), battery removed. (Q16) Find the new capacitance. (Q17) Compare the new stored energy with the old. (Q18) Along which direction can a test charge be moved inside the gap with no work?

Dielectrics

An insulating material of dielectric constant \(\kappa \ge 1\) filling the gap:

\[ E = \frac{E_0}{\kappa}, \qquad C = \kappa C_0, \qquad \varepsilon_0\oint\kappa\vec E\cdot d\vec A = q_{\text{free}} \]
What each letter means
\(E,\ E_0\)
the field inside the dielectric, and the field the same plate charge would make with an empty gap, N/C
\(\kappa\)
dielectric constant of the insulating material (a pure number, \(\ge 1\); 1 for vacuum or air)
\(C,\ C_0\)
the capacitance with and without the dielectric, F
\(\oint\)
integral over a closed surface (one with an inside and an outside, like a balloon); the circle on the sign is what marks it as closed
\(q_{\text{free}}\)
the free charge enclosed (the charge on the plates), C; the dielectric's own bound charge is accounted for by \(\kappa\)
\(\sigma,\ \sigma_i\)
the plate's surface charge density and the induced (bound) density on the dielectric's faces, C/m²
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet

Molecular model (8.5): the field polarizes the molecules (aligns permanent dipoles or induces dipoles). The net effect is an induced surface charge \(-\sigma_i\) on the dielectric face next to the \(+\) plate and \(+\sigma_i\) next to the \(-\) plate, partially cancelling the plate charge. The field inside is \(E\) \(= (\sigma - \sigma_i)/\varepsilon_0\) \(= \sigma/(\kappa\varepsilon_0)\), so \(\sigma_i = \sigma(1 - 1/\kappa)\). A conductor is the \(\kappa \to \infty\) limit (complete cancellation, \(E = 0\)).

The mechanism of a dielectric, and why the battery decides what happens

A dielectric is an insulator: its electrons cannot flow, but every molecule can stretch. In the gap field, each molecule's electrons shift slightly toward the positive plate and its nuclei toward the negative plate (or, for molecules like water that are dipoles already, the dipoles rotate to line up). Inside the material these tiny shifts cancel neighbor against neighbor, but at the two faces they do not: the face next to the \(+\) plate ends up with a thin layer of negative charge, the face next to the \(-\) plate with positive charge. These bound charges make a field opposing the plates' field, so the total field inside the dielectric is smaller, \(E = E_0/\kappa\), where \(\kappa\) measures how easily the material polarizes. A metal is the extreme case, \(\kappa\to\infty\): its electrons move all the way and cancel the field completely.

A weaker field for the same plate charge means a smaller \(\Delta V = Ed\), and therefore a larger \(C = Q/\Delta V\). That is all "\(C = \kappa C_0\)" says.

Why the battery matters. Inserting the slab lowers the voltage for the plates' current charge. If the battery is disconnected, the charge has nowhere to go: \(Q\) is fixed, \(\Delta V\) drops, and the stored energy \(Q^2/2C\) drops (the slab is actually pulled into the gap; the missing energy went into that pull). If the battery is connected, it notices the voltage sag and pumps in more charge until \(\Delta V\) is back to its own value: \(Q\) rises to \(\kappa Q_0\), and the energy \(\tfrac12 CV^2\) rises, supplied by the battery. Same slab, opposite answers to "did the energy go up?", decided entirely by whether the charge or the voltage was held fixed.

An uncharged conducting slab works the same way but more so: its faces take on \(\mp Q\) fully, the field inside it is zero, and the effective gap shrinks by its thickness, \(C = \varepsilon_0A/(d - t)\).

The bound charge on a dielectric's faces
Section 8.5 (molecular model)
A dielectric of constant \(\kappa\) fills the gap of a capacitor whose plates carry density \(\pm\sigma\). Find the bound (induced) density \(\sigma_i\) on the dielectric's faces.

  1. Field from the plates and the bound layers

    WhyInside the dielectric, the plates contribute \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) and the bound layers (opposite sign, facing each plate) contribute \(-\sigma_i/\varepsilon_0\).

    \(\displaystyle E\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma - \sigma_i}{\varepsilon_0}\)

  2. The dielectric reduces the field by κ

    \(\displaystyle E = \dfrac{E_0}{\kappa}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{\kappa\varepsilon_0}\)

  3. Set equal and solve

    WhyCancel \(\varepsilon_0\), then isolate \(\sigma_i\).

    \(\displaystyle \sigma - \sigma_i\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\sigma}{\kappa}\) \(\displaystyle \Rightarrow \sigma_i\) \(\displaystyle = \sigma\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\kappa}\right)\)

    MeansVacuum (\(\kappa = 1\)): no bound charge. A metal (\(\kappa \to \infty\)): \(\sigma_i = \sigma\), complete cancellation.

σᵢ = σ(1 − 1/κ)
A capacitor half filled with a dielectric

\(A = 5\ \mathrm{cm^2}\), \(d = 1\ \mathrm{mm}\), a slab with \(\kappa = 1.5\) fills half the gap (thickness \(d/2\)), and the charge is fixed at \(Q = 6\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{C}\). (Q20) Find \(\Delta V\). (Q21) Find \(C\).

    \(\displaystyle A = 5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2},\) \(\displaystyle d\) \(\displaystyle = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m},\) \(\displaystyle \tfrac d2\) \(\displaystyle = 5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}\)

    WhySet by the plate charge: \(E_0 = Q/(\varepsilon_0A)\).

    \(\displaystyle E_0\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{6\times10^{-11}}{(8.85\times10^{-12})(5\times10^{-4})}\) \(\displaystyle = 1.36\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/m}\)

    WhyReduced by \(\kappa\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{E_0}{\kappa}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{1.36\times10^{4}}{1.5}\) \(\displaystyle = 9.04\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{V/m}\)

    MeansQ20 answered.

    WhyTreat each half as its own capacitor with gap \(d/2\).

    No slab: \(\displaystyle C_0 = \varepsilon_0A/d\) \(\displaystyle = 4.42\ \mathrm{pF}\). Full slab: \(\displaystyle \kappa C_0 = 6.64\ \mathrm{pF}\).

    MeansHalf a slab lands in between, and never simply at "κ/2."

Two dielectric layers
Fall 2018, Question 26
The bottom half of the gap (thickness \(d/2\)) is filled with \(\kappa_1\) and the top half with \(\kappa_2\). Find \(C\) in terms of \(C_0 = \varepsilon_0A/d\).

  1. Each layer as its own capacitor

    WhyGap \(d/2\) doubles the empty value, then the dielectric multiplies by \(\kappa\).

    \(\displaystyle C_1\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\kappa_1\varepsilon_0A}{d/2}\) \(\displaystyle = 2\kappa_1C_0,\) \(\displaystyle C_2\) \(\displaystyle = 2\kappa_2C_0\)

  2. Layers along the field: series

    WhyThe same charge passes through both layers.

    \(\displaystyle C = \dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{(2\kappa_1C_0)(2\kappa_2C_0)}{2\kappa_1C_0 + 2\kappa_2C_0}\)

  3. Simplify

    WhyCancel a factor \(2C_0\) from top and bottom.

    \(\displaystyle C\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{2\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1 + \kappa_2}\,C_0\)

  4. Check

    WhySet \(\kappa_1 = \kappa_2 = \kappa\).

    \(\displaystyle \dfrac{2\kappa^2}{2\kappa}C_0\) \(\displaystyle = \kappa C_0\ \checkmark\)

  5. If the two were side by side instead

    WhyEach covers half the area over the full gap: parallel.

    \(\displaystyle C\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{\kappa_1C_0}{2} + \dfrac{\kappa_2C_0}{2}\) \(\displaystyle = \tfrac12(\kappa_1 + \kappa_2)C_0\)
C = 2κ₁κ₂C₀/(κ₁ + κ₂)
What each letter means
\(\kappa_1,\ \kappa_2\)
the dielectric constants of the two slabs
\(d\)
the full gap, m; each slab is \(d/2\) thick
\(A\)
the plate area, m²
\(C_0\)
the empty-gap capacitance, \(\varepsilon_0A/d\)
\(C_1,\ C_2\)
the capacitance of each half treated as its own capacitor, F
\(C\)
the capacitance of the combination, F
\(\varepsilon_0\)
permittivity of free space, \(8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2/(N\,m^2)}\); a constant of nature, given on the equation sheet
Full dielectric with the battery removed
Fall 2015, Questions 16–18
\(C_0 = 1.61\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\) is charged to \(85.5\ \mathrm{V}\), so \(q = 1.38\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\). The battery is disconnected, then a slab with \(\kappa = 2.65\) fills the gap. Find the new capacitance, the new voltage, and compare the energies.

  1. What is fixed?

    WhyThe battery is disconnected, so the charge cannot change.

    \(\displaystyle q\) \(\displaystyle = 1.38\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\ \text{(fixed)}\)

  2. New capacitance

    WhyA full dielectric multiplies \(C\) by \(\kappa\).

    \(\displaystyle C_1 = \kappa C_0\) \(\displaystyle = (2.65)(1.61\times10^{-11})\) \(\displaystyle = 4.27\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\)

  3. New voltage

    Why\(V = q/C\), and \(C\) went up by \(\kappa\), so \(V\) goes down by \(\kappa\).

    \(\displaystyle V_1 = \dfrac{85.5}{2.65}\) \(\displaystyle = 32.3\ \mathrm{V}\)

  4. Energies

    WhyCharge fixed: use \(q^2/2C\).

    \(\displaystyle U_1 = \dfrac{q^2}{2C_1}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{q^2}{2\kappa C_0}\) \(\displaystyle = \dfrac{U_0}{\kappa}\)

    MeansU₀ > U₁.

C₁ = 4.27×10⁻¹¹ F V₁ = 32.3 V U₀ > U₁
Trap

If the battery had stayed connected, \(U_1 = \tfrac12\kappa C_0V^2\) \(= \kappa U_0 \gt U_0\). The same physical action gives opposite answers for "does the energy go up or down" depending on the battery. Read the problem statement for the words "disconnected," "removed," "isolated," or "remains connected."

Before the exam

Exam Strategy, Decision Map, and the Trap List

How to pick the method in ten seconds, and the twenty mistakes the distractors are built around.

Decision map: what is given, what is asked

You are asked for…Given…Do thisSection
Force on a chargea few point chargesCoulomb magnitudes, arrows by sign rule, components, sum. Or find \(\vec E\) first and use \(\vec F = q\vec E\).5.3
\(\vec E\) at a pointa few point charges\(kq/r^2\) each, away from +, toward −, components, sum. Use symmetry to zero a component.5.4
\(\vec E\) at a pointa rod, ring, arc, disk (finite object, low symmetry)Set up \(\int k\,dq/r^2\) with \(dq = \lambda\,dx\) or \(\lambda R\,d\theta\); include the trig factor; kill a component by symmetry; check the far limit.5.5
\(\vec E\) at a pointsphere, infinite cylinder/line, infinite sheet (high symmetry), possibly layeredGauss's law: \(Q_{\text{enc}}\) inside a sphere/cylinder through the point; \(E = kQ_{\text{enc}}/r^2\) or \(2k\lambda_{\text{enc}}/r\) or \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) per sheet. Conductors: \(E=0\) inside, induced charges on surfaces.6.3, 6.4
Flux through a surfacea closed surface\(Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\), full stop. Shape, size, position of charge inside: irrelevant.6.2
Flux through a surfacean open flat surface in a uniform field\(EA\cos\theta\) with \(\theta\) to the normal.6.1
Induced surface chargeconductor with a cavity / shell / slabGaussian surface inside the metal encloses zero: inner surface \(= -q_{\text{inside}}\); outer \(=\) net \(-\) inner. For slabs between sheets: total field inside the slab \(= 0\).6.4, 6.5
Potential energy of a set of charges; work to assemblepoint charges at given positions\(\sum_{\text{pairs}}kq_iq_j/r_{ij}\). Signs matter, no components.7.1
Speed after releasecharges and masses\(\Delta K = -\Delta U\); if both move, add momentum conservation.7.1
\(V\) at a pointpoint charges\(\sum kq_i/r_i\), scalar. Work to bring in \(q\): \(qV\).7.2
\(V\) or \(\Delta V\)a field you know (uniform, or from Gauss)\(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec l\): uniform gives \(-Ed\) along \(\vec E\); \(1/r^2\) gives \(kQ(1/r_2 - 1/r_1)\); \(1/r\) gives \(-2k\lambda\ln(r_2/r_1)\); inside a conductor, no change.7.3, 7.4
\(\vec E\) from \(V\)a graph or formula for \(V\)minus the slope: \(E_x = -dV/dx\).7.3
Compare \(\Delta V\)'s or \(E\)'san equipotential / field-line mapcount lines crossed; spacing ↔ strength; \(\vec E\) ⟂ equipotentials, high to low \(V\).7.5
\(C\)a geometry\(\varepsilon_0A/d\), \(2\pi\varepsilon_0L/\ln(b/a)\), \(4\pi\varepsilon_0ab/(b-a)\); with dielectric, times \(\kappa\); conducting slab of thickness \(t\): use gap \(d-t\).8.1
\(Q\), \(V\), or \(U\) of one capacitor in a networka circuitreduce to \(C_{\text{eq}}\), get total \(Q\), unwind: series share \(Q\), parallel share \(V\).8.2
What changes when a slab is inserted or the gap changesbattery connected or notDisconnected: \(Q\) fixed, use \(U = Q^2/2C\). Connected: \(V\) fixed, use \(U = \tfrac12CV^2\).8.4

Scaling questions (no calculator needed)

  • Point charge: \(F, E \propto 1/r^2\); double \(r\) → quarter. \(V, U \propto 1/r\); double \(r\) → half.
  • Infinite line: \(E \propto 1/r\). Infinite sheet: \(E\) independent of \(r\).
  • Inside a uniform insulating sphere or cylinder: \(E \propto r\).
  • Flux through a closed surface: independent of its size and shape.
  • Parallel plates: \(C \propto A/d\); doubling \(A\) and halving \(d\) quadruples \(C\).
  • Fixed \(Q\): \(U \propto 1/C\). Fixed \(V\): \(U \propto C\).
  • Two capacitors in series: \(C_{\text{eq}}\) is less than the smaller one; equal ones give half. In parallel: sum.

The trap list

  1. Flux angle. \(\Phi = EA\cos\theta\) uses the angle between \(\vec E\) and the normal. A plate "at 30° to the field" has \(\theta = 60^\circ\).
  2. \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) vs. \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\). Free sheet: \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) each side. Surface of a conductor: \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) just outside. Between capacitor plates: \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) (two sheets adding).
  3. Vectors vs. scalars. \(\vec F\) and \(\vec E\): components. \(U\) and \(V\): signed numbers, no cosines. Never add field magnitudes from different directions.
  4. Newton's third law. The force on the big charge equals the force on the small one in magnitude, always.
  5. Zero-field location. Like charges: between, nearer the smaller. Opposite charges: outside, on the smaller charge's side. Independent of the test charge.
  6. Who does the work. \(\Delta U = -W_{\text{field}}\) \(= +W_{\text{you}}\) (at constant speed). "Work required" and "work you do" mean \(W_{\text{you}} = q\,\Delta V\). Field pushes a charge toward lower \(U\).
  7. \(E = 0\) does not mean \(V = 0\). Inside a conductor \(V\) is constant and equal to the surface value. Conversely, \(V = 0\) at a point between \(+q\) and \(-q\) while \(E \ne 0\) there.
  8. Logarithms for cylinders. \(\Delta V = -2k\lambda\ln(r_2/r_1)\), and the reference point cannot be infinity. The \(1/r\) form belongs to spheres.
  9. Battery connected or not. Decides whether \(Q\) or \(V\) is fixed, and therefore whether \(U\) rises or falls when \(C\) changes.
  10. Series vs. parallel sharing. Series: same \(Q\). Parallel: same \(V\). "Same voltage as \(C_1\)" means a parallel partner, never a series partner (unless the capacitances happen to be equal).
  11. Induced charge bookkeeping. Inner surface of a conductor around charge \(q\): exactly \(-q\). Outer surface: net charge minus inner. A neutral conductor does not change the field outside itself.
  12. Distance dependence by geometry. Point \(1/r^2\); line \(1/r\); sheet constant. Mixing these up produces the wrong power in "which expression" questions.
  13. Dipoles. Torque is zero at \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\); \(U\) is lowest at \(0^\circ\), highest at \(180^\circ\), zero at \(90^\circ\); net force is zero in a uniform field for every orientation.
  14. Calculator quadrant. \(\tan^{-1}(F_y/F_x)\) with \(F_x \lt 0\) needs \(+180^\circ\). Sketch the resultant first.
  15. Units. cm to m before squaring; nC \(= 10^{-9}\), pC \(= 10^{-12}\), μC \(= 10^{-6}\); \(\mu\)g \(= 10^{-9}\) kg. Keep \(k = 8.99\times10^9\) or \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\), not both.
  16. Charge sharing. Identical conductors touching split the total equally. Different-size spheres connected by a wire equalize \(V\), so \(Q \propto R\).
  17. Ring and arc limits. On-axis ring field is zero at the center and \(kQ/h^2\) far away. The arc's \(dq\) uses \(\lambda R\,d\theta\), and \(\lambda = Q/(\text{arc length})\), not \(Q/(2\pi R)\) unless it is a full ring.
  18. Gauss's law is always true, sometimes useless. For a cube of charge, no surface makes \(E\) constant; the law still gives the flux.
  19. Pairs, not charges. \(U_{\text{total}}\) has one term per pair. Three charges: three terms. Four: six. The "work to add one more charge" is only the new pairs.
  20. Sign of \(\lambda\), \(\sigma\), \(\rho\). Carry the sign through \(Q_{\text{enc}}\): a negative enclosed charge means an inward field. In multi-layer problems, the direction flips wherever \(Q_{\text{enc}}\) changes sign.

Day-of checklist

  • TI-30 (non-graphing), cover off; no phone.
  • Skim the provided sheet once at the start so you know where each formula sits (Appendix reproduces it).
  • For every vector problem: draw the arrows first, then compute.
  • For every Gauss problem: write the list of layers and their surface charges before touching a formula.
  • For every capacitor circuit: write the structure in words ("\(C_1\) and \(C_2\) parallel, then series with \(C_3\)") before reducing.
  • Check units and order of magnitude of every numeric answer against the choices; distractors are usually off by a factor of 2, \(\pi\), 10, or a sign.
