Hour Exam 1, Spring 2014

Q1Electric fields A positively charged rod is brought near (not touching) an electroscope; the electroscope is briefly grounded; then the rod is removed. Which is NOT true? (a) Negative charges flow from ground to the electroscope. (b) The leaves repel each other when the rod is moved away. (c) Positive charges are induced on the electroscope when the rod is moved away.

With the + rod nearby, electrons in the electroscope are drawn toward the rod, leaving the leaves positive. Grounding lets electrons flow in from ground to neutralize the positive far side (a is true). Remove the ground, then the rod: the extra electrons spread out, the electroscope is net negative, and the like-charged leaves repel (b is true). Nothing positive is "induced" once the rod is gone; the object is simply negatively charged. Statement (c) is false.

Answer: c §5.1
Q2Gauss's law Three parallel infinite planes, left to right: \(+\sigma\), \(-2\sigma\), \(-2\sigma\). Point A is between the first two; B is between the last two. Find \(E_A/E_B\). Options: ∞, 3/4, 1, 5, 2.

Each sheet contributes \(|\sigma_i|/2\varepsilon_0\), away from positive, toward negative. Work in units of \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\), taking right as positive.

At A: \(+\sigma\) is to the left (push right): \(+1\). Middle \(-2\sigma\) is to the right (pull right): \(+2\). Far \(-2\sigma\) to the right: \(+2\). \(E_A = 5\).

At B: \(+\sigma\) far left: \(+1\). Middle \(-2\sigma\) now to the left (pull left): \(-2\). Right \(-2\sigma\): \(+2\). \(E_B = 1\). Ratio \(= 5\).

Answer: d §6.5
Q3Electric fields \(Q_1 = +5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at (0, 4 cm), \(Q_2 = +5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at (0, −4 cm), \(Q_3 = -7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at (−3 cm, 0). P is at (3 cm, 0). Direction of \(\vec E\) at P due to \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) only: zero, −x, or +x?

\(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are equal, positive, and mirror images across the x-axis. Their fields at P point away from each charge; the y-parts cancel and the x-parts both point in \(+x\).

Answer: c (+x) §5.4
Q4Electric fields Same charges. A 1 C charge is placed at P. What is the x-component of the net force on it from all three charges? Options: +1.3×10⁷, +4.1×10⁶, −1.3×10⁷, +3.0×10⁴, −4.1×10⁶ N.

\(F_x = (1\ \mathrm{C})E_x\). From \(Q_1\): distance \(\sqrt{3^2+4^2} = 5\ \mathrm{cm}\); \(E = k(5\times10^{-6})/(0.05)^2\) \(= 1.80\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{N/C}\); x-part \(= E\cdot(3/5) = 1.08\times10^{7}\). Same from \(Q_2\): total \(2.16\times10^{7}\) in \(+x\).

From \(Q_3\) (negative, 6 cm to the left of P): field points toward \(Q_3\), i.e. \(-x\): \(k(7\times10^{-6})/(0.06)^2\) \(= 1.75\times10^{7}\).

\(E_x\) \(= 2.16\times10^7 - 1.75\times10^7\) \(= +4.1\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N/C}\); \(F_x = +4.1\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N}\).

Answer: b §5.4
Q5Electric fields A uniformly charged semicircle (right half of a circle, radius \(r = 5\ \mathrm{cm}\)) has \(Q = +15\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). What is \(\lambda\)? Options: 150, 95, 48 μC/m.

Arc length of a semicircle is \(\pi r\): \(\lambda = Q/(\pi r)\) \(= 15\times10^{-6}/(\pi\times0.05)\) \(= 9.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C/m}\) \(= 95\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\). (150 would be \(Q/(2r)\), 48 would be \(Q/(2\pi r)\), a full ring.)

Answer: b §5.5
Q6Electric fields Which expression gives \(E_x\) at the origin due to this semicircle? (θ is measured from the +x axis; the arc runs from −π/2 to π/2.) Options include \(-\int\frac{k\lambda}{r}\sin\theta\,d\theta\), \(-\int\frac{k\lambda}{r}\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta\), 0, \(-\int\frac{k\lambda}{r^2}\cos\theta\,d\theta\), \(-\int\frac{k\lambda}{r}\cos\theta\,d\theta\).

\(dq = \lambda r\,d\theta\); every element is at distance \(r\), so \(dE = k\lambda r\,d\theta/r^2\) \(= k\lambda\,d\theta/r\). The field at the origin from a positive element at angle \(\theta\) points from the element toward the origin, i.e. along \((-\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)\). So \(E_x\) \(= -\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{k\lambda}{r}\cos\theta\,d\theta\) \(= -2k\lambda/r\). The \(1/r^2\) version forgot the \(r\) from \(dq\); the \(\sin\theta\) version is the y-component (which integrates to zero).

Answer: e §5.5
Q7Electric fields What point charge at P(−r, 0) would make the net field at the origin vanish? No such charge / positive / negative.

The arc's field at the origin points in \(-x\) (away from the arc, which is on the right). To cancel it we need a field in \(+x\) at the origin from a charge at \((-r,0)\), i.e. a field pointing away from that charge: positive. Magnitude needed: \(kq/r^2 = 2k\lambda/r\), so \(q = 2\lambda r = 2Q/\pi\), which exists.

Answer: b (positive) §5.5
Q8Flux \(q_1 = +3\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at the origin, \(q_2 = -6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at x = 4 cm. A Gaussian sphere of radius 2 cm surrounds \(q_2\). Patch \(da_1\) is on the side facing \(q_1\) (x = 2 cm), \(da_2\) on the far side (x = 6 cm). Compare field-line densities \(n_1\) and \(n_2\).

Line density ∝ \(|E|\). At \(da_1\): \(q_2\) (2 cm away, negative) pulls toward itself, \(+x\): \(k(6\times10^{-6})/0.02^2\) \(= 1.35\times10^{8}\). \(q_1\) (2 cm away, positive) pushes away, also \(+x\): \(6.7\times10^{7}\). Total \(2.0\times10^{8}\). At \(da_2\): \(q_2\) pulls in \(-x\): \(1.35\times10^{8}\); \(q_1\) (6 cm away) pushes \(+x\): \(7.5\times10^{6}\). Net \(1.27\times10^{8}\). So \(n_1 \gt n_2\).

Answer: c §6.2
Q9Flux Net flux through that Gaussian sphere? Options: −3.4×10⁵, −3×10⁻⁶, −6.8×10⁵, 6.8×10⁵, −6 N·m²/C.

Only \(q_2\) is inside: \(\Phi = q_2/\varepsilon_0\) \(= -6\times10^{-6}/8.85\times10^{-12}\) \(= -6.8\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C}\). \(q_1\) affects the local density (Q8) but not the net flux.

Answer: c §6.2
Q10Gauss's law Insulating sphere of radius \(a = 6\ \mathrm{cm}\) with \(Q = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) spread uniformly through its volume, inside a concentric uncharged conducting shell of radius \(b = 10\ \mathrm{cm}\). Field magnitude at (4 cm, 0)? Options: 3×10⁷, 0.72×10⁷, 1.3×10⁷, 2×10⁷, 4.5×10⁷ N/C.

Inside the insulator, \(E = kQr/a^3\) \(= 8.99\times10^9(8\times10^{-6})(0.04)/(0.06)^3\) \(= 1.33\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{N/C}\). The shell contributes nothing inside (no enclosed shell charge).

Answer: c §6.3
Q11Gauss's law Surface charge density on the inner surface of the shell at \(b = 10\ \mathrm{cm}\)? Options: 8×10⁻⁶, 0, −6.4×10⁻⁵ C/m².

The inner surface holds \(-Q = -8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) (so the field in the metal is zero). \(\sigma\) \(= -8\times10^{-6}/(4\pi\times0.1^2)\) \(= -6.4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\).

Answer: c §6.4
Q12Gauss's law An infinite line charge \(\lambda = 1\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\), parallel to z, is added through (−30 cm, 0). Find \(\vec E\) at P = (−20 cm, 0). Options: −7.0×10⁶, 2.0×10⁶, −1.6×10⁶, 7.4×10⁶, 1.8×10⁵ N/C (all \(\hat x\)).

Line: 10 cm to the left of P, positive, pushes P in \(+x\): \(2k\lambda/r\) \(= 2(8.99\times10^9)(10^{-6})/0.1\) \(= 1.8\times10^{5}\). Sphere system: P is outside the shell (20 cm from the origin); enclosed charge \(+8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\); field points away from the origin, i.e. \(-x\): \(kQ/r^2\) \(= 8.99\times10^9(8\times10^{-6})/0.04\) \(= 1.8\times10^{6}\). Net \(E_x = 0.18\times10^6 - 1.8\times10^6\) \(= -1.6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{N/C}\).

Answer: c §6.5
Q13Work and energy Charges \(q\) at (0,0), \(q\) at (0,a), \(q\) at (a,0), and \(2q\) at (a,a). Work to assemble from infinity? Options: \(\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}(5)\), \(\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}(3+\frac1{\sqrt2})\), \(\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}(\frac4{\sqrt3})\), \(\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}(2+\sqrt2)\), \(\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}(6+\frac3{\sqrt2})\).

Six pairs. Sides (length \(a\)): \(q\cdot q\), \(q\cdot q\), \(q\cdot2q\), \(q\cdot2q\) → \(6q^2/a\). Diagonals (length \(a\sqrt2\)): \(q\cdot2q\) and \(q\cdot q\) → \(3q^2/(a\sqrt2)\). Total \(\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}(6 + 3/\sqrt2)\). Options with \(q\) instead of \(q^2\) have wrong units.

Answer: e §7.1
Q14Potential Which sketch represents V along the horizontal dotted line through M = (a/2, a/2)? (a) two humps with a dip between them, (b) a single asymmetric peak, (c) a valley.

All charges are positive, so \(V \gt 0\) everywhere and \(V \to 0\) far away. Along \(y = a/2\), \(V\) is large near \(x = 0\) (two charges at distance \(a/2\)) and near \(x = a\) (charges \(q\) and \(2q\) at distance \(a/2\)), with a dip at M in between; the right hump is taller because of the \(2q\).

Answer: a §7.2
Q15Electric fields A positive charge is placed at M. Direction of the force? Zero / right / down and left.

M is the center of the square. The fields from \(q\) at (0,a) and \(q\) at (a,0) are equal and opposite at the center: they cancel. \(q\) at the origin pushes toward (a,a) (up-right); \(2q\) at (a,a) pushes toward the origin (down-left) with twice the magnitude. Net: down and left. Equivalently, the force on a positive charge points from high \(V\) to low \(V\), away from the biggest charge.

Answer: c §5.4
Q16Capacitance Circuit: \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are vertical branches sharing the same two nodes; \(C_3\) (and a closed switch) sits in the top wire between those nodes and the battery; \(C_4\) is a branch across the battery. \(C_1 = 6\), \(C_2 = 8\), \(C_3 = 12\), \(C_4 = 10\ \mu\mathrm{F}\); \(Q_1 = 5.83\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). Are \(C_3\) and \(C_4\) in series, parallel, or neither?

\(C_3\) is in series with the \(C_1\)∥\(C_2\) block; that whole string is in parallel with \(C_4\). \(C_3\) alone is neither in series nor in parallel with \(C_4\) (they do not share the same charge, nor the same voltage).

Answer: b (neither) §8.2
Q17Capacitance \(C_{1234}\)? Options: 6.1, 36, 8, 160, 16 μF.

\(C_{12} = 14\); series with \(C_3\): \(14\times12/26 = 6.46\); parallel with \(C_4\): \(6.46 + 10 = 16.5\ \mu\mathrm{F}\).

Answer: e §8.2
Q18Capacitance \(V_3\)? Options: 7.8, 2.1, 1.1, 0.97, 14 V.

\(V_1 = 5.83/6 = 0.972\ \mathrm{V} = V_2\). \(Q_{12} = 14\times0.972\) \(= 13.6\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) \(= Q_3\). \(V_3 = 13.6/12 = 1.13\ \mathrm{V}\).

Answer: c §8.2
Q19Capacitance \(V_{\text{battery}}\)? Options: 2.1, 0.97, 1.1 V.

\(V_{\text{bat}}\) \(= V_{12} + V_3\) \(= 0.972 + 1.13\) \(= 2.1\ \mathrm{V}\).

Answer: a §8.2
Q20Capacitance Parallel plates, \(A = 5\ \mathrm{cm^2}\), \(d = 1\ \mathrm{mm}\), a dielectric slab \(\kappa = 1.5\) of thickness \(d/2\) fills half the gap. With \(Q = 6\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{C}\) fixed, find \(\Delta V\). Options: 4.5, 14, 2.7, 6.8, 11 V.

\(E_0 = Q/(\varepsilon_0A)\) \(= 6\times10^{-11}/(8.85\times10^{-12}\times5\times10^{-4})\) \(= 1.36\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/m}\). \(\Delta V\) \(= E_0(d/2) + (E_0/\kappa)(d/2)\) \(= 6.78 + 4.52\) \(= 11.3\ \mathrm{V}\).

Answer: e §8.4
Q21Capacitance Capacitance of this configuration? Options: 4.4, 5.3, 22 pF.

\(C = Q/\Delta V\) \(= 6\times10^{-11}/11.3\) \(= 5.3\ \mathrm{pF}\). (4.4 pF is the empty capacitor.)

Answer: b §8.4

Hour Exam 1, Spring 2015

Q1Electric fields \(Q_1 = 7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at (−L,0), \(Q_2 = -10.5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at (0,0), \(Q_3 = 7\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at (L,0), \(L = 1.3\ \mathrm{m}\). \(Q_4 = -10.5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at (0,h), \(h = 2.6\ \mathrm{m}\). x-component of the force on \(Q_4\)? Options: 0.147, −0.07, −0.217, 0.077 N, zero.

\(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) are equal and symmetric about the y-axis, so their x-pulls on \(Q_4\) cancel; \(Q_2\) is directly below \(Q_4\) and gives no x-force.

Answer: e (zero) §5.3
Q2Electric fields y-component of the force on \(Q_4\)? Options: zero, 0.00674, −0.00979, 0.147, −0.287 N.

\(Q_2\) on \(Q_4\): both negative, repulsive, up: \(k(10.5\times10^{-6})^2/2.6^2\) \(= 0.1466\ \mathrm{N}\). \(Q_1\) on \(Q_4\): attractive, toward \(Q_1\); \(r^2 = 1.69 + 6.76 = 8.45\); \(F = k(7)(10.5)\times10^{-12}/8.45\) \(= 0.0782\ \mathrm{N}\); y-part \(-0.0782(2.6/2.907) = -0.0699\). Same from \(Q_3\). \(F_y = 0.1466 - 0.1399\) \(= +0.0067\ \mathrm{N}\).

Answer: b §5.3
Q3Potential Conducting spheres \(r_1 = 20\ \mathrm{mm}\), \(q_1 = 0.4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) and \(r_2 = 5\ \mathrm{mm}\), \(q_2 = 0.12\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), far apart. Potential difference between their surfaces? Options: 3.6×10⁴, 1.8×10⁵, 2.16×10⁵ V.

\(V_1 = kq_1/r_1\) \(= 8.99\times10^9(0.4\times10^{-6})/0.02\) \(= 1.80\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\); \(V_2\) \(= 8.99\times10^9(0.12\times10^{-6})/0.005\) \(= 2.16\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\). Difference \(3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\). (The other options are the individual potentials.)

Answer: a §7.2
Q4Potential If connected by a thin wire, which way does positive charge flow? None / 1 to 2 / 2 to 1.

Positive charge flows from higher potential to lower: sphere 2 (\(2.16\times10^5\ \mathrm{V}\)) to sphere 1 (\(1.80\times10^5\ \mathrm{V}\)). Equal charges do not mean equal potentials; the smaller sphere is at higher \(V\).

Answer: c §7.2
Q5Gauss's law Sheets \(\sigma_1 = +5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at x = 0 and \(\sigma_2 = -9.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at x = 0.8 m; a neutral conducting slab occupies 0.2–0.4 m. \(E_x\) at x = 0.9? Options: −0.254×10⁶, 0.536×10⁶, −0.536×10⁶ V/m.

At x = 0.9 both sheets are to the left. \(\sigma_1\) pushes right, \(\sigma_2\) pulls left; the neutral slab contributes nothing outside itself. \(E_x\) \(= (5 - 9.5)\times10^{-6}/(2\times8.85\times10^{-12})\) \(= -2.54\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V/m}\).

Answer: a §6.5
Q6Gauss's law Induced charge density on the left face of the slab (x = 0.2)? Options: −7.25, −2.25, −5, −2.5, −14.5 μC/m².

Inside the slab the sheets alone give: \(\sigma_1\) (to the left) pushes right, \(+5\); \(\sigma_2\) (to the right, negative) pulls right, \(+9.5\); total \(+14.5\) in units of \(\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}/2\varepsilon_0\). The slab's faces \(\sigma_L\) and \(\sigma_R = -\sigma_L\) contribute \(\sigma_L/\varepsilon_0 = 2\sigma_L\) in the same units inside the slab. Zero total requires \(2\sigma_L = -14.5\), so \(\sigma_L = -7.25\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) (and \(\sigma_R = +7.25\)).

Answer: a §6.5
Q7Gauss's law Sheet \(\sigma\) at x = 0; line \(\lambda\) (along z) at x = d. \(E_x\) due ONLY to the line at a point on the x-axis at distance r from the sheet (0 < r < d)? Options: \(\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}\), \(\frac{-\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(d-r)}\), \(\frac{-\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}\), \(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\), \(\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(d-r)}\).

The point is \(d - r\) from the line. A positive line pushes the point (which is to its left) toward \(-x\): \(E_x = -\lambda/[2\pi\varepsilon_0(d-r)]\). Distance is measured to the line, not to the sheet.

Answer: b §6.3
Q8Electric fields There is a point with \(E = 0\) between the sheet and the line. What can you conclude about the signs of \(\lambda\) and \(\sigma\)?

The sheet's field \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) points \(+x\) if \(\sigma \gt 0\); the line's field points \(-x\) if \(\lambda \gt 0\). They can cancel only if they point opposite ways, which requires the same sign for both (both positive or both negative).

Answer: a (same sign) §6.5
Q9Electric fields Position of the zero? Options: \(r = \lambda/\pi\sigma\), \(r = d - \lambda/\pi\sigma\), \(r = d + \lambda/\pi\sigma\).

\(\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) \(= \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0(d-r)}\Rightarrow d - r\) \(= \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\sigma}\Rightarrow r\) \(= d - \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\sigma}\).

Answer: b §6.5
Q10Gauss's law Insulating sphere of radius R, uniform \(\rho\). \(|E|\) at \(r \gt R\)? Options: \(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho}{r^2}\), \(\frac{1}{3\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho R^2}{r}\), \(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho R^3}{r^2}\), \(\frac{1}{3\rho\varepsilon_0}\frac{R^3}{r^2}\), \(\frac{1}{3\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho R^3}{r^2}\).

\(Q = \rho\tfrac43\pi R^3\); \(E = Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2)\) \(= \rho R^3/(3\varepsilon_0r^2)\).

Answer: e §6.3
Q11Gauss's law \(|E|\) at \(r \lt R\)? Options: \(\rho r^2/3\varepsilon_0\), \(\rho R/6\varepsilon_0\), \(\rho r/3\varepsilon_0\), \(\rho R/3\varepsilon_0\), \(\rho r/6\varepsilon_0\).

\(E\,4\pi r^2\) \(= \rho\tfrac43\pi r^3/\varepsilon_0\Rightarrow E\) \(= \rho r/3\varepsilon_0\).

Answer: c §6.3
Q12Gauss's law Which graph shows \(|E|\) vs r? The sketches: (a) straight rise to R then a curved decay; (b) straight rise then straight fall; (c) curved (concave-up) rise then decay; (d) concave-down rise then decay; (e) straight rise then straight fall to zero. The answer choices are labeled a=e, b=c, c=d, d=b, e=a.

Linear rise inside (\(E \propto r\)), continuous at R, then \(1/r^2\) decay (a curve, not a line). That is sketch (a), which is answer choice (e).

Answer: e (sketch a) §6.3
Q13Electric fields A rod of length 2 m with \(Q_{\text{rod}} = 18\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) lies from (−L,0) to (L,0); \(Q_1\) sits at (−L,h). Linear charge density of the rod? Options: 36, 9, 4.5 μC/m.

\(\lambda = Q/\text{length}\) \(= 18/2\) \(= 9\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\).

Answer: b §5.5
Q14Electric fields Expression for \(\vec E\) at P = (0,h) due to the point charge and the rod? Options: (a) \(\frac{kQ_1}{L^2}\hat x\); (b) \(k\lambda\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{dx}{x^2+h^2}\hat y + \frac{kQ_1}{L^2}\hat x\); (c) \(k\lambda\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{dx}{x^2+h^2}\hat y\); (d) \(k\lambda\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{x\,dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\hat y + \frac{kQ_1}{L^2}\hat x\); (e) \(k\lambda\int_{-L}^{L}\frac{h\,dx}{(x^2+h^2)^{3/2}}\hat y + \frac{kQ_1}{L^2}\hat x\).

\(Q_1\) is at the same height as P, a distance L to the left, so its field at P is \(kQ_1/L^2\) in \(\hat x\). The rod is symmetric about P's x-position, so only \(E_y\) survives; each element contributes \(k\lambda\,dx/(x^2+h^2)\) times the projection factor \(h/\sqrt{x^2+h^2}\). That is (e). Option (b) omits the projection; (d) uses the x-projection, which integrates to zero.

Answer: e §5.5
Q15Electric fields A second charge \(Q_2\) is placed at (L,h). What value makes the total field at (0,h) zero? \(Q_2 = Q_1\) / not possible / \(Q_2 = -Q_1\).

Both point charges lie on the horizontal line through P, so they can only produce x-components there. The rod's field at P is purely in y and is nonzero; no charge at (L,h) can cancel it.

Answer: b (not possible) §5.5
Q16Capacitance A parallel-plate capacitor (area A, gap d, charge Q, isolated). A conducting slab of thickness d/2 is inserted in the middle. Relation between C' and C? C' = C, C/2, or 2C.

The field is zero inside the slab, so the effective gap is \(d - d/2 = d/2\): \(C' = \varepsilon_0A/(d/2) = 2C\).

Answer: c §8.4
Q17Capacitance Energy before, U, and after, U'? U' = U, U' > U, U' < U.

Q is fixed (isolated). \(U' = Q^2/2C' = Q^2/4C = U/2\).

Answer: c §8.4
Q18Potential In the "before" capacitor (plates horizontal, y vertical), in which direction can a charge be moved between the plates with no external work? Parallel to y / always necessary / parallel to x.

Along an equipotential, which for parallel plates is a plane parallel to the plates: the x-direction.

Answer: c §7.5
Q19Capacitance Solid conducting cylinder radius \(r_1\), charge Q, inside a hollow conducting cylinder (inner \(r_2\), outer \(r_3\)) with −Q, length L. If \(r_2\) is decreased slightly (L, \(r_1\), \(r_3\) fixed), does C decrease, increase, or stay the same?

\(C = 2\pi\varepsilon_0L/\ln(r_2/r_1)\). Smaller \(r_2\) means a smaller logarithm and a larger C. Physically, a narrower gap holds the same Q at a smaller \(\Delta V\).

Answer: b (increases) §8.1
Q20Capacitance The gap is filled with gasoline (\(\kappa = 2\)). New capacitance relative to the previous? \(C_0/2\), \(C_0\), \(2C_0\).

A dielectric multiplies the capacitance by \(\kappa\): \(C_1 = 2C_0\).

Answer: c §8.4
Q21Capacitance Six capacitors: \(C_1 = 10\), \(C_2 = 16\), \(C_3 = 50\), \(C_4 = 6\), \(C_5 = 20\), \(C_6 = 40\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). \(C_1\), \(C_2\), \(C_4\), \(C_5\) each connect the top rail to the bottom rail; the middle branch from top rail to bottom rail is \(C_3\), the 12 V battery, then \(C_6\) in series. Equivalent capacitance? Options: 142, 92.6, 15.6 μF.

Outer four in parallel: \(52\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). In series with \(C_3\) and \(C_6\): \(1/C_{\text{eq}}\) \(= 1/50 + 1/52 + 1/40\) \(= 0.0642\), \(C_{\text{eq}} = 15.6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). (142 is the sum of all six, 92.6 is another wrong grouping.)

Answer: c §8.2
Q22Capacitance Which capacitors have the same charge? \(C_1\) and \(C_4\) / \(C_3\) and \(C_6\) / \(C_4\) and \(C_5\).

Series elements carry the same charge: \(C_3\) and \(C_6\) (each carries the full \(Q = C_{\text{eq}}E\)). \(C_4\) and \(C_5\) are in parallel (same voltage, different charges).

Answer: b §8.2
Q23Capacitance Energy stored in \(C_3\)? Options: 350, 1120, 3600 μJ.

\(Q = 15.6\times10^{-6}\times12\) \(= 1.87\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}\). \(U_3 = Q^2/2C_3\) \(= (1.87\times10^{-4})^2/(10^{-4})\) \(= 3.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J}\) \(= 350\ \mu\mathrm{J}\). (3600 μJ would be \(\tfrac12C_3E^2\), wrongly assuming the full 12 V across \(C_3\).)

Answer: a §8.3
Q24Work and energy Water molecule: O has −2e, each H has +e at \(10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\) from O; the H–H separation is \(1.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\). Potential energy of the configuration (zero at infinite separation)? Options: 1.45×10⁻¹⁸, −7.76×10⁻¹⁸, −9.22×10⁻¹⁸ J.

\(U\) \(= ke^2\left[\dfrac{-2}{10^{-10}} + \dfrac{-2}{10^{-10}} + \dfrac{1}{1.6\times10^{-10}}\right]\) \(= (8.99\times10^9)(2.56\times10^{-38})(-4\times10^{10} + 0.625\times10^{10})\) \(= -7.8\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\). (−9.22 omits the H–H repulsion.)

Answer: b §7.1
Q25Work and energy If the H–O–H angle opens from 105° to 180° with O–H distances fixed, the potential energy will: decrease / stay the same / increase.

Only the H–H term changes; the two H's move farther apart (from \(1.6\) to \(2.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\)), so the positive repulsion term shrinks and \(U\) decreases (becomes more negative).

Answer: a §7.1

Hour Exam 1, Fall 2015

Q1Electric fields \(q_1 = 4.2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at the origin, \(q_2 = 6.3\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at x = d = 0.85 m. Which plot shows \(E_x(x)\) along the axis (positive = pointing right)? The candidates differ in the sign of the divergences on each side of each charge and whether the middle region crosses zero.

Both charges are positive, so their fields point away from them on both sides. Left of \(q_1\): both fields point left (negative), diverging to \(-\infty\) at \(x \to 0^-\). Between: just right of \(q_1\), \(+\infty\); just left of \(q_2\), \(-\infty\); it crosses zero in between (closer to \(q_1\), the smaller charge). Right of \(q_2\): \(+\infty\) at \(d^+\), decaying to zero. The plot with exactly this pattern is (c). Plot (b) has the middle region wrong; (a) shows both charges as sinks; (d) treats them as opposite signs; (e) has a flat middle.

Answer: c §5.4
Q2Electric fields y-component of \(\vec E\) at P, 0.425 m directly above \(q_2\)? Options: 37400, 3.33×10⁵, 18700, 3.56×10⁵, 3.14×10⁵ N/C.

From \(q_2\): \(k(6.3\times10^{-6})/0.425^2\) \(= 3.14\times10^{5}\), straight up. From \(q_1\): \(r = \sqrt{0.85^2 + 0.425^2}\) \(= 0.950\ \mathrm{m}\), \(E = 4.18\times10^{4}\), y-part \(= 4.18\times10^4(0.425/0.950)\) \(= 1.87\times10^{4}\). \(E_y = 3.33\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\).

Answer: b §5.4
Q3Electric fields Magnitude of \(\vec E\) at P? Options: 3.14×10⁵, 3.7×10⁵, 3.35×10⁵ N/C.

\(E_x = 4.18\times10^4(0.85/0.950)\) \(= 3.74\times10^{4}\). \(|E|\) \(= \sqrt{(3.33\times10^5)^2 + (3.74\times10^4)^2}\) \(= 3.35\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\).

Answer: c §5.4
Q4Electric fields Identical conducting spheres 1 and 2 each have \(Q = 3.8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\). A third identical neutral sphere touches 1, then 2, then is removed. Final charge on sphere 2? Options: 2.85, 5.7, 1.9 μC.

Touch 1: each \(Q/2 = 1.9\). Touch 2: \((1.9 + 3.8)/2 = 2.85\ \mu\mathrm{C}\).

Answer: a §5.2
Q5Electric fields With sphere 1 at x = 0 and sphere 2 at x = d, which region contains the zero-field point? \(d \lt x\), \(0 \lt x \lt d\), \(x \lt 0\).

Both spheres are positive: the zero is between them, nearer sphere 1 (the smaller charge, 1.9 vs 2.85).

Answer: b §5.4
Q6Electric fields Two curved rods form a circle of radius R: the top semicircle carries +q, the bottom −q. Direction of \(\vec E\) at the center? +x, −x, −y, zero, +y.

The top +q pushes the center away from the top: down. The bottom −q pulls the center toward the bottom: down. Both add to \(-y\).

Answer: c §5.5
Q7Electric fields Which integral gives \(E_x\) due to the top semicircle (+q), with θ measured from the y-axis? Options: \(\int\frac{kq\,d\theta}{R^2}\), \(\int\frac{kq\cos\theta\,d\theta}{\pi R^2}\), \(\int\frac{kq\sin\theta\,d\theta}{\pi R^2}\), \(\int\frac{kq\sin\theta\,d\theta}{R^2}\), \(\int\frac{kq\cos\theta\,d\theta}{R^2}\) (all from −π/2 to π/2).

\(\lambda = q/(\pi R)\), \(dq = \lambda R\,d\theta\) \(= (q/\pi)d\theta\), \(dE = kq\,d\theta/(\pi R^2)\). With θ from the y-axis, the x-projection is \(\sin\theta\). \(E_x\) \(= \int\frac{kq\sin\theta\,d\theta}{\pi R^2}\), which integrates to zero by symmetry, as it should. The options without \(\pi\) used the wrong \(\lambda\); \(\cos\theta\) would be the y-component.

Answer: c §5.5
Q8Work and energy +Q is moved from distance a to a closer distance b from an infinite positive line λ. Sign of the work done by the field? Zero / positive / negative.

The field pushes +Q away from the line; the displacement is toward it. Force opposite displacement: negative work.

Answer: c §7.1
Q9Work and energy Magnitude of the change in potential energy? Options: \(|2k\lambda Q(1/b - 1/a)|\), \(|2k\lambda Q\ln(b/a)|\), \(|2k\lambda Q(a-b)|\).

\(\Delta U = Q\Delta V\) \(= -Q\int_a^b\frac{2k\lambda}{r}dr\) \(= -2k\lambda Q\ln(b/a)\). Line charge means a logarithm.

Answer: b §7.3
Q10Gauss's law Solid conducting sphere, R = 0.4 m, Q = 5×10⁻⁶ C. \(|E|\) at r = 0.8 m? Options: 2.81×10⁵, 1.41, 70300 N/C.

\(E = kQ/r^2\) \(= 4.50\times10^4/0.64\) \(= 7.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\).

Answer: c §6.3
Q11Potential V at r = 0.8 m (zero at infinity)? Options: 0, −1.13×10⁵, −56300, 1.13×10⁵, 56300 V.

\(V = kQ/r\) \(= 4.50\times10^4/0.8\) \(= 5.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\), positive for positive Q.

Answer: e §7.2
Q12Potential V at r = 0.1 m (inside the conductor)? Options: 0, 4.5×10⁵, −4.5×10⁵, 1.13×10⁵, −1.13×10⁵ V.

Inside a conductor \(E = 0\), so \(V\) is constant and equals the surface value \(kQ/R = 4.50\times10^4/0.4\) \(= 1.13\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\). It is not zero, and it is not \(kQ/r\) with r = 0.1 (that gives \(4.5\times10^5\), a distractor).

Answer: d §7.4
Q13Capacitance 9 V battery. Two boxes in series: the left box has \(C_2\) in its top edge and \(C_1\) in its bottom edge (joined by the box's sides); the right box has \(C_4\) top and \(C_3\) bottom. \(C_1 = 5.8\), \(C_2 = 11.6\), \(C_3 = 17.4\), \(C_4 = 23.2\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). Which capacitor has the same voltage as \(C_1\)? \(C_2\) / \(C_3\) / none.

\(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are the two edges of the same box, connected between the same two nodes: parallel, same voltage.

Answer: a §8.2
Q14Capacitance Equivalent capacitance? Options: 3.48×10⁻⁵, 5.8×10⁻⁵, 4.35×10⁻⁶, 1.38×10⁻⁵, 1.22×10⁻⁵ F.

\(C_{12} = 17.4\), \(C_{34} = 40.6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\); series: \(17.4\times40.6/58 = 12.2\ \mu\mathrm{F}\).

Answer: e §8.2
Q15Capacitance Charge on \(C_1\)? Options: 1.1×10⁻⁴, 5.48×10⁻⁵, 7.31×10⁻⁵, 3.65×10⁻⁵, 2.74×10⁻⁵ C.

\(Q_{\text{tot}}\) \(= 12.2\times10^{-6}\times9\) \(= 1.10\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}\) (that is option a, the total, a distractor). \(V_{12}\) \(= 1.10\times10^{-4}/17.4\times10^{-6}\) \(= 6.3\ \mathrm{V}\). \(Q_1 = 5.8\times10^{-6}\times6.3\) \(= 3.65\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C}\).

Answer: d §8.2
Q16Capacitance Parallel plates \(A = 0.0226\ \mathrm{m^2}\), \(d = 0.0124\ \mathrm{m}\), charged to \(V_0 = 85.5\ \mathrm{V}\), then the battery is disconnected. Charge on the positive plate? Options: 1.38, 2.07, 2.76 (×10⁻⁹ C).

\(C_0 = \varepsilon_0A/d\) \(= 8.85\times10^{-12}(0.0226)/0.0124\) \(= 1.61\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\); \(q = C_0V_0\) \(= 1.38\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C}\).

Answer: a §8.1
Q17Capacitance A dielectric slab of thickness d and \(\kappa = 2.65\) fills the gap. \(C_1\)? Options: 4.27×10⁻¹¹, 6.09×10⁻¹², 1.61×10⁻¹¹ F.

\(C_1 = \kappa C_0\) \(= 2.65\times1.61\times10^{-11}\) \(= 4.27\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\).

Answer: a §8.4
Q18Capacitance Compare \(U_0\) (before) and \(U_1\) (after). \(U_0 = U_1\), \(U_0 \lt U_1\), \(U_0 \gt U_1\).

Battery disconnected: q fixed. \(U = q^2/2C\), and C grew by 2.65, so \(U_1 = U_0/2.65\): \(U_0 \gt U_1\).

Answer: c §8.4
Q19Gauss's law Three infinite planes: a neutral conducting slab on the left (faces \(\sigma_L\), \(\sigma_R\)), then two insulating planes each with \(\sigma = 5\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\) to its right. P lies between the two insulating planes. Contribution to \(E_x\) at P from the right plane only? Options: −5.65×10¹¹, −2.82×10¹¹, 2.82×10¹¹, 5.65×10¹¹, 0 N/C.

P is to the left of the right plane, which is positive, so its field at P points left: \(-\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) \(= -5/(2\times8.85\times10^{-12})\) \(= -2.82\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{N/C}\).

Answer: b §6.5
Q20Gauss's law Induced charge on the right side of the conducting slab? Options: −10, −2.5, −5 C/m².

Inside the slab both planes (to the right) push left: external field \(-2(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0)\) \(= -\sigma/\varepsilon_0\). The slab's faces contribute \(\sigma_L/\varepsilon_0\) inside; cancellation requires \(\sigma_L = +\sigma = +5\), hence \(\sigma_R = -5\ \mathrm{C/m^2}\).

Answer: c §6.5
Q21Flux Gaussian box \(S_1\) encloses the whole conducting slab; box \(S_3\) (four times wider in x) encloses the right plane. Compare total fluxes: \(\Phi_1 \gt \Phi_3\), \(\Phi_1 \lt \Phi_3\), \(\Phi_1 = \Phi_3\).

\(S_1\) encloses \(\sigma_L + \sigma_R = 0\): \(\Phi_1 = 0\). \(S_3\) encloses positive charge \(\sigma A\): \(\Phi_3 \gt 0\). The width of the box does not matter.

Answer: b §6.2
Q22Gauss's law Hollow insulating cylinder, inner a = 0.45 m, outer b = 0.675 m, \(\rho = 3\ \mathrm{C/m^3}\); neutral metal tube c = 0.9 to d = 1.125 m. \(|E|\) at r = 0.743 m? Options: 4.89, 5.78, 7.27 (×10¹⁰ N/C).

\(\lambda = \rho\pi(b^2 - a^2)\) \(= 3\pi(0.4556 - 0.2025)\) \(= 2.39\ \mathrm{C/m}\). \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0r)\) \(= 2.39/(2\pi\times8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.743)\) \(= 5.78\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{N/C}\).

Answer: b §6.3
Q23Gauss's law \(|E|\) at r = 0.99 m? Options: 4.34×10¹⁰, 0, 5.45×10¹⁰ N/C.

0.9 < 0.99 < 1.125: inside the metal, \(E = 0\).

Answer: b §6.4
Q24Gauss's law Charge per unit length induced on the inner surface of the tube? Options: −4.29, −0.759, −7.63, −1.09, −2.39 C/m.

Exactly minus the enclosed charge per length: \(-2.39\ \mathrm{C/m}\).

Answer: e §6.4
Q25Gauss's law If the (neutral) conducting tube were removed, the field at r = 1.69 m would: increase / remain unchanged / decrease.

The enclosed charge for r = 1.69 m is the insulator's \(\lambda\) either way (the tube's \(-2.39\) and \(+2.39\) cancel). Unchanged.

Answer: b §6.4
Q26Flux A sphere, a blob-shaped surface, and a sphere around a cube, each enclosing total charge Q. Compare the total fluxes.

All equal, \(Q/\varepsilon_0\). Gauss's law does not care about shape.

Answer: b §6.2
Q27Potential Field-line map with dashed equipotentials (equal steps). G and H are near the bottom where lines are dense; A is near G, D is far up where lines are sparse. Compare \(V_{GH}\) with \(V_{AD}\).

Count equipotentials crossed. G to H crosses two spacings; A to D also crosses two spacings, even though the path is much longer (the lines are far apart where the field is weak). Same number of lines, same \(\Delta V\).

Answer: c §7.5

Hour Exam 1, Fall 2018

Q1Electric fields Square of side a = 0.5 m, Q = 7 μC: +2Q at the top-left corner, −Q at the bottom-left, +Q at the bottom-right; P is the empty top-right corner. y-component of the force on +2Q? Options: −1.14, 4.77, −1.76, −4.77, −2.28 N.

\(kQ^2/a^2\) \(= 8.99\times10^9(49\times10^{-12})/0.25\) \(= 1.762\ \mathrm{N}\). From −Q (directly below, distance a, attractive): \(2\times1.762 = 3.52\ \mathrm{N}\) downward. From +Q (diagonal, distance \(a\sqrt2\), repulsive, pointing up-left): magnitude \(2\times1.762/2 = 1.762\ \mathrm{N}\), y-part \(+1.762/\sqrt2 = +1.246\ \mathrm{N}\). \(F_y = -3.52 + 1.25 = -2.28\ \mathrm{N}\).

Answer: e §5.3
Q2Work and energy Work required to create this configuration from infinity? Options: −0.881, −2.79, 3.89, −1.4, −3.89 J.

\(kQ^2/a = 0.881\ \mathrm{J}\). Pairs: \((2Q)(-Q)/a \to -2\); \((-Q)(Q)/a \to -1\); \((2Q)(Q)/(a\sqrt2)\to +1.414\). Sum \(-1.586\times0.881 = -1.40\ \mathrm{J}\).

Answer: d §7.1
Q3Potential Electric potential at P? Options: 2.02, −3.99×10⁵, 2.89×10⁵ V.

\(kQ/a = 1.259\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\). P is a from +2Q (\(+2\)), a from +Q (\(+1\)), \(a\sqrt2\) from −Q (\(-0.707\)): \(V = 1.259\times10^5\times2.293\) \(= 2.89\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}\).

Answer: c §7.2
Q4Work and energy You bring −2Q from infinity to P. The work you do is: zero / positive / negative.

\(W_{\text{you}}\) \(= qV_P\) \(= (-2Q)(+2.89\times10^5) \lt 0\). The negative charge is attracted toward the net-positive configuration; you hold it back.

Answer: c §7.2
Q5Flux A negative point charge −q sits inside a cylinder (length L, radius R), closer to end A than end B. Net flux through the whole surface? Options: \(\frac{L}{R}\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\), \(-q/\varepsilon_0\), \(q/\varepsilon_0\).

\(Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0\) \(= -q/\varepsilon_0\). Position and dimensions are irrelevant.

Answer: b §6.2
Q6Flux Sign of the flux through end A? \(\Phi_A = 0\), \(\gt 0\), \(\lt 0\).

The field of a negative charge points inward toward it everywhere, so on every part of the surface \(\vec E\cdot d\vec A \lt 0\). \(\Phi_A \lt 0\) (and \(\Phi_B \lt 0\) too, smaller in magnitude).

Answer: c §6.2
Q7Gauss's law Insulating sphere (radius a, charge \(Q_{\text{sphere}}\) uniform) inside a conducting shell (inner b, outer c, net \(Q_{\text{shell}}\)). \(|E|\) at \(r \lt a\)? Options: \(kQ_s a/r^3\), \(kQ_s r/a^3\), \(kQ_s/r^2\).

\(Q_{\text{enc}} = Q_s r^3/a^3\), so \(E = kQ_s r/a^3\).

Answer: b §6.3
Q8Gauss's law \(\vec E\) at \(a \lt r \lt b\)? Options: \(k(Q_s - Q_{sh})\hat r/r^2\), \(kQ_{sh}\hat r/r^2\), 0, \(k(Q_s + Q_{sh})\hat r/r^2\), \(kQ_s\hat r/r^2\).

Only the sphere's charge is enclosed: \(kQ_s\hat r/r^2\). The shell's charges (inner \(-Q_s\), outer \(Q_{sh} + Q_s\)) are outside the Gaussian surface.

Answer: e §6.4
Q9Gauss's law Charge on the outer surface of the shell? \(Q_{sh} + Q_s\), \(Q_{sh} - Q_s\), \(Q_{sh}\).

Inner surface: \(-Q_s\). Outer \(= Q_{sh} - (-Q_s) = Q_{sh} + Q_s\).

Answer: a §6.4
Q10Potential V inside the conducting shell (\(b \lt r \lt c\)), zero at infinity? Options: 0, \(kQ_{sh}/c + kQ_s/r\), \(kQ_{sh}/r\), \(k(Q_s + Q_{sh})/c\), \(k(Q_s + Q_{sh})/r\).

Outside, \(V = k(Q_s + Q_{sh})/r\). Integrating inward, \(V\) reaches \(k(Q_s + Q_{sh})/c\) at the outer surface and stays constant through the metal (E = 0 there).

Answer: d §7.4
Q11Gauss's law Line charge +λ at the center of a thick conducting cylindrical shell (inner \(r_1\), outer \(r_2\)) with net −λ/3. Points A (\(r_A \lt r_1\)), B (in the metal), C (\(r_C \gt r_2\)). Order \(|E_A|\), \(|E_B|\), \(|E_C|\).

\(E_A = 2k\lambda/r_A\); \(E_B = 0\); \(E_C = 2k(\lambda - \lambda/3)/r_C\) \(= 2k(2\lambda/3)/r_C\). \(r_A \lt r_C\) and \(\lambda \gt 2\lambda/3\), so \(|E_A| \gt |E_C| \gt |E_B|\).

Answer: a §6.4
Q12Gauss's law λ = 1.3 C/m, \(r_1 = 0.15\), \(r_2 = 0.20\), \(r_C = 0.35\ \mathrm{m}\). \(|E_C|\)? Options: 8.9, 6.7, 0, 13, 4.5 (×10¹⁰ N/C).

\(\lambda_{\text{enc}}\) \(= 1.3 - 0.433\) \(= 0.867\ \mathrm{C/m}\). \(E = 2(8.99\times10^9)(0.867)/0.35\) \(= 4.45\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{N/C}\). (6.7×10¹⁰ uses the full λ.)

Answer: e §6.4
Q13Gauss's law Sheets \(\sigma_1 = +8\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at x = 0.6 and \(\sigma_2 = -6.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\) at x = 0.8; neutral conducting slab from 0 to 0.2. \(E_x\) at C (x = 0.7)? Options: 0.452, 0.819, 0.085 (×10⁶ V/m).

Between the sheets: \(\sigma_1\) (left, +) pushes right; \(\sigma_2\) (right, −) pulls right. \(E_x\) \(= (8 + 6.5)\times10^{-6}/(1.77\times10^{-11})\) \(= 8.19\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V/m}\).

Answer: b §6.5
Q14Gauss's law Induced charge density on the right side of the slab? Options: 0, −1.5, 1.5, 0.75, −0.75 μC/m².

Inside the slab (both sheets to the right): \(\sigma_1\) pushes left (\(-8\)), \(\sigma_2\) pulls right (\(+6.5\)): \(-1.5\) in units of \(\mu\mathrm{C/m^2}/2\varepsilon_0\). The slab supplies \(2\sigma_L\) in those units; \(2\sigma_L = +1.5\Rightarrow\sigma_L\) \(= +0.75\), \(\sigma_R = -0.75\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^2}\).

Answer: e §6.5
Q15Potential \(V_B - V_A\) for A at x = 0.2 and B at x = 0.5? Options: 0.136, −0.246, 0.025, −0.136, 0.11 (×10⁶ V).

Between the slab and \(\sigma_1\) the field is uniform: \(E_x\) \(= (-8 + 6.5)\times10^{-6}/(1.77\times10^{-11})\) \(= -8.47\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/m}\). \(V_B - V_A = -E_x\Delta x\) \(= +8.47\times10^4\times0.3\) \(= 2.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\).

Answer: c §7.3
Q16Electric fields Ring of radius R in the x-y plane with total +Q. Charge density λ? \(Q/(\pi R^2)\), \(Q/R\), \(Q/(2\pi R)\).

Circumference \(2\pi R\): \(\lambda = Q/(2\pi R)\).

Answer: c §5.5
Q17Electric fields Which integral gives \(E_z\) at height h on the axis? (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{k\lambda R\,d\theta}{h^2+R^2}\); (b) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{k\lambda R\,d\theta}{h^2+R^2}\frac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+R^2}}\); (c) same with \(\frac{R}{\sqrt{h^2+R^2}}\); (d) \(\int\frac{k\lambda R\,d\theta}{\sqrt{h^2+R^2}}\frac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+R^2}}\); (e) \(\int\frac{k\lambda\,d\theta}{h^2+R^2}\frac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+R^2}}\).

\(dq = \lambda R\,d\theta\), \(r^2 = h^2 + R^2\), axial projection \(h/\sqrt{h^2+R^2}\): (b). (a) has no projection; (c) projects onto the wrong side; (d) has \(1/r\) instead of \(1/r^2\); (e) drops the R from \(dq\).

Answer: b §5.5
Q18Electric fields For \(h \gg R\), the field magnitude is approximately: \(kQ/R^2\), \(k\lambda/h^2\), \(kQ/h^2\).

\(kQh/(h^2+R^2)^{3/2} \to kQh/h^3\) \(= kQ/h^2\): a point charge.

Answer: c §5.5
Q19Potential Long insulating cylinder (radius R, length L, +Q uniform) with \(V(R) = 0\). Which equation gives V at \(r \gt R\)? (a) \(-\int_0^r\frac{Q}{2\pi rL\varepsilon_0}dr\); (b) \(-\int_\infty^r\); (c) \(-\int_R^r\).

\(V(r) = V(R) - \int_R^r E\,dr\) with \(V(R) = 0\) and \(E = Q/(2\pi\varepsilon_0Lr)\) outside. The lower limit must be the reference point R. Starting from 0 would pass through the interior where the field formula is different; starting from ∞ diverges.

Answer: c §7.4
Q20Potential Which graph shows V inside and outside? (a) rises to a peak at R then decays; (b) a cusp at R; (c) highest at r = 0, decreasing, passing through zero at R and continuing down.

Positive charge, so V decreases outward everywhere. Inside, \(E \propto r\) so V falls as an inverted parabola from its maximum on the axis; it hits zero at R (by definition) and continues to fall as \(-\ln(r/R)\) outside. Graph (c).

Answer: c §7.4
Q21Capacitance Five identical capacitors (C = 25 μF), battery V = 5 V. Layout: top wire has \(C_5\) then the battery; bottom wire has \(C_4\) then \(C_2\); \(C_3\) connects the node between \(C_5\) and the battery to the node between \(C_4\) and \(C_2\); \(C_1\) is the right side. \(C_1\) and \(C_3\) are in: neither / series / parallel.

\(C_1\) carries the full loop charge; \(C_3\) carries only part of it (it shares the node with the \(C_5\)–\(C_4\) path). Not the same charge, not the same voltage: neither.

Answer: a §8.2
Q22Capacitance \(C_4\) and \(C_5\) are in: neither / parallel / series.

They are joined by the plain left wire with nothing else attached: series.

Answer: c §8.2
Q23Capacitance Equivalent capacitance? Options: 62.5, 9.38, 87.5 μF.

\(C_5\)–\(C_4\) series: 12.5; parallel with \(C_3\): 37.5. Series with \(C_1\) and \(C_2\): \(1/(1/25 + 1/25 + 1/37.5)\) \(= 9.38\ \mu\mathrm{F}\).

Answer: b §8.2
Q24Capacitance Energy stored in \(C_2\)? Options: 312, 44, 117, 235, 23.5 μJ.

\(Q = C_{\text{eq}}V\) \(= 9.38\times5\) \(= 46.9\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) on \(C_2\). \(U_2 = Q^2/2C\) \(= (4.69\times10^{-5})^2/(5\times10^{-5})\) \(= 4.4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{J}\) \(= 44\ \mu\mathrm{J}\). (312 μJ is \(\tfrac12CV^2\) with the whole 5 V, wrong.)

Answer: b §8.3
Q25Capacitance Parallel plates, area 0.055 m², separation 0.002 m; Q = +0.42 μC moved from the bottom plate to the top. Voltage with empty gap? Options: 1040, 1730, 1210 V.

\(C_0\) \(= 8.85\times10^{-12}(0.055)/0.002\) \(= 2.43\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{F}\); \(V_0 = Q/C_0\) \(= 0.42\times10^{-6}/2.43\times10^{-10}\) \(= 1.73\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{V}\).

Answer: b §8.1
Q26Capacitance Dielectric fills the gap: bottom half (thickness d/2) has \(\kappa_1\), top half \(\kappa_2\). Capacitance in terms of \(C_0\)? \(C_0\frac{2\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}\), \(C_0(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)\), \(C_0\frac{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}{2}\).

Stacked layers are in series: \(C_i = 2\kappa_iC_0\); \(C\) \(= \dfrac{(2\kappa_1C_0)(2\kappa_2C_0)}{2\kappa_1C_0+2\kappa_2C_0}\) \(= \dfrac{2\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}C_0\). The \((\kappa_1+\kappa_2)/2\) form is the side-by-side (parallel) case.

Answer: a §8.4

Homework 1–7: What Each Problem Tests

The syllabus promises exam problems "of similar style" to the homework. Each row gives the concept, the method, and the result where the numbers are fully specified in the printout.

Homework 1 · Coulomb's law

ProblemConceptMethod and result
1. \(Q_2\) floating above \(Q_1 = +5\ \mathrm{nC}\), \(m = 5.5\ \mu\mathrm{g}\), \(d = 35\ \mathrm{cm}\)Force balanceFree-body: weight down, electric force up, so repulsive: \(Q_2\) positive. \(|Q_2| = mgd^2/(kQ_1)\) \(= 0.147\ \mathrm{nC}\).
2. \(q_1\), \(q_2\), \(q_3\) on a line at angle θ with a springSuperposition along a line; equilibrium with a spring\(\vec F\) \(= kq^2(1/r^2 + 1/(2r)^2)(\cos\theta\,\hat i + \sin\theta\,\hat j)\); \(q_2\) moves toward \(q_3\); spring force \(-k_s\Delta r\) along the same line; at equilibrium the distances are \(r + \Delta r\) and \(2r - \Delta r\).
3. \(+5.9\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at 0, \(-1.1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at 0.21 mZero net force locationOpposite signs: outside, on the small charge's side: \(x = 0.370\ \mathrm{m}\). Both positive: between, \(x = 0.147\ \mathrm{m}\).
4. Triangle, net force on the lower-right charge (symbolic)2D vector sumOne Coulomb term per other charge; direction by sign rule; write \(\hat i\), \(\hat j\) parts using the triangle's angles. See 5.3.
5. \(q_1 = 2.5\), \(q_2 = q_3 = -1.5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) triangle, \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) on \(q_1\)2D vector sum, numericBoth negative charges attract \(q_1\); each force magnitude \(k(2.5)(1.5)\times10^{-12}/r^2\) with its own side length; resolve along the figure's axes and add.
6. Square with four charges, force on lower-right (symbolic)2D vector sum with a diagonalTwo edge neighbors at distance \(d\), one diagonal at \(d\sqrt2\) contributing \(1/(2d^2)\) times \(\cos45^\circ = 1/\sqrt2\) to each component.
7. Electrons in \(-6\ \mathrm{nC}\); removed for \(+1.1\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)Quantization\(N = |q|/e\): \(3.75\times10^{10}\); \(6.9\times10^{12}\).
8. Foam balls, \(N = 10^6\) protons each, \(d = 2.3\ \mathrm{m}\)\(q = Ne\), Coulomb\(Q = Ne = 1.6\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{C}\); \(F = kQ^2/d^2\) \(= 4.3\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{N}\).
9. Two 71 nC charges, \(F = 1.2\ \mathrm{N}\)Solve Coulomb for r\(d = \sqrt{kq^2/F}\) \(= \sqrt{8.99\times10^9(71\times10^{-9})^2/1.2}\) \(= 6.1\ \mathrm{mm}\).

Homework 2 · Electric fields

ProblemConceptMethod and result
1. \(Q_1 = +0.35\ \mathrm{nC}\) at origin, \(Q_2 = -6.5\ \mathrm{nC}\) at 14.5 cm, P 4.5 cm above \(Q_2\)Field components from two charges\(Q_1\): \(r = \sqrt{14.5^2 + 4.5^2}\) \(= 15.2\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(E = 136\ \mathrm{N/C}\); \(E_x = 136(14.5/15.2) = 130\), \(E_y = 136(4.5/15.2) = 40\ \mathrm{N/C}\). \(Q_2\): \(E = k(6.5\times10^{-9})/0.045^2\) \(= 2.89\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\) pointing down (toward the negative charge): \(E_{y,2} = -2.89\times10^{4}\). Net \(E_y = -2.88\times10^{4}\), \(|E| \approx 2.88\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N/C}\), angle \(\tan^{-1}(E_y/E_x) \approx -89.7^\circ\).
2. Equilateral triangle, side 27 cm, \(q_a = 2.7\), \(q_b = -9.9\), \(q_c = 1.9\ \mathrm{nC}\); field at the centerSuperposition with 120° geometryCenter-to-vertex distance \(r = s/\sqrt3 = 15.6\ \mathrm{cm}\), so \(E_i = kq_i/r^2\): 999, 3660, 703 N/C. Directions: away from \(q_a\) and \(q_c\), toward \(q_b\), each along its vertex's radial line (120° apart). Resolve with the figure's orientation and add. The \(-9.9\ \mathrm{nC}\) term dominates, so the result points roughly toward \(q_b\).
3. Arc, \(\theta_0 = 53^\circ\), \(\lambda = -29.5\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\), \(R = 1.1\ \mathrm{m}\)Integration on an arc\(|E|\) \(= (2k|\lambda|/R)\sin(\theta_0/2)\) \(= 2.15\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\) along the symmetry axis, pointing toward the (negative) arc; the perpendicular component is zero.
4. Semicircle, \(R = 17.4\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(Q = 34.7\ \mathrm{nC}\)Integration; unit-vector answer\(\vec E\) \(= -\int\frac{k\lambda}{R}(\cos\theta\,\hat i + \sin\theta\,\hat j)d\theta\) over the arc; for a semicircle the result is \(2k\lambda/R = 2kQ/(\pi R^2)\) \(= 6.6\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{N/C}\) along the axis, away from the arc.
5. Rod on the x-axis, point beyond the endIntegration along the axis\(dq = (q/L)dx\), \(r = a + L - x\), \(\vec E\) \(= \frac{kq}{L}\int_0^L\frac{dx}{(a+L-x)^2}\hat i\) \(= \frac{kq}{a(a+L)}\hat i\); numeric \(7.8\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N/C}\).

ProblemConceptMethod and result

Aluminum sphere \(-q\) (radius a) inside copper shell \(+Q\) (b to c)Gauss then integrate; equipotentials; field lines\(E_r\): \(k(Q-q)/r^2\) (r > c); 0 (b–c); \(-kq/r^2\) (a–b); 0 (r < a). \(V\): \(k(Q-q)/r\); \(k(Q-q)/c\); \(k(Q-q)/c - kq(1/r - 1/b)\); \(k(Q-q)/c - kq(1/a - 1/b)\). Equipotentials: whole conductors and concentric spheres. Lines run from the copper inner surface inward to the aluminum, and from the copper outer surface to infinity.
2. Aluminum cylinder radius R, λ, zero at 2RLog potential with a reference\(E_r = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0r)\) outside, 0 inside. \(V\) \(= -\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\frac{r}{2R}\) outside; \(\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln2\) inside. Equipotentials: coaxial cylinders and the interior. Field lines: radial, from the surface outward, densest just outside.

Metal pipe radius a, σ, zero at 3aSame with \(\lambda = 2\pi a\sigma\)\(E_r = \sigma a/(\varepsilon_0r)\) outside, 0 inside. \(V\) \(= -\frac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln\frac{r}{3a}\) outside; \(\frac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln3\) inside. Shift to zero at 2a: add \(V_{\text{shift}}\) \(= \frac{\sigma a}{\varepsilon_0}\ln\frac23\).
4. Coaxial cylinders \(\pm Q\), length LCylindrical capacitor\(|\Delta V|\) \(= \frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0L}\ln\frac ba\).
5. Plates \(-\sigma\) at y = 0 (V = 0) and \(+\sigma\) at y = dUniform field, linear potential\(\vec E = 0\) outside; \(-(\sigma/\varepsilon_0)\hat j\) between. \(V = 0\) (y < 0); \(\sigma y/\varepsilon_0\) (between); \(\sigma d/\varepsilon_0\) (y > d). Equipotentials: planes ⟂ y between the plates, whole volumes outside. Lines ∥ y from y = d to y = 0, only between the plates.

Homework 7 · Capacitance (and one Gauss's-law superposition)

ProblemConceptMethod and result
1. Plates \(\pm28.7\ \mathrm{nC}\), \(A = 0.0247\ \mathrm{m^2}\), \(d = 9.98\ \mathrm{cm}\)\(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\); scaling\(C = 2.19\ \mathrm{pF}\); \(\Delta V = 1.31\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}\); doubling Q leaves C at 2.19 pF; \(2A\), \(d/4\): \(17.5\ \mathrm{pF}\), \(\Delta V = 1.64\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{V}\).
2. Derive the energy density\(u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\)\(C_0 = \varepsilon_0A/d\); \(E = V_0/d\); \(U = \tfrac12C_0V_0^2\) \(= \tfrac12\varepsilon_0AdE^2\); volume \(Ad\); \(u = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\).
3. Plane \(\sigma_P = 2\sigma_0\) and a sphere (surface density \(\sigma_S = 6\sigma_0\), radius R) whose center is \(d = 5R\) from the planeSuperposition of a sheet field and a sphere fieldPlane: \(\sigma_0/\varepsilon_0\) away from the plane. Sphere (outside it): \(kQ/r^2\) with \(Q = 4\pi R^2(6\sigma_0)\), i.e. \(6\sigma_0R^2/(\varepsilon_0r^2)\), away from the sphere. Between plane and sphere they oppose: \(\sigma_0/\varepsilon_0\) \(= 6\sigma_0R^2/(\varepsilon_0(5R - d_0)^2)\Rightarrow 5R - d_0\) \(= \sqrt6R\Rightarrow d_0\) \(= 2.55R\) from the plane. (Inside the shell the sphere's field is zero, so no cancellation there; beyond the sphere both fields point the same way.)

Letters in these integrals
\(x\)
position along a rod, measured from one end or from the foot of the perpendicular, m
\(h\)
perpendicular distance from the rod or disk to the field point, m
\(a,\ L\)
a rod's length or the distance from its end to the point, m
\(\theta\)
the angle of a charge element seen from the field point or the arc's center
\(\theta_0\)
the total opening angle of an arc
\(r\)
radius or distance from a center or axis, m
\(u\)
a substitution variable that stands in for a messier expression while integrating
\(\rho = Ar\)
a density that grows with radius; \(A\) is a given constant with units C/m⁴
